title: Add intensity levels (lite, full, ultra) to caveman mode
body:
Closes #10

## Summary

- **Lite** — drop filler and pleasantries, keep normal grammar. Professional but no fluff
- **Full** — existing default, unchanged. Classic caveman
- **Ultra** — maximum compression. Telegraphic, abbreviations, arrow notation

Triggered via `/caveman lite`, `/caveman full`, `/caveman ultra` (Codex: `$caveman lite|full|ultra`).
Level persists until changed or session ends.

## Before / After

**Before:** One mode — full caveman or nothing.

**After:** Three levels, same React re-render example side-by-side in the README:

> **🪶 Lite:** "Your component re-renders because you create a new object reference each render. Inline object props fail shallow comparison every time. Wrap it in `useMemo`."
>
> **🪨 Full:** "New object ref each render. Inline object prop = new ref = re-render. Wrap in `useMemo`."
>
> **🔥 Ultra:** "Inline obj prop → new ref → re-render. `useMemo`."

## Changes

- `skills/caveman/SKILL.md` — added intensity levels section, level-specific rules, examples, updated description and triggers
- `plugins/caveman/skills/caveman/SKILL.md` — synced copy
- `caveman.skill` — rebuilt archive
- `README.md` — added 3-column lite/full/ultra comparison in Before/After section + intensity levels trigger table under Usage

## Test plan

- [ ] `/caveman lite` produces professional tone without filler but keeps full grammar
- [ ] `/caveman full` matches existing default behavior (no regression)
- [ ] `/caveman ultra` produces maximum compression with abbreviations and arrows
- [ ] Level persists across messages until explicitly changed
- [ ] "stop caveman" / "normal mode" still reverts to normal

title: Add Auto-Clarity: full sentences for security warnings and destructive ops
body:
## What

Adds an **Auto-Clarity** section to `SKILL.md`. Caveman drops compressed grammar and uses full sentences for responses where fragmentation risks misunderstanding or harm — then resumes caveman immediately after.

## Why

Current `Boundaries` section covers code blocks and git commits but leaves a gap: destructive confirmations, security warnings, and multi-step sequences where fragment order matters. A caveman response like `Delete all users. Run: DROP TABLE users;` skips the warning that should precede it.

## When Auto-Clarity triggers

- Security warning or destructive action confirmation (delete, drop, force-push)
- Irreversible action — data loss possible
- Multi-step sequence where fragment order risks misread
- Error diagnosis needing precise cause → effect chain
- User explicitly confused or asking for clarification

## Before / After

**Before** (caveman, no guard):
> Delete all users. Run: `DROP TABLE users;`

**After** (auto-clarity kicks in):
> **Warning:** This will permanently delete all rows in the `users` table and cannot be undone. To proceed, run:
> ```sql
> DROP TABLE users;
> ```
> Caveman resume. Verify backup exist first.

---
Orthogonal to PR #11 (intensity levels). No conflict.

title: Add GitHub Action to auto-sync SKILL.md copies on push to main
body:
## What

Adds a GitHub Action (`.github/workflows/sync-skill.yml`) that automatically syncs the canonical `skills/caveman/SKILL.md` to all duplicate locations after any push to `main` that touches it.

## Why

`SKILL.md` exists in 4 places:
- `skills/caveman/SKILL.md` ← canonical (per CONTRIBUTING.md)
- `caveman/SKILL.md`
- `plugins/caveman/skills/caveman/SKILL.md`
- `caveman.skill` (ZIP)

Currently contributors must sync manually, which is error-prone and undocumented. This action makes it automatic and invisible.

## How it works

1. Triggers on push to `main` when `skills/caveman/SKILL.md` changes
2. Copies canonical file to both directory duplicates
3. Rebuilds `caveman.skill` ZIP (`caveman/SKILL.md` inside)
4. Auto-commits if any file changed

`CONTRIBUTING.md` updated to say: only edit `skills/caveman/SKILL.md`, CI handles the rest.

## No action needed from contributors

After this merges, contributors edit one file, open a PR, and the sync happens automatically post-merge.

title: README makes two inaccurate claims about token savings
body:
First, I want to say that this is a super fun project! 
Now wanted to clarify some stuff you probably already know but I feel frames this project dishonestly.

### 1. Tokens ≠ Words

The README uses "tokens" and "words" interchangeably ("75% less word", "few token do trick"). 
Tokens are subword units — "polymorphism" can be 3+ tokens, "useMemo" is 2. The 69→19 
counts in the examples don't appear to be validated with an actual tokenizer, and look 
closer to word counts on cherry-picked examples.

### 2. The skill itself costs input tokens

The skill file (~1.28 KB, ~300–350 tokens) is injected as context on **every request**. 
The README only accounts for output token savings, but:

- Input tokens are also billed
- The skill overhead is **fixed per request**, regardless of response length
- For short responses, the overhead can exceed the savings

The net cost is: `(output tokens saved) - (skill input tokens added)`. Break-even only 
happens above a certain response length. The "75% less cost" claim doesn't hold for 
short interactions.

---

Happy to submit a PR with corrected wording if you're open to it.

title: Feature: Localized trigger words (non-English activation)
body:
## Summary

The caveman skill currently only triggers on English phrases (`caveman mode`, `less tokens`, `be brief`). Users who work in mixed-language environments (e.g., German + English codebases) would benefit from localized trigger words.

## Proposed Addition

Add support for localized trigger phrases in the SKILL.md description field. Example for German:

| Trigger | Language | Meaning |
|---------|----------|---------|
| `kurz&knapp` | German | "short & concise" — natural German idiom for brevity |
| `kurz bitte` | German | "brief please" |
| `weniger text` | German | "less text" |

The German expression **"kurz&knapp"** is a very common idiom (literally "short & tight") that perfectly maps to caveman mode's intent. It's the natural thing a German-speaking developer would say when wanting compressed output.

## Suggested Implementation

In `SKILL.md` description block, extend the trigger list:

```yaml
description: >
  ...Use when user says "caveman mode", "talk like caveman",
  "use caveman", "less tokens", "be brief", "kurz&knapp",
  or invokes /caveman...
```

And in the `## Boundaries` section:

```markdown
- "stop caveman", "normal mode", "ausführlich", "verbose": revert
```

## Why This Matters

- Claude Code is used globally, not just by English speakers
- Trigger words should feel natural in the user's working language
- Zero cost: just a few extra strings in the description field
- Could be extended to other languages (French: "sois bref", Spanish: "sé breve", etc.)

## Context

I'm using a local distillation of your caveman concept with German triggers and it works great. Thought the upstream skill would benefit from this too.

title: feat: Add 文言文 (Classical Chinese) mode — terse, literary, ancient
body:
## 🎋 Request: 文言文 (Classical/Literary Chinese) Mode

### What
Add a new intensity level for 文言文 — Classical Chinese (文言文) — the ultra- terse, literary register used in ancient Chinese texts like the 道德经, 論語, and 史記.

### Why
Classical Chinese is arguably the most token-efficient literary register ever standardized. A single character can carry the semantic weight of an entire English phrase. If caveman-speak saves ~65% tokens in English, 文言文 could achieve similar or greater compression while adding a rich, distinctive voice.

**Examples of the compression power of 文言文:**

| English (verbose) | 文言文 | Savings |
|---|---|---|
| "The reason your React component re-renders is because you are creating a new object reference on each render cycle" | 物頻出新參照，致重繪 | ~85% |
| "I would be happy to help you fix the authentication middleware bug" | 吾樂助君修 Middleware 之 bug | ~80% |
| "Sure, let me take a look at that for you" | 善，吾觀之 | ~90% |
| "It might be worth considering that the token expiry check uses less-than instead of less-than-or-equal" | 期滿檢查誤用 <，宜改 ≤ | ~85% |

### How it would work
```
/caveman wenyan    # Classical Chinese mode
/caveman wenyan-lite  # Less intense literary compression
/caveman wenyan-full # Maximum classical terseness
```

Example output:
```
Input: "Your PostgreSQL connection pool is leaking connections because you're not properly closing them in a finally block"
Wenyan-Full: 池漏 connection，未以 finally 閉之
Wenyan-Lite: Connection 池洩漏，finally 中未閉
```

### Technical notes
- Chinese characters are typically 1 token each in modern LLMs (vs 3-4 chars per token for English), so character-for-character it is already more token-efficient
- The challenge is guiding the LLM to produce classical-style Chinese without modern 白话 (vernacular) additions
- Could be implemented as a prompt/rule pack similar to the existing caveman rules
- Intensity levels could control how classical vs. modern-vernacular the output is

### Why this is different from caveman
- **Caveman**: drops English articles/fillers → works well for English
- **文言文**: fundamentally different language register — no articles, no subject-verb separation, highly idiomatic, ancient literary tradition

### References
- 道德經 (Tao Te Ching) — ~5,000 characters, entire philosophical text
- Classical Chinese averages 1 character per concept vs. English's ~5-6 characters per word

---

Would love to hear thoughts — is this something the project is open to? Happy to help prototype if there's a direction.

title: Fix path regex and prevent backup file overwriting
body:
## Summary

Fixed 3 bugs in the caveman-compress scripts:

### 1. PATH_REGEX Bug in `validate.py`
- **Problem**: The regex `(\./|\../|/|[A-Za-z]:\\)[\w\-/\\\.]+` incorrectly matched relative paths like `src/file.js` as `rc/` instead of the full path.
- **Fix**: Changed to `(?:\./|\.\./|/|[A-Za-z]:)?[\w\-/\\\.]+` using non-capturing group with optional prefix.
- **Impact**: This bug could cause false positive warnings during validation when comparing file paths in compressed vs original files.

### 2. Backup File Overwriting in `compress.py`
- **Problem**: Running compression twice on the same file would silently overwrite the `.original.md` backup, potentially losing important content.
- **Fix**: Added check that aborts with a warning if backup already exists.
- **Impact**: Prevents accidental data loss.

### 3. Empty `__init__.py`
- **Problem**: The module couldn't be properly imported as a package.
- **Fix**: Added `__all__` exports and `__version__` for proper imports.
- **Impact**: Improves module usability.

## Test Plan

- Verified PATH_REGEX correctly handles: `./src/file.tsx`, `src/file.js`, `/usr/bin`, Windows paths
- Verified backup protection triggers when running compression twice on same file
- Verified module imports correctly with `from caveman_compress.scripts import validate`

title: feat: add eval harness measuring real token savings (refs #18)
body:
## Summary

Adds an \`evals/\` directory with a minimal harness that measures real token compression per skill against a verbose LLM baseline. Closes the gap on #18 (README's token-savings claims being unverified).

## How it works

\`cases.yaml\` holds golden pairs:
- \`input\` — the user question
- \`baseline\` — a typical verbose, hedged LLM answer (the thing caveman replaces)
- \`outputs\` — per-skill, per-level caveman answer **taken verbatim from each \`SKILL.md\` example**

\`measure.py\` counts tokens with \`tiktoken\` (\`cl100k_base\`) and reports savings as \`1 − (caveman / baseline)\`, averaged across cases. No LLM calls, no API key, deterministic, runs in CI for free.

## Current results (2 cases)

| Skill | Lite | Full | Ultra |
|-------|------|------|-------|
| **abathur** | −82% | −79% | −86% |
| **caveman** | −82% | −84% | −89% |
| **caveman-cn** | −71% | −73% | −82% |
| **caveman-es** | −79% | −81% | −88% |

The actual savings exceed the README's "~75%" claim.

## Why this design

- **No LLM in the loop** → reproducible, free, runs in CI
- **Sources outputs from \`SKILL.md\` examples** → measures what skills actually promise, not invented reference data
- **Tight scope** → does not grade quality, faithfulness, latency, or cost. Those are separate problems

A future v2 could add \`evals/llm_run.py\` that calls a real model with each skill loaded for held-out questions.

## Run

\`\`\`bash
uv run --with tiktoken --with pyyaml python evals/measure.py
\`\`\`

Refs #18.

title: Add token-compression eval harness with three-arm methodology
body:
Closes #18.

## Why

The README currently claims `~75% token savings` with no underlying measurement. This PR adds a real, auditable eval harness and shows the honest number is meaningfully lower.

## How

Three arms per prompt, all using the same model:

| Arm | System prompt |
|-----|---------------|
| `__baseline__` | none |
| `__terse__` | `Answer concisely.` |
| `<skill>` | `Answer concisely.\n\n{SKILL.md}` |

The honest delta for any skill is **`<skill>` vs `__terse__`** — this isolates the skill from the generic "be terse" effect. An earlier draft of this harness compared skills against a no-skill baseline plus an aggressive activation wrapper, which inflated every number. Three independent reviewers (simplification / first-principles / scope-discipline lenses) flagged that as the load-bearing flaw, so it's gone.

Two scripts:
- `evals/llm_run.py` — calls `claude -p --system-prompt …` per (prompt, arm), writes `snapshots/results.json` with metadata (model, CLI version, timestamp). Requires `claude` CLI logged in.
- `evals/measure.py` — reads the snapshot, counts tokens with tiktoken `o200k_base`, prints a markdown table with median / mean / min / max / stdev. No network, no auth, runs in CI.

The snapshot is committed to git as the source of truth so any change to the numbers is reviewable as a diff.

## Initial results (claude-opus-4-6, n=10)

Reference arms:
- baseline (no system prompt): 1948 tokens total
- terse control (`Answer concisely.`): 2045 tokens total (+5% vs baseline — opus does not compress on the bare instruction)

Skills, measured against the terse control:

| Skill | Median | Mean | Min | Max | Stdev |
|-------|--------|------|-----|-----|-------|
| **caveman-cn** | −54% | −49% | −10% | −93% | 27% |
| **caveman** | −50% | −46% | −0% | −88% | 25% |
| **caveman-es** | −48% | −37% | +14% | −72% | 31% |
| **compress** | −21% | −22% | +18% | −57% | 22% |



![Skill compression chart](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sebastianbreguel/caveman/feat/eval-harness-llm/evals/snapshots/results.png)

Real range is **−22% to −49% mean**, not −75%. The README headline should be updated to match (separate change, not in this PR).

## What this does NOT measure

- **Fidelity** — a skill that returned `k` to everything would score −99% and "win". A future v2 could add a judge-model rubric.
- **Cost** — skills add input tokens on every call. Output savings are not the full economic picture.
- **Cross-model behavior** — only the model used to generate the snapshot (currently opus-4-6).
- **Exact Claude tokens** — `tiktoken o200k_base` is OpenAI's BPE and only an approximation. Ratios between arms are meaningful; absolute numbers are approximate.
- **Statistical significance** — single run per (prompt, arm) at default temperature. The min/max/stdev columns let the reader eyeball noise; this is not a powered experiment.

## Test plan

- [x] `uv run python evals/llm_run.py` regenerates the snapshot
- [x] `uv run --with tiktoken python evals/measure.py` reads the snapshot and prints the table
- [x] Snapshot committed and reviewable as a diff
- [ ] Maintainer verifies they can reproduce the run with their own `claude` CLI auth

title: feat: optional SessionStart hook + visible [CAVEMAN] statusline badge
body:
Hey Julius — first off, thanks for caveman. It's a beautifully simple idea and I've gotten a lot of value out of it.

This PR adds an **optional** addition for Claude Code users: a `SessionStart` hook that auto-loads the caveman ruleset at session start, plus a documented pattern for showing a persistent `[CAVEMAN]` badge in the statusline.

## Why

Claude Code `SessionStart` hooks inject their stdout as a hidden system-reminder that Claude sees but the user doesn't. That means when you wire caveman into a SessionStart hook, you get the behavior but no visual proof it actually fired. Users end up wondering \"is caveman mode on right now?\" and there's no way to check short of asking Claude.

The flag-file pattern in this PR solves that:

1. The hook writes a tiny file at `~/.claude/.caveman-active`
2. The user's statusline script checks for that flag and prepends a badge when present
3. The user now has persistent, passive confirmation caveman is loaded

## What's in the PR

- `hooks/caveman-activate.js` — ~30 lines, Node stdlib only, no dependencies. Writes the flag, emits the ruleset.
- `README.md` — one new subsection under **Install** titled *Optional: SessionStart Hook + Visible Mode Badge*. Explains the hook, the `settings.json` snippet, the statusline snippet, and why the flag file exists.

Both the hook and the statusline snippet are clearly marked **Claude Code only** — Cursor/Codex/other users can ignore this entire section. The core skill install works exactly as before if the hook isn't wired up.

## What's NOT in the PR

- No changes to any `SKILL.md` files
- No changes to `plugin.json` / `marketplace.json` / any manifest
- No changes to the compress tool, benchmarks, evals, or sub-skills
- No renaming, no branding changes, nothing speculative

Just the hook file, the README section explaining how to use it, and a pointer to the flag-file bridge pattern.

## Testing

I've been running this pattern in my own setup for the last couple sessions. The hook writes the flag reliably, the statusline picks it up on every render, and the badge disappears cleanly if I delete the flag file. Node stdlib only, no transitive deps.

## If you don't want it

Totally understand — your repo is already minimal and this adds a harness-specific path. Close without pressure, I'll keep it in my own fork. Either way, appreciate the work you've put into caveman and wanted to offer it back. 🪨

*(Note: this PR comes from my \`jccidc/caveman-harness\` fork, which has a few other Claude Code-specific additions on top. Those are deliberately **not** in this PR — this one is the single cleanest addition I thought might be useful upstream.)*

title: fix(docs): use ANSI-C quoting for bash statusline badge example
body:
Small docs fix — the bash statusline snippet in \`hooks/README.md\` has a real bug.

## Problem

The current snippet uses double-quoted escape sequences:

\`\`\`bash
caveman_text=\"\033[38;5;172m[CAVEMAN]\033[0m\"
\`\`\`

Bash does **not** interpret backslash escapes inside double quotes. Users who copy-paste this get the literal 19-character string \`\033[38;5;172m[CAVEMAN]\033[0m\` in their statusline instead of a colored badge.

You can verify with \`printf\`:

\`\`\`bash
$ caveman_text=\"\033[38;5;172m[CAVEMAN]\033[0m\"
$ printf '%s\n' \"\$caveman_text\" | cat -v
\033[38;5;172m[CAVEMAN]\033[0m
\`\`\`

No ESC character — just literal text.

## Fix

Switch to ANSI-C quoted strings (\`\$'...'\`), which bash does interpret:

\`\`\`bash
caveman_text=\$'\033[38;5;172m[CAVEMAN]\033[0m'
\`\`\`

For the mode-variant line that needs to interpolate \`\${caveman_suffix}\`, adjacent string concatenation preserves both the ANSI-C literal portions and the double-quoted expansion:

\`\`\`bash
caveman_text=\$'\033[38;5;172m[CAVEMAN:'\"\${caveman_suffix}\"\$']\033[0m'
\`\`\`

Verified with \`bash -c ... | cat -v\`:

\`\`\`
^[[38;5;172m[CAVEMAN]^[[0m
^[[38;5;172m[CAVEMAN:ULTRA]^[[0m
\`\`\`

\`^[\` is the visible representation of ESC (0x1B). Both variants now produce real escape sequences, and the badge renders with color in a terminal.

## Scope

- 2 lines changed in \`hooks/README.md\`
- No other files touched
- No behavior change — purely a docs fix so copy-paste works

This is one of a small batch of docs and install.sh quality-of-life PRs I'm sending today. Each one is independent and can be merged in any order. Close any that don't fit your vision — no pressure. 🪨

title: feat(install): check for node availability and back up settings.json
body:
Two small safety improvements to `hooks/install.sh`. Both purely additive — no behavior change on the happy path, only on failure modes.

## 1. Fail fast if node is missing

The script uses `node -e` to merge the hook config into `~/.claude/settings.json`, but doesn't check that node is on PATH first. Claude Code itself ships node, but users running `install.sh` via curl pipe on a fresh machine (before installing Claude Code) hit a cryptic error from inside the heredoc.

Adds a `command -v node` check at the top with a helpful message:

```bash
if ! command -v node >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "ERROR: 'node' is required to install the caveman hooks (used to merge"
  echo "       the hook config into ~/.claude/settings.json safely)."
  echo "       Install Node.js from https://nodejs.org and re-run this script."
  exit 1
fi
```

## 2. Back up `settings.json` before the node merge

The script now copies `$SETTINGS` to `$SETTINGS.bak` before running the node rewrite. If the merge fails mid-write (disk full, interrupted script, node crash, power loss), the user can recover their config from the backup instead of losing it.

```bash
cp "$SETTINGS" "$SETTINGS.bak"
```

This matters more now that the script wires up **two** hook entries (SessionStart + UserPromptSubmit) in a single `node -e` write. More state at risk per transaction.

## Scope

- 1 file changed: `hooks/install.sh`
- +13 lines, -0 lines
- Syntax-checked with `bash -n`
- No new dependencies, no new flags, no new behavior on the happy path

Second PR in a small batch today. Independent of the others — can be merged in any order. Close if it doesn't fit your vision. 🪨

title: feat(hooks): add uninstall.sh companion to install.sh
body:
Symmetric uninstaller for users who installed the hooks via `hooks/install.sh` (not via the plugin system). Currently `hooks/README.md` documents uninstall as three manual steps — this script automates them.

## What it does

1. Removes `caveman-activate.js` and `caveman-mode-tracker.js` from `~/.claude/hooks` if present (idempotent — skips missing files)
2. Uses node to filter out the caveman `SessionStart` and `UserPromptSubmit` entries from `~/.claude/settings.json`. Preserves all non-caveman hook entries. Drops event keys that become empty (e.g. if `UserPromptSubmit` only had the caveman tracker, the `UserPromptSubmit` key is removed entirely to keep settings.json tidy)
3. Removes the `~/.claude/.caveman-active` flag file
4. Backs up settings.json to `settings.json.bak` before editing, same policy as the install.sh safety PR
5. Gracefully degrades if node is missing — prints a warning with the settings.json path and tells the user to edit manually
6. Prints a reminder that plugin users should disable the plugin instead of running this script

## Verified

Node JSON-filter logic tested in isolation against a settings.json containing:

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [
      { "hooks": [ {"command": "node /path/caveman-activate.js"} ] },
      { "hooks": [ {"command": "node /path/unrelated-hook.js"} ] }
    ],
    "UserPromptSubmit": [
      { "hooks": [ {"command": "node /path/caveman-mode-tracker.js"} ] }
    ],
    "PostToolUse": [
      { "hooks": [ {"command": "node /path/some-other-hook.js"} ] }
    ]
  },
  "someOtherField": "preserve me"
}
```

Result after running the filter:
- 2 caveman entries removed (as expected)
- `unrelated-hook` preserved in `SessionStart`
- `UserPromptSubmit` key dropped (was only caveman-mode-tracker)
- `PostToolUse` entirely preserved
- `someOtherField` preserved

## Scope

title: fix: handle nested fences + strip LLM output wrapper in caveman-compress
body:
## Summary

Two bugs caused `caveman-compress` to reliably fail on files that contain fenced code blocks showing markdown (e.g. report templates, output format examples, docs about markdown). Both are fixed here with no behavior change for the happy path.

### 1. Fence parser mispairs nested / variable-length fences

`validate.py` used:

```python
CODE_BLOCK_REGEX = re.compile(r"```.*?```", re.DOTALL)
```

This pairs fences greedily left-to-right. When a file has an outer 4-backtick fence wrapping an inner 3-backtick snippet (common in docs about markdown and in report templates that illustrate code output), the regex parses it as two separate blocks — so `extract_code_blocks(original) != extract_code_blocks(compressed)` even when nothing inside changed. Tilde fences (`~~~`) weren't supported at all.

**Fix:** replaced with a line-based fence parser following CommonMark rules. A fenced block opens on a line starting with 3+ backticks or tildes (with up to 3 leading spaces), and closes on a line with a matching fence char of at least the same length and no info string. Variable-length fences, tilde fences, and nested blocks all parse correctly.

### 2. Claude wraps full output in `` ```markdown ... ``` ``

`compress.py` passes Claude's stdout straight through without stripping any wrapper. The model frequently wraps its entire response in a fence (even when prompted not to), which:

- fails code-block validation (inner real blocks no longer match the original)
- burns the retry budget on a fix that can't succeed
- ends with the file restored and the user thinking compression "just doesn't work on this file"

**Fix:** added `strip_llm_wrapper()` that removes an outer `` ``` ``-or-`~~~` fence only when it wraps the entire output. Inner fences preserved exactly. Applied to both the `anthropic` SDK path and the `claude` CLI fallback. Also strengthened the compression prompt with an explicit "do not wrap the output in an outer fence" rule.

## Test plan

- [x] Unit-style smoke test on a file with three fenced blocks (one ` ``` `, one tilde, one 4-backtick wrapping 3-backtick) — all three extract correctly
- [x] `strip_llm_wrapper()` round-trips ` ```markdown ... ``` ` correctly, preserves inner ` ```py ... ``` ` exactly
- [x] End-to-end run on a real ~6KB command file with two fenced output-format blocks — validation passes on first attempt where the old parser would hit max retries and restore

## Notes

- No change to the extractor's public API — still returns `list[str]`
- `strip_llm_wrapper()` is conservative: it only strips when a single outer fence wraps the *entire* stripped output, so normal responses without a wrapper are untouched

title: wenyan: add -simp suffix for 简体 output
body:
## Before

User: `/caveman wenyan`
Caveman: 物出新參照，致重繪。useMemo .Wrap之。   ← only 繁體 available

User: asks in 简体 / wants simplified
Caveman: 物出新參照，致重繪。useMemo .Wrap之。   ← still 繁體, no way to switch

## After

User: `/caveman wenyan` (or `wenyan-lite` / `wenyan-ultra`)
Caveman: 物出新參照，致重繪。useMemo .Wrap之。   ← default 繁體, unchanged

User: `/caveman wenyan-lite-simp`
Caveman: 组件频重绘，以每绘新生对象参照故。以 useMemo 包之。

User: `/caveman wenyan-full-simp`
Caveman: 物出新参照，致重绘。useMemo .Wrap之。

User: `/caveman wenyan-ultra-simp`
Caveman: 新参照→重绘。useMemo Wrap。

## Why

Wenyan currently only emits 繁體 because every few-shot example in `SKILL.md` is 繁體, even though 文言文 itself has no inherent script. This adds a composable `-simp` suffix to each wenyan intensity (`wenyan-lite-simp`, `wenyan-full-simp`, `wenyan-ultra-simp`) as a first-class switch, grounded by parallel 简体 examples in the React demonstration block. Default remains 繁體 — zero breaking change.

## Design notes

- **Suffix, not a new mode family** — composes with existing `wenyan-lite/full/ultra` instead of doubling the mode count, keeps the `/caveman <mode>` single-arg grammar, and leaves the 3-row intensity table intact.
- **Flag declared where wenyan is defined** — inline addition to the `wenyan-full` table row (the canonical wenyan entry) rather than a bolted-on section.
- **Few-shot over rules** — script bias was created by examples, so the fix is examples. Adding one 简体 row per intensity gives the model symmetric grounding; no magic-word rule needed.
- **Diff stat: `+4 −1`, one file.** Per CONTRIBUTING.md, only `skills/caveman/SKILL.md` is touched; the other 3 SKILL.md copies and `caveman.skill` are left for CI auto-sync.

## Known follow-up (not in this PR)

`hooks/caveman-mode-tracker.js` will fall the new `-simp` args through to `'full'` on the statusline badge. Functional behavior (model output) is unaffected because the model reads the user's `/caveman` command from the prompt directly, not from the flag file. Happy to add a tracker patch in this PR or a follow-up — let me know the preference.

title: Failed with non-blocking status code: node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1458
body:
On Windows, ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} in .claude-plugin/plugin.json is not expanded before the hook command runs. It resolves to an empty string, so node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/caveman-mode-tracker.js
  becomes node /hooks/caveman-mode-tracker.js, which Node on Windows resolves to C:\hooks\caveman-mode-tracker.js and fails with MODULE_NOT_FOUND.

  Error

  UserPromptSubmit hook error
  Failed with non-blocking status code:
  node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1458
  Error: Cannot find module 'C:\hooks\caveman-mode-tracker.js'
    code: 'MODULE_NOT_FOUND'

  Same error fires on SessionStart. Both hooks in plugin.json use ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}.

  Environment

  - Windows 11 Pro
  - Node.js v25.6.1
  - Install path: C:\Users\Username\\.claude\plugins\cache\caveman\caveman\92f892f2b997\ (ASCII, no spaces)

  What I verified

  - ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is not substituted by Claude Code before the shell sees the command.
  - $env:CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT (PowerShell env var syntax) also fails after /reload-plugins — Claude Code isn't injecting the env var into the hook subprocess on Windows either.
  - Hardcoding the absolute install path in plugin.json works.

  Suggested fix

  Resolve the hook script path from within the Node script itself using __dirname, instead of depending on ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} expansion by the caller. A small launcher that require()s the real hook by
  relative path would work on every platform regardless of how Claude Code handles the variable.

title: feat: add Japanese (日本語) compression modes to caveman
body:
`Before`: Many word. おそらく、検討してみてください、確かに、そうです、. Wall hit face.

`After`: 「新参照毎レンダ。インライン`obj prop`→再レンダ。`useMemo`で包め。」Brain same. Mouth small.

`Why`: Japanese very token heavy. Now 3 tier squeeze like wenyan. No extra rule bloat + Colleagues = happy!

`Research`: 
<details>
  <summary>Japanese (日本語) Mode — Token Efficiency</summary>

---

## Intensity Levels

| Level | Trigger | Description |
|---|---|---|
| nihongo-lite | `/caveman nihongo-lite` | 常体短文. Grammar intact, filler gone, readable |
| nihongo-full | `/caveman nihongo` | Full 日本語. Subject dropping, 体言止めOK, ~70% compression |
| nihongo-ultra | `/caveman nihongo-ultra` | Maximum terseness, ~75% compression |

---


## The Right Comparison (IMO)

The wenyan research compared verbose English prose to 文言文 output. The same frame applies here: **the baseline is verbose English AI prose, not standard Japanese prose.** Nihongo mode does not translate to natural conversational Japanese — it produces maximally terse, kanji-heavy technical Japanese using grammatical compression features that have no English equivalent.

Standard Japanese prose is indeed ~77% more token-expensive than English prose with GPT-4o (Castillo, 2025 — tiktoken on parallel text: English 432 tokens, Japanese 767 tokens for the same content). But nihongo-ultra is not standard Japanese prose. The compression mechanisms below close that gap dramatically and then some when measured against the verbose English baseline.

---

## Examples・Token Savings

Baseline: verbose English AI output (what the model produces without caveman mode)

| English (verbose) | 日本語 (nihongo-ultra) | Savings vs verbose English |
|---|---|---|
| "The reason your React component re-renders is because you are creating a new object reference on each render cycle" | 新参照→再レンダ | ~75% |
| "I would be happy to help you fix the authentication middleware bug" | authミドルウェアバグ、修正する | ~70% |
| "Your PostgreSQL connection pool is leaking connections because you are not properly closing them in a finally block" | プールがconn漏れ。finally未閉 | ~72% |
| "The authentication middleware is not properly validating the JWT token signature" | authミドルウェア、JWT署名未検証 | ~70% |
| "I would recommend using useMemo to memoize the expensive computation" | 重計算→useMemoで記憶 | ~75% |
| "This function will return the sum of all elements in the array" | 配列全要素の和を返す | ~78% |
| "Sure, let me take a look at that for you" | 確認する | ~85% |

Token savings are measured with `cl100k_base` / GPT-4o tokenizer against the full verbose English phrasing.

---

## Compression Mechanics (a lot like wenyan)

Japanese enables a class of compression that English structurally cannot:

**1. Pro-drop (主語省略)**
Japanese is a pro-drop language — subjects and objects are omitted when recoverable from context. English grammar requires explicit subjects in almost every clause. A response that would need "I", "you", "it", "the function", "this component" in English drops all of them in Japanese.

> English: "You should close the connection in a finally block"
> Japanese: `finallyでconn閉じる` (subject gone, object compressed)

**2. 体言止め (Taigen-dome — noun-terminal sentences)**
Japanese can end sentences with a noun phrase rather than a full predicate. English cannot. This drops the entire verb structure — often 3–5 tokens — while remaining grammatically complete and natural to a native reader.

> English: "The problem is that the connection is not being closed" (~10 tokens)
> Japanese: `conn未閉が問題` (noun-terminal, ~5 tokens)

**3. Particle omission**
In terse register, Japanese particles (は/が/を/に) can be dropped when meaning is unambiguous. Combined with pro-drop, this removes most of the grammatical glue English is forced to articulate.

**4. Kanji semantic density**
A kanji character encodes roughly 12 bits of information vs ~6 bits for a Latin letter (Shannon entropy; see also Castillo 2025 character-count data). One kanji = one token in modern tokenizers (GPT-4o, Claude) yet carries the meaning of 2–4 English words. Technical kanji compounds — `認証` (authentication), `接続` (connection), `検証` (validation) — encode multi-word English concepts in 2 characters / 2 tokens.

This is the same mechanism that makes wenyan efficient. Nihongo-ultra front-loads kanji and technical abbreviations, minimising hiragana/katakana filler that would otherwise inflate token count.

**5. Arrow notation and symbolic connectives**
`→` for causation/implication replaces "because", "therefore", "which causes", "resulting in" — each of which is 1–2 tokens in English but expresses only connective meaning. Japanese technical writing already uses this convention natively.

---

## Why 日本語?

### Honest comparison to wenyan

Wenyan is the more extreme compression register (hands down). Classical Chinese has no hiragana/katakana filler, and its grammar is even more telegraphic than Japanese — wenyan-full achieves ~85-90% reduction, nihongo-ultra achieves ~70-75%. 

**Nihongo's case is different, not weaker:**

**Accessibility.** Wenyan requires classical Chinese literacy — a specialised skill even for native Mandarin speakers. Modern Japanese, even in terse form, is readable to the ~125 million Japanese speakers worldwide. The compression is available to a far larger audience without specialised training.

**Validated by independent research.** SynthLang (ruvnet, 2024–2025) — a dedicated token-efficiency research project — explicitly uses Japanese kanji as its core logographic compression substrate, citing 70–90% reduction from verbose English prompts. SynthLang chose Japanese over other options precisely because its kanji-based writing encodes high semantic density while remaining interpretable to both humans and LLMs.

**Character economy.** The same content that requires 2,053 English characters uses only 1,081 Japanese characters (Castillo, 2025) — a 47% reduction in character count. Characters ≈ semantic payload per glyph. Japanese packs more meaning per character than English; standard tokenisers just aren't optimised for it. Modern tokenisers (GPT-4o, Claude 3+) have significantly improved their Japanese vocabulary coverage, closing much of the token-fertility gap documented in older benchmarks.

**Grammatical compression English cannot replicate.** The pro-drop + 体言止め combination eliminates entire grammatical categories that English is structurally forced to articulate. English caveman mode compresses English — it cannot drop subjects or use noun-terminal clauses because English grammar prohibits it. Nihongo mode achieves comparable compression ratios via a completely different and linguistically legitimate mechanism.

**The information-theoretic argument.** The dylancastillo benchmark shows Chinese achieves the same 2,053-character English content in 707 characters and 531 tokens. Japanese achieves it in 1,081 characters but 767 tokens — the overhead comes almost entirely from hiragana/katakana grammatical particles. Nihongo mode targets this directly: maximise kanji, drop particles where legal, use 体言止め to eliminate verb forms. The result closes the gap with Chinese significantly.

### Summary

Wenyan mode is the most efficient. Nihongo mode is the most efficient for the 125 million people who read Japanese and don't read classical Chinese. Both are logographically grounded, both beat verbose English by 70–85%, and both operate on the same core principle: dense characters carrying more semantic weight per token than English words.

---

## Sources

- Castillo, D. (2025). *Japanese is the most expensive language in terms of input tokens.* tiktoken benchmark on 9 languages using GPT-4o tokeniser. https://dylancastillo.co/til/counting-tokens.html
- ruvnet. (2024). *SynthLang: A hyper-efficient prompt language inspired by Japanese logographics.* GitHub: https://github.com/ruvnet/SynthLang
- Cohen. (2025). *SynthLang: A hyper-efficient prompt language inspired by Japanese.* LinkedIn. https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/効-synthlang-hyper-efficient-prompt-language-inspired-japanese-cohen-ixjac
- Artfish AI. (2023). *All languages are NOT created (tokenized) equal.* https://www.artfish.ai/p/all-languages-are-not-created-tokenized
- Castillo (2025) character data: EN 2053 chars / 432 tokens; JP 1081 chars / 767 tokens; ZH 707 chars / 531 tokens
- StackExchange / jovanni. (2013). *Japanese language "compression ratio."* Kanji ≈ log₂(3000) ≈ 12 bits vs alphabet ≈ log₂(60) ≈ 6 bits. https://japanese.stackexchange.com/questions/13155
- Craig Trim. (2026). *Why Non-English Speakers Pay More for AI.* Medium. https://medium.com/@craigtrim/why-non-english-speakers-pay-more-for-ai-eb6db7d5b67c
- Baloney, T. (2024). *CJK (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) LLM/AI best practices.* https://tonybaloney.github.io/posts/cjk-chinese-japanese-korean-llm-ai-best-practices.html

</details>

title: feat: make default caveman mode configurable
body:
## Summary

- Add `hooks/caveman-config.js` — shared config resolver with XDG-compliant path resolution across all platforms
- Remove hard-coded `'full'` default from `caveman-activate.js` and `caveman-mode-tracker.js`, replaced with `getDefaultMode()` call
- Update `install.sh` to include the new config module

### Config resolution order

1. `CAVEMAN_DEFAULT_MODE` environment variable (highest priority)
2. Config file `defaultMode` field at:
   - `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/caveman/config.json` (any platform, if `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set)
   - `~/.config/caveman/config.json` (macOS / Linux fallback)
   - `%APPDATA%\caveman\config.json` (Windows fallback)
3. `'full'` (unchanged default)

### Example config

```json
{ "defaultMode": "ultra" }
```

Or per-harness via environment variable:

```bash
CAVEMAN_DEFAULT_MODE=lite
```

## Test plan

Manual smoke tests — all passing:

### Test 1: No config (default behavior)
```
$ node -e "const c = require('./hooks/caveman-config'); console.log('default:', c.getDefaultMode()); console.log('configPath:', c.getConfigPath()); console.log('configDir:', c.getConfigDir());"
default: full
configPath: /Users/matt/.config/caveman/config.json
configDir: /Users/matt/.config/caveman
```

### Test 2: Environment variable override
```
$ CAVEMAN_DEFAULT_MODE=ultra node -e "const c = require('./hooks/caveman-config'); console.log('default:', c.getDefaultMode());"
default: ultra
```

### Test 3: XDG config file override
```
$ mkdir -p /tmp/caveman-xdg-test/caveman
$ echo '{"defaultMode":"lite"}' > /tmp/caveman-xdg-test/caveman/config.json
$ XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/tmp/caveman-xdg-test node -e "const c = require('./hooks/caveman-config'); console.log('default:', c.getDefaultMode());"

```

### Validation
- [x] No config → defaults to `full` (backward compatible)

title: feat(skills): add caveman-debug skill
body:
## Summary

Adds a `caveman-debug` skill — one-line debug findings in the format `<file>:L<line>: <error>. <root cause>. <fix>.` Same family as `caveman-commit` and `caveman-review`, specialized for diagnosis (stack traces, repro reports, post-mortems) instead of commit messages or PR review.

Also adds two debug-flavored prompts to `evals/prompts/en.txt` so the eval harness exercises the new skill on its target distribution after the next snapshot refresh.

## Why

Verbose Claude debug output is the worst offender for "wall of text" — every diagnosis starts with "Looking at the stack trace, I can see…" before getting to the actual `file:line`. A skill that constrains output to **location → error → root cause → fix** saves the most tokens precisely where users have the lowest tolerance for fluff (you're in the middle of a fire drill, you don't want a five-paragraph essay).

It also fills an obvious gap in the skill family: there's a skill for writing the commit, a skill for reviewing the PR, and a skill for compressing memory — but nothing for the debugging step in between.

## Before / After

**Before (verbose Claude):**

> "Looking at the stack trace, it seems like the error is happening in the user authentication middleware. The JWT token might be expired but the validation isn't catching it properly. You should probably take a closer look at how the expiry is being checked."

**After (`caveman-debug`):**

> ```
> auth/middleware.ts:L42 🔴 crash: `TypeError: Cannot read 'iat' of undefined`.
> `jwt.verify` returns `null` on expired token, code assumes object.
> Fix: `if (!decoded) return res.status(401).end();` before `decoded.iat`.
> Repro: 1) login 2) wait > exp 3) GET /me → 500.
> ```

Same diagnosis. ~5x fewer tokens. Actionable file:line + concrete fix + minimal repro.

The skill includes severity prefixes (`🔴 crash` / `🟠 wrong` / `🟡 flaky` / `🔵 perf`) that mirror `caveman-review`'s `bug/risk/nit/q` convention, plus an Auto-Clarity escape hatch for production data corruption, security findings, and onboarding contexts where the *why* still needs spelling out.

## Files changed

- `skills/caveman-debug/SKILL.md` — new file, 77 lines, follows the structural conventions of `skills/caveman-commit/SKILL.md` and `skills/caveman-review/SKILL.md` (frontmatter → opening line → Rules → Examples → Auto-Clarity → Boundaries).
- `evals/prompts/en.txt` — appends 2 prompts:
  - `Stack trace ends in `TypeError: Cannot read property 'email' of undefined at UserController.show (controllers/user.js:42:18)`. Where do I look first?`
  - `A test passes locally but fails in CI with `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432`. How do I debug it?`

## Notes for maintainer

- **Eval snapshot needs refresh**: `evals/snapshots/results.json` has to be regenerated (`uv run python evals/llm_run.py`) for the new skill and prompts to appear in `measure.py` output. I left it untouched because it's already stale relative to the current `skills/` layout (still has `caveman-cn` / `caveman-es` arms removed in `e6df0d6`, missing arms for `caveman-commit` / `caveman-review` / `compress`) — felt safer to leave the refresh as one atomic step on your end with the `claude` CLI authenticated.
- **Not bundled with the plugin** (`plugins/caveman/skills/`) — same precedent as `caveman-commit`, `caveman-review`, `compress`, which all live only under `skills/`. Happy to bundle in a follow-up if you'd prefer.
- **No `README.md` skills-table row added** — your existing pattern (per git log) has been to add those rows yourself post-merge. Not pre-empting.

## Test plan

- [x] `skills/caveman-debug/SKILL.md` YAML frontmatter parses (`yaml.safe_load`)
- [x] `evals/llm_run.py:67` discovery loop picks up `caveman-debug` (verified by simulating the same `Path('skills').iterdir()` filter)
- [x] `evals/prompts/en.txt` is well-formed (12 lines, no blanks, no trailing whitespace)
- [x] Only `skills/caveman-debug/SKILL.md` and `evals/prompts/en.txt` touched — nothing in `caveman/`, `plugins/`, `.cursor/`, or `caveman.skill` (those are auto-synced from `skills/caveman/SKILL.md` only, per `.github/workflows/sync-skill.yml`)
- [ ] **Maintainer:** refresh eval snapshot to confirm `caveman-debug` posts a real compression delta on the new debug prompts

title: Codex plugin packages broken compress skill stubs instead of a real SKILL.md/scripts directory
body:
## Summary
The Codex plugin install ships `plugins/caveman/skills/compress/SKILL.md` as a one-line path pointer instead of an actual skill file with YAML frontmatter. The companion `scripts` entry is also shipped as a one-line path pointer instead of a real directory.

## User-visible failure
Codex reports:

```text
Skipped loading 1 skill(s) due to invalid SKILL.md files.
...\skills\compress\SKILL.md: missing YAML frontmatter delimited by ---
```

## Root cause
The packaged plugin contains:

```text
plugins/caveman/skills/compress/SKILL.md -> ../../../../caveman-compress/SKILL.md
plugins/caveman/skills/compress/scripts  -> ../../../../caveman-compress/scripts
```

Those pointer-style files are not resolved by the Codex plugin loader, so it reads the literal file contents and rejects `SKILL.md` as invalid markdown frontmatter.

## Expected
The packaged plugin should contain a real `SKILL.md` file with frontmatter and a real `scripts/` directory so the `compress` skill can load and run after install.

## Proposed fix
Replace the pointer files in `plugins/caveman/skills/compress/` with the actual packaged skill content and script files.

title: feat(compress): respect CAVEMAN_MODEL on the claude CLI fallback path
body:
## Summary

Extend the existing `CAVEMAN_MODEL` env var support to the `claude --print` CLI fallback path.

The Anthropic SDK path in `call_claude()` already honors `CAVEMAN_MODEL` — see line 44 where it does `os.environ.get("CAVEMAN_MODEL", "claude-sonnet-4-5")`. But the CLI fallback (used when `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is unset or the `anthropic` package isn't installed — i.e., the common Claude Code plugin path) hardcodes whatever `claude --print` defaults to, ignoring the same env var.

This PR closes the gap so behavior is consistent across both paths.

## Why this matters

The CLI fallback path is the common one for users running caveman as a Claude Code plugin. Those users can't install `anthropic` into Claude Code's bundled Python environment, and many of them aren't using a raw API key — they use CLI auth. Today, those users have no way to change the model: `CAVEMAN_MODEL` is silently ignored on their execution path.

Concretely: running caveman compression on ~100 files against Opus costs about 5–10× what the same pass costs against Haiku, and the output quality is indistinguishable for this mechanical task (the existing regex validator catches both models' mistakes equivalently). Cost-conscious plugin users should be able to opt into the cheaper model just like API-key users already can.

## Usage

Session-wide (in shell rc):
```bash
export CAVEMAN_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
```

Per-call:
```bash
CAVEMAN_MODEL=claude-sonnet-4-6 caveman:compress big_file.md
```

Unset or empty → previous behavior, no `--model` flag passed to `claude --print`.

## Design notes

- **Non-breaking**: zero behavior change for users who don't set the env var. The `--model` flag is only appended if `CAVEMAN_MODEL` is non-empty, same pattern the SDK path already uses.
- **Consistent with SDK path**: same env var name, same "unset = default" semantics, so documentation can cover both paths together.
- **Retry path stays cheap**: if validation fails and `build_fix_prompt` runs, it re-enters `call_claude()`, which re-reads the env var — so the retry also uses the cheaper model.
- **Error messages updated**: `Claude call failed` now includes which model was in effect (`default` if unset), which helps debug cheap-model failures when they happen.

## Test plan

- [x] With `CAVEMAN_MODEL` unset, the constructed subprocess command is byte-identical to before (`["claude", "--print"]`).
- [ ] With `CAVEMAN_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`, compression produces valid output on a representative file (verified on a ~150 KB auto-memory directory).
- [ ] With `CAVEMAN_MODEL=nonexistent-model`, the error message clearly reports the invalid model.
- [ ] Retry path (forced by corrupting a code block) uses the same model as the initial call.

## Alternatives considered

- **A new env var for the CLI path** — rejected. Having one knob `CAVEMAN_MODEL` that works on both paths is simpler for users and for documentation.
- **Adding a `--model` CLI flag to the skill** — rejected. Skills are invoked via Claude Code's `Skill` tool, so an env var is easier to thread through than a flag.

## Scope

Touches only `caveman-compress/scripts/compress.py`. No README changes (the existing `CAVEMAN_MODEL` documentation, if any, applies equally to both paths now). Happy to add a README section clarifying the env var works on both paths if the maintainer wants.

title: fix: use portable shebangs and add run-hook.sh wrapper (#65)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #65

- Shell scripts used `#!/bin/bash` which fails if bash isn't at `/bin/bash` (NixOS, some containers, some BSD-derived systems)
- Plugin hook commands called `node` directly — fails when node is only reachable via nvm, Volta, or fnm (not on the default PATH in non-interactive shells like CI runners or plugin hooks)

Plugin hook error: /bin/sh: line 1: node: command not found

title: fix: Copilot/Cline mode selector (#88)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #88

The mode selector was broken for Copilot VS Code and Cline because `rules/caveman-activate.md` (the always-on rule injected as system context) listed mode names but gave no behavior descriptions. Without knowing what "ultra" or "wenyan-ultra" *does*, the AI had nothing to switch to.

- **Before:** `Switch level: /caveman lite|full|ultra|wenyan` — 4 modes, no definitions, wenyan sub-modes missing
- **After:** all 6 modes listed with brief behavior definitions; `/caveman ultra` now works in hookless agents

Also included: configurable default mode via `CAVEMAN_DEFAULT_MODE` env var or `~/.config/caveman/config.json` — allows users to set a persistent default without a `/caveman` command each session.

## Why good

Hookless agents (Copilot, Cline) can only follow mode instructions that are *defined* in the system context they receive. Adding the mode behavior table to the always-on rule is the minimal fix that makes mode switching work without any hook infrastructure.

## Before / After

**Before** (`rules/caveman-activate.md`, mode section):
```
Switch level: /caveman lite|full|ultra|wenyan
```
Copilot sees this → doesn't know what ultra means → no change in output.

**After:**
```
Level: full (default). Switch: `/caveman lite|full|ultra|wenyan-lite|wenyan-full|wenyan-ultra`
- lite: drop filler/hedging, keep articles and full sentences
- full: drop articles, fragments OK, short synonyms
- ultra: abbreviate (DB/auth/fn/req/res/impl), arrows for causality (X → Y), one word when possible
- wenyan-lite: semi-classical Chinese, grammar intact, filler gone
- wenyan-full: full 文言文, maximum classical terseness
- wenyan-ultra: extreme classical abbreviation
```
Copilot sees this → knows ultra = abbreviations + arrows → mode switch works.

## Verification

- [x] Baseline tests: all 7 checks pass (no pre-existing failures)
- [x] Post-fix tests: no regressions, all 7 checks still pass
- [x] New test: `verify_rule_completeness()` — checks all 6 modes present in rule file (would have failed on old code)
- [x] Synced copies updated: `.github/copilot-instructions.md` and `.clinerules/caveman.md` match source
- [x] README table updated: Cline and Copilot mode switching `—` → `Y⁵` with footnote

title: Meta-compression of SKILL.md and Spanish localization
body:
I have applied the Caveman philosophy to its own instructions. This PR introduces "efficiency from within" by compressing the core skill and expanding accessibility.
**Changes:**
1. **Meta-Compression of `SKILL.md`**: Reduced the instruction footprint from **3.7KB to 1.9KB (-48%)**. This saves critical input tokens on every turn.
2. **Spanish Localization**: Added `SKILL.es.md` for high-efficiency technical Spanish communication.
3. **Terminal Utilities**: Added `commands/caveman-pipe` to summarize terminal input (like `git diff`) instantly.
**Before (SKILL.md):**
> "Respond terse like smart caveman. All technical substance stay. Only fluff die. ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No revert after many turns. No filler drift. Still active if unsure. Off only: "stop caveman" / "normal mode"."

**After (SKILL.md):**
> "Respond terse like smart caveman. Substance stay. Fluff die. ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift. Off: "stop caveman" / "normal mode"."
**Why this change is better:**
The meta-compressed prompt is significantly more token-efficient. By using fewer tokens in the system prompt, we free up more of the agent's context window for actual project code, satisfying the core goal: **"Why use many token when few do trick"**.

title: Migrate CLI to argparse and fix relative execution pathing
body:
Migrate the compress CLI to `argparse` to add configuration flags, and inject `sys.path.insert` to fix direct execution errors.

**Example**

* **Before:** `python cli.py` fails with an ImportError. The script hard-aborts if a backup exists, and the max file size is permanently locked at 500KB.
* **After:** `python cli.py` runs perfectly from any directory. Users can now run `python cli.py --force --max-size 10000 --retries 5` to easily bypass backups and configure limits natively.

**Why good**
1. Removes the `ImportError` crash when running the script directly from the terminal. 
2. Gives users command-line control over edge cases (large files, existing backups) without having to manually edit source code.

title: caveman-compress silently overwrites inline code and commands despite "Validation passed"
body:
## Title
`caveman-compress` reports success while rewriting inline code and commands because validation never checks inline backticks

## Summary
`caveman-compress` promises to preserve inline code, commands, file paths, and other technical content exactly, but its validator does not check inline code spans at all. As a result, the tool can print `Validation passed`, return success, and overwrite the source file even when inline commands or environment variables were changed.

## Impact
This matters because the tool is designed to rewrite always-loaded memory files such as `CLAUDE.md`. Those files often contain commands, env vars, flags, file names, and other precise technical instructions inside backticks. A successful run can silently mutate that technical content while presenting the result as safe and validated.

Affected users are contributors relying on `caveman-compress` to shrink memory/context files without changing meaning. The failure mode is subtle: the backup exists, the command succeeds, and the live file is still overwritten with incorrect instructions.

## Environment
- Repository: `JuliusBrussee/caveman`
- Investigated at commit: `8bab5c739e133b0a637b7e0fd1a732d47b414fe9`
- Host: Linux WSL2 (`Linux GEOVANI-PC 6.6.87.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2 x86_64`)
- Python: `3.12.3`
- Reproduction did not require network access or a real Claude call; `scripts.compress.call_claude` was mocked locally to make the behavior deterministic.

## Evidence
1. The user-facing contract explicitly says technical content is preserved exactly.
   - `caveman-compress/SKILL.md:48-57` says inline code, file paths, commands, and env vars must be preserved exactly.
   - `caveman-compress/SKILL.md:82-83` says: inline code inside backticks must be preserved exactly.
   - `caveman-compress/README.md:129-141` says inline code, commands, file paths, headings, dates, and version numbers are not touched.
   - `caveman-compress/README.md:43` says validations passed and file paths were preserved exactly.

2. The compression prompt enforces that contract, but only at prompt level.
   - `caveman-compress/scripts/compress.py:69-75` instructs the model not to modify inline backticks, URLs, headings, file paths, or commands.

3. The validator does not enforce that contract.
   - `caveman-compress/scripts/validate.py:156-160` only calls:
     - `validate_headings`
     - `validate_code_blocks`
     - `validate_urls`
     - `validate_paths`
     - `validate_bullets`
   - There is no validator for inline code spans, commands, env vars, or other backtick-delimited technical content.
   - `validate_paths()` only emits a warning (`validate.py:126-131`), not an error.
   - `validate_bullets()` only emits a warning (`validate.py:134-144`), not an error.

4. Success is keyed only off `result.is_valid`, so warnings do not block overwrite.
   - `caveman-compress/scripts/compress.py:153-157` treats validation as passed when there are no errors.
   - Because inline code is never checked, modified inline commands can still produce `Validation passed`.

5. Direct validator repro: changed inline code produces a clean success result.

```bash
python3 - <<'PY'
import sys, tempfile
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, '/path/to/repo/caveman-compress')
from scripts.validate import validate

original = "# Title\nRun `npm install` and set `NODE_ENV=production`.\n"
compressed = "# Title\nRun `yarn install` and set `NODE_ENV=development`.\n"

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    orig = Path(tmp) / "orig.md"
    comp = Path(tmp) / "comp.md"
    orig.write_text(original)
    comp.write_text(compressed)
    result = validate(orig, comp)
    print("is_valid:", result.is_valid)
    print("errors:", result.errors)
    print("warnings:", result.warnings)
PY
```

Observed output:

```text
is_valid: True
errors: []
warnings: []
```

6. End-to-end repro: `compress_file()` reports success and overwrites the source file with changed inline commands.

```bash
python3 - <<'PY'
import sys, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from unittest.mock import patch

sys.path.insert(0, '/path/to/repo/caveman-compress')
from scripts.compress import compress_file

original = "# Title\nRun `npm install` and set `NODE_ENV=production`.\n"
corrupted = "# Title\nRun `yarn install` and set `NODE_ENV=development`.\n"

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    path = Path(tmp) / "CLAUDE.md"
    path.write_text(original)
    with patch("scripts.compress.call_claude", return_value=corrupted):
        print("compress_file_returned:", compress_file(path))
    print("source_contents:")
    print(path.read_text())
PY
```

Observed output:

```text
Processing: /tmp/.../CLAUDE.md
Compressing with Claude...

Validation attempt 1
Validation passed
compress_file_returned: True
source_contents:
# Title
Run `yarn install` and set `NODE_ENV=development`.
```

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Clone the repository and `cd` into it.
2. Run the following command from the repo root:

```bash
python3 - <<'PY'
import sys, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from unittest.mock import patch

sys.path.insert(0, 'caveman-compress')
from scripts.compress import compress_file

original = "# Title\nRun `npm install` and set `NODE_ENV=production`.\n"
corrupted = "# Title\nRun `yarn install` and set `NODE_ENV=development`.\n"

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    path = Path(tmp) / "CLAUDE.md"
    path.write_text(original)
    with patch("scripts.compress.call_claude", return_value=corrupted):
        ok = compress_file(path)
    print("returned:", ok)
    print(path.read_text())
PY
```

3. Observe that the command prints `Validation passed`.
4. Observe that the function returns `True`.
5. Observe that the rewritten file now contains `yarn install` and `NODE_ENV=development` instead of the original inline code.

## Expected Behavior
If inline code, commands, env vars, or other preserved technical spans change, validation should fail and the run should not be reported as successful. A successful compression should not be able to change those backtick-delimited instructions.

## Actual Behavior
Inline code changes are invisible to the validator, so the run is treated as valid. `compress_file()` returns success and overwrites the source file even though the technical instructions inside backticks were changed.

## Root Cause Analysis
The core mismatch is between the preservation contract and the validator implementation:

- The prompt and docs define inline backticks and commands as immutable.
- The validator never extracts or compares inline code spans.
- The success path only looks at `result.is_valid`, which is set only by validator errors.
- Since no inline-code validator exists, those mutations never become errors.

There is a secondary gap for other “must preserve exactly” content: path mismatches are warnings, not errors, so even some detected drift would not block a successful overwrite.

## Proposed Fix
Add explicit validation for every content type the tool promises to preserve exactly, especially:

- inline code spans
- env vars
- commands/examples that appear inside inline code
- path-like tokens that are currently warning-only

At minimum, any mismatch in those preserved spans should become a hard validation error, not a warning.

## Optional Patch Sketch
```python
INLINE_CODE_REGEX = re.compile(r"`([^`\n]+)`")

def extract_inline_code(text: str) -> list[str]:
    return INLINE_CODE_REGEX.findall(text)

def validate_inline_code(orig: str, comp: str, result: ValidationResult) -> None:
    if extract_inline_code(orig) != extract_inline_code(comp):
        result.add_error("Inline code not preserved exactly")

def validate(original_path: Path, compressed_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
    result = ValidationResult()
    orig = read_file(original_path)
    comp = read_file(compressed_path)

    validate_headings(orig, comp, result)
    validate_code_blocks(orig, comp, result)
    validate_inline_code(orig, comp, result)
    validate_urls(orig, comp, result)
    validate_paths(orig, comp, result)  # likely promote to error for exact-preserve content
    validate_bullets(orig, comp, result)
    return result
```

If you want stronger safety, stage compressed output in a temp file and only overwrite the source after validation fully passes.

## Risk / Regression Notes
After fixing this, it would be worth testing:

- inline code with commands and env vars, e.g. `` `npm install` `NODE_ENV=production` ``
- multiple inline code spans on one line
- escaped backticks / multi-backtick inline spans
- inline paths on Unix and Windows
- markdown files with both fenced code blocks and inline code
- cases where prose changes are allowed but inline technical spans must remain byte-for-byte identical

## Maintainer Value
This is worth maintainer attention because it breaks the main trust guarantee of `caveman-compress`: “compress prose, preserve technical content.” The current behavior can silently change operational instructions in a file that loads every session, while still claiming validation success. Fixing this would materially improve safety, user trust, and the credibility of the tool’s documented guarantees.

title: fix: per-turn reinforcement in UserPromptSubmit hook
body:
## The problem

Caveman's SessionStart hook injects the full ruleset once per session. This works great in isolation, but falls apart when other plugins inject competing style instructions on every turn.

I run caveman alongside an output-style plugin (explanatory mode). That plugin emits a style reminder via `<system-reminder>` on every user message. Caveman's one-shot injection from SessionStart quietly loses the priority fight — the model sees "be educational and verbose" on every turn but only saw "drop articles, fragments OK" once at the start. As it turns out, recency and repetition win in LLM attention. Caveman was active but the model wrote full verbose prose anyway.

## The fix

The mode-tracker hook already fires on every `UserPromptSubmit` — it just didn't emit anything. This adds a short structured reminder (via `hookSpecificOutput`) when the flag file exists. The full rules from SessionStart stay in context; this simply keeps them visible in the model's attention window.

The reminder uses the same `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` JSON format that Claude Code expects from hooks — no raw stdout.

## What changes

`hooks/caveman-mode-tracker.js`: after processing mode changes and deactivation, checks if the flag file exists and emits a one-line reinforcement. Silent-fails on all filesystem errors, same as existing code.

## Testing

Ran with an active output-style plugin that previously caused caveman to be ignored. With the reinforcement, caveman style persists across turns.

title: fix: natural language activation/deactivation in mode tracker
body:
## The problem

The README tells users they can say "talk like caveman" to activate. And they can — the model reads the prompt and starts speaking caveman. But the `UserPromptSubmit` hook only matched `/caveman` commands, so the flag file never got written and the statusline badge never appeared.

In other words: the model was in caveman mode, but the hook system didn't know about it. The flag file and statusline were out of sync with actual behavior.

## The fix

The mode-tracker now matches natural language activation phrases: "activate caveman", "turn on caveman mode", "talk like caveman", "enable caveman", etc. Same for deactivation: "stop caveman", "disable caveman", "turn off caveman mode".

A negative guard prevents "stop caveman" from triggering activation (it contains "caveman" after all). Deactivation runs after activation in the control flow, so even if both somehow matched, deactivation wins.

Natural language activation uses `getDefaultMode()` to respect `CAVEMAN_DEFAULT_MODE` and `config.json`, same as the `/caveman` command path.

## What changes

`hooks/caveman-mode-tracker.js`:
- New natural language activation block before the `/caveman` command block
- Expanded deactivation regex to match "disable", "deactivate", "turn off" in addition to existing "stop caveman" and "normal mode"

title: feat: add Thai language auto-detection and filler compression rules
body:
## What this adds

When the user writes in Thai, caveman now automatically detects it and applies Thai-specific filler rules at the current intensity level (lite/full/ultra). No `/caveman thai` command needed — language detection is automatic. Same principle as wenyan for Chinese, but Thai-specific.

## How the filler list was derived

The drop list wasn't guessed — it was derived from analysis of real Thai-language conversations in actual Claude Code sessions. Extracted user messages containing Thai text, counted frequency, and verified which words carry zero semantic payload vs. which are context-dependent.

**Top Thai fillers found (ranked by frequency in real usage):**

| Word/Phrase | What it is | Safe to always drop? |
|---|---|---|
| ก็ | Padding softener "also/just" | Yes |
| อะ/อ่ะ/วะ | Informal sentence particles | Yes |
| นะ | Softener particle | Yes |
| เออ | Opener filler "yeah/uh" | Yes |
| แบบว่า/แบบ | Hedge "like" | Yes |
| ก็คือ | Intro starter "well, it is..." | Yes |
| แล้วก็ | Redundant clause chaining | Yes |
| เลย | Trailing emphasis | Yes |
| อยู่ | Trailing stative particle | Yes |
| ถ้าเกิดว่า | Verbose conditional → ถ้า | Yes (shorten) |
| เหรอ/เหรอวะ | Question particles | Yes |

Context-dependent (keep when meaningful): `คือ` (definition), `แค่` (meaningful limit), `น่าจะ` (genuine uncertainty), `ใช่ไหม` (seeking confirmation).

## Before / After

**"ทำไม React component ถึง re-render?"**

Without caveman:
> "อ่ะ คือก็แบบว่า component มันก็ re-render เพราะว่ามันก็สร้าง object reference ใหม่ทุกครั้งเลยนะครับ ก็น่าจะลองใช้ useMemo ดูนะครับ"

With Thai caveman (full):
> "Object ref ใหม่ทุก render. Inline prop = ref ใหม่ = re-render. ใช้ `useMemo`."

**"อธิบาย database connection pooling"**

Without caveman:

❯ are you using the caveman plugin

● Yes. Full mode.

❯ is it making you faster and burning less tokens?

❯ how much plugin overhead is there on every prompt?

  tokens input overhead per turn.

❯ so for programming like what we have been doing in this chat, what is the average token response size before i turned on caveman?

title: compress skill broken on Windows: symlinks checked out as text files
body:
## Problem

On Windows (Git for Windows / MSYS2), the `skills/compress/` skill fails to load because `SKILL.md` and `scripts` are git symlinks pointing to `../../caveman-compress/`. By default, Windows Git checks out symlinks as plain text files containing the link target path, so the skill content is unreachable.

## Repro

- OS: Windows 11 Pro
- Git: Git for Windows (default, `core.symlinks` not set globally)
- Plugin version: `63e797cd753b` (installed via marketplace)

After install:

```
$ ls -la ~/.claude/plugins/cache/caveman/caveman/63e797cd753b/skills/compress/
-rw-r--r-- 31 SKILL.md      # contains literal text: ../../caveman-compress/SKILL.md
-rw-r--r-- 30 scripts       # contains literal text: ../../caveman-compress/scripts
```

Invoking `/caveman:compress` from Claude Code hits `SKILL.md` but reads only the link text, so the skill cannot execute.

Other skills (`caveman/`, `caveman-commit/`, `caveman-help/`, `caveman-review/`) work fine — they ship real files, not symlinks.

## Workaround (applied locally)

Replace broken symlinks with real copies:

```bash
cd ~/.claude/plugins/cache/caveman/caveman/63e797cd753b
rm skills/compress/SKILL.md skills/compress/scripts
cp caveman-compress/SKILL.md skills/compress/SKILL.md
cp -r caveman-compress/scripts skills/compress/scripts
```

This gets wiped on the next plugin update.

## Suggested fix

Any of:

1. Replace the symlinks under `skills/compress/` with the real files (simplest, works everywhere).
2. Keep a single canonical location (either `caveman-compress/` at repo root, or `skills/compress/`) and drop the duplicate + symlinks.
3. Document requiring `git config --global core.symlinks true` on Windows — but that also requires Developer Mode / admin on most setups, so option 1 or 2 is friendlier.

Happy to send a PR if the maintainer prefers option 1.

title: caveman-compress: UnicodeEncodeError on Windows (cp1252) crashes before reporting validation errors
body:
## Problem

On Windows, running `caveman-compress` with the default console codepage (cp1252) crashes with `UnicodeEncodeError` the moment the script tries to print the `❌` (U+274C) glyph — which happens on every validation failure and on the fallback error branch in `cli.py`.

The real failure (the validation error list) never reaches the user, because the print itself raises before the errors are shown. The script then dies without restoring the original file, leaving the compressed-but-unvalidated content in place and a half-written `<file>.original.md`.

## Repro

- Python 3.14, Windows 11
- Default stdout encoding: `cp1252`
- File: any 40KB+ natural-language markdown (triggered here on a 46KB CLAUDE.md)

```
Validation attempt 1
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../scripts/compress.py", line 159, in compress_file
    print("\u274c Validation failed:")
UnicodeEncodeError: 'charmap' codec can't encode character '\u274c' in position 0

During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:
  File ".../scripts/cli.py", line 68, in main
    print(f"\n\u274c Error: {e}")
UnicodeEncodeError: 'charmap' codec can't encode character '\u274c' in position 2
```

Occurrences of the problem glyph:
- `scripts/compress.py:159` — `print("❌ Validation failed:")`
- `scripts/compress.py:167` — `print("❌ Failed after retries — original restored")`
- `scripts/cli.py:29, 33, 60, 68` — error branches

## Workaround

Run with `PYTHONUTF8=1` or `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` in the environment. Neither is set by default on Windows.

## Suggested fix

Any of:

1. **Force UTF-8 stdout at process start** (cleanest — no user env required):
   ```python
   import sys
   sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding='utf-8', errors='replace')
   sys.stderr.reconfigure(encoding='utf-8', errors='replace')
   ```
   Put this at the top of `cli.py` / `__main__.py`.

2. Replace the `❌` glyphs with ASCII (`[FAIL]`, `ERROR:`) — safest, works on the oldest terminals too.

3. Document `PYTHONUTF8=1` as a Windows requirement.

## Secondary concern

When `print(...)` raises inside the validation-failed branch, the outer `try/except` in `cli.py` prints another `❌` and also raises, so `compress_file` never reaches its own cleanup path that restores the original file. Whatever the root cause, the script should restore the original on any unexpected exception, not just on `MAX_RETRIES` exhaustion.

Happy to send a PR if you'd like.

title: feat: add native Copilot CLI extension and installer
body:
## Summary

- add native Copilot CLI extension under `.github/extensions/caveman/`
- add installer scripts for per-repo and `--global` installs
- add canonical shared sources in `lib/` for parser + config resolver, with CI sync into runtime copies
- update README / CLAUDE / verification so Copilot CLI path is documented and validated
- add regression tests for extension behavior, installer behavior, and config resolution

## Before

- Copilot CLI only had static-instructions path; no native extension install path
- no Copilot CLI auto-activation, slash commands, or one-shot skills via native runtime
- default-mode config resolution could drift between runtimes; `~/.config/caveman/config.json` on Windows could be ignored by extension copy

## After

- Copilot CLI can install Caveman natively per repo or globally
- auto-activation, `/caveman` commands, one-shot skills, and mode switching work in Copilot CLI
- parser and config resolver each have one canonical source with synced runtime copies
- verification checks extension syntax without requiring Copilot CLI SDK outside Copilot CLI runtime

## Why this implementation

Copilot CLI has native extension discovery from repo `.github/extensions/` and user `~/.copilot/extensions/`. `npx skills add` would only install static instructions, so it cannot provide native `onSessionStart` / `onUserPromptSubmitted` hooks, slash commands, one-shot skills, or repo/global extension install.

Installer script exists because extension has to be copied into one of Copilot CLI's discovery locations. `--global` covers user-wide install; repo-targeted install covers checked-in project setup.

Shared `lib/` sources follow repo's existing sync pattern for generated/runtime consumers and reduce drift risk between hook runtime and Copilot extension runtime.

## Concerns / tradeoffs

- this does **not** use same install path as other agent integrations. That difference is intentional and platform-driven, not arbitrary.
- no persistent status badge in Copilot CLI because there is no statusline API there.
- kept scope to one feature: native Copilot CLI integration. Docs/tests/sync changes are support for that one integration, not a wider harness rewrite.

## Non-goals

- no change to core caveman behavior / SKILL semantics
- no change to other agent install paths
- no attempt to force generic cross-harness installer abstraction

## Verification

- `node tests/test_caveman_config.mjs`
- `node tests/test_extension_integration.mjs`
- `node tests/test_copilot_installer.mjs`
- `node --check .github/extensions/caveman/extension.mjs`
- manual smoke check: `node scripts/install-copilot-extension.mjs --global --force`

title: Hook commands break on paths with spaces
body:
## Bug

The hook commands in `plugin.json` don't quote `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, so they break for any user whose home directory path contains a space (e.g. `/Users/Tyler Laprade/`).

```json
"command": "node ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/caveman-activate.js"
```

The shell splits the unquoted expansion at the space, so Node.js receives `/Users/Tyler` as the file argument and fails:

```
node:internal/modules/cjs/loader:1459
  throw err;
  ^

Error: Cannot find module '/Users/Tyler'
```

Both the `SessionStart` and `UserPromptSubmit` hooks are affected.

## Fix

Quote the variable in both hook commands in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`:

```json
"command": "node \"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/caveman-activate.js\""
```

```json
"command": "node \"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/caveman-mode-tracker.js\""
```

## Repro

Have a macOS user with a space in their username, install the plugin, start a Claude Code session. Both hooks error on every session start and every prompt submit.
