title: dead_load:skills is self-invalidating: reporting a dead skill marks it used (plus 4 related measurement defects)
body:
# `dead_load:skills` is self-invalidating: reporting a dead skill marks it used

**Version:** caveman 1.2.5 (binary_release bin-v1.1.3), macOS, Claude Code transcripts
**Sink:** `dead_load:skills` — `"detection": "structured+substring_guard"`

## Summary

`dead_load:skills` decides a skill is unused by searching scanned transcripts for its
name. The report's own output is written into the transcript of the session that ran it.
So the act of reporting a dead skill makes it look used on the next run, and the finding
erases itself.

This is not drift and not a stale cache. It is a measurement whose output is an input to
the next measurement, with no marker distinguishing "genuinely used" from "named in a
report".

## Reproduction

Three `caveman learn report --json` runs inside one Claude Code session, roughly five
minutes apart. **No skills installed, removed, or invoked between runs. No config
changed.** Same window, same `sessions_scanned: 1329`.

| run | `evidence.skill_count` | `tokens_per_turn` | `dead_load` penalty | Cave Score |
|-----|------------------------|-------------------|---------------------|------------|
| 1   | **19**                 | 75                | 2                   | 73         |
| 2   | **7**                  | 27                | 2                   | 73         |
| 3   | **0** (sink absent)    | —                 | 0                   | **75**     |

The 12 that disappeared between run 1 and run 2 are *exactly* the 12 that run 1 printed
in `evidence.skills`, which caps at 12 entries:

    ios-fix, ios-qa, ios-sync, land-and-deploy, landing-report, make-pdf,
    office-hours, open-gstack-browser, pair-agent, plan-ceo-review,
    plan-devex-review, plan-eng-review

19 - 12 = 7, which is run 2's count exactly.

Run 2 named its remaining 7 (`plan-tune`, `qa-only`, `setup-browser-cookies`,
`setup-deploy`, `setup-gbrain`, `skillify`, `sync-gbrain`). Those 7 were then discussed
in the session, and run 3 emits no `dead_load:skills` sink at all.

All 19 are still installed:

    $ for s in <the 19>; do [ -d ~/.claude/skills/$s ] || echo "MISSING: $s"; done
    checked 19 named-dead skills; still installed: 19; missing: 0

## Why this matters more than the token count

1. **It fails silently and in the flattering direction.** Nothing errors. The sink
   quietly shrinks and the Cave Score rises, so the tool reports improvement where
   nothing improved. A user running `learn` weekly sees dead load "resolved" by
   observation alone.

2. **It cannot be worked around by the user.** The consent-gated editing skill
   (`caveman-learn`) instructs the agent to *show the candidate skills to the user*
   before proposing a fix. Following the documented workflow is what destroys the
   evidence. The more correctly the skill is followed, the faster the sink empties.

3. **It contaminates the `applied` ledger.** If a user gates some skills and then runs
   `caveman learn applied dead_load:skills`, the subsequent "improved" verdict is
   partly or wholly the artifact above, not the fix. The longitudinal verdicts
   (improved / unchanged / regressed) inherit the defect.

4. **The same guard shape presumably backs other detections.** Anything deciding "not
   used in N sessions" by substring over transcripts has this property wherever its own
   output lands in a scanned transcript.

## Suggested fixes, cheapest first

- **Exclude the tool's own output from the scanned corpus.** Skip tool-result blocks
  whose content parses as `caveman.learn.v*` JSON, and assistant turns produced in
  response to them. Cheapest and closes the direct loop.
- **Require a use signal stronger than a substring.** A skill invocation appears
  structurally in Claude Code transcripts (a `Skill` tool call, or a `<command-name>`
  block). `structured+substring_guard` suggests the structured path already exists and
  the substring pass is a fallback widening it — consider making the substring pass
  *narrowing only*, or dropping it.
- **If the substring pass stays, mark what it decided.** Emit per-skill *why* a skill
  was excluded (`structured_invocation` vs `substring_only`) so a consumer can tell a
  real use from a mention. A count that cannot distinguish the two reports the same
  number for two different states.

## Note

Reported with `basis: inferred` numbers straight from `caveman learn report --json`;
the run-to-run deltas above are the whole of the claim and are reproducible by running
the command three times in one session.

---

## Two further defects in the same guard, found while acting on its output

Acting on run 1's list surfaced two more problems. Together with the self-invalidation
above, `dead_load:skills` is wrong in both directions at once.

### (a) A skill whose name is a common word can never be reported dead

The substring guard matches a skill's name anywhere in a transcript. On this machine
55 skill directories are non-functional (see (b)), and the guard flagged 19. The 36 it
could not flag include:

    learn  review  qa  ship  guard  browse  health  freeze  spec
    canary  careful  codex  diagram  retro  scrape  connect-chrome

These are ordinary English words that appear in normal conversation with a coding
agent. `review` and `learn` in particular appear in almost every session. **A skill so
named is structurally undetectable by this guard**, regardless of whether it is used,
installed, or even loadable. The 19 that got flagged were flagged mainly because they
carry distinctive hyphenated names (`open-gstack-browser`, `plan-devex-review`).

So the sink under-reports, and it under-reports *non-randomly* — biased toward exactly
the skills whose names are least likely to collide.

### (b) It charges tokens for skills that load nothing

All 19 it flagged are **dangling symlinks**:

    $ readlink ~/.claude/skills/ios-fix/SKILL.md
    /Users/mikejones/.claude/skills/gstack/ios-fix/SKILL.md
    $ [ -d /Users/mikejones ] || echo "NO SUCH USER DIR"
    NO SUCH USER DIR

55 of 87 skill directories are in this state, every one pointing into the same
nonexistent home (an account-rename or machine-migration artifact). The agent host
cannot read them, does not list them, and loads no description for them — none of the
55 appears in the harness's available-skills listing.

`dead_load:skills` nevertheless priced 19 of them at **75 tokens/turn**
(`tokens_per_day_rate: 117255`) and applied a Cave Score penalty of 2. That figure is
derived from directory presence, not from what the host actually loads.

The user-visible consequence is the wrong remedy. The report says *"consider gating
skills with no detected use"*. Gating a dangling symlink returns nothing, because it
was already costing nothing. The actual defect on this machine — 55 broken installs,
one stale path, a whole skill suite silently non-functional for weeks — is a
correctness problem the token framing hides. A user who follows the suggestion tidies
19 of the 55 and never learns the other 36 are broken too.

### Suggested additions to the fixes above

- **Resolve the skill before pricing it.** If `SKILL.md` is unreadable, its cost is 0.
  Report it under a different heading — *broken install*, not *dead load* — because the
  remedy is repair or removal, not gating.
- **Require word-boundary or structured matching**, and treat a name that is a common
  English word as unmatchable: report it as `undetectable_by_name` rather than silently
  omitting it. An omitted skill and a used skill currently produce the same output.

---

## Secondary, unrelated: `learn savings` exits 1 with no diagnostic

Same version. With no fixes yet recorded via `learn applied`:

    $ caveman learn savings
    Command failed: /Users/mikejones-mabookair/.caveman/bin/caveman-proxy learn savings
    $ echo $?
    1

Same with `--json`. The subcommand is documented in `caveman learn --help`, and the
`caveman-learn` skill instructs the agent to present its output, so an agent following
the skill hits an unexplained failure. If the cause is simply an empty ledger, an empty
result and a message would be better than exit 1 — as written, "no fixes recorded yet"
and "the ledger is broken" produce the same output.

---

## Fourth defect: `config_tax` reports 0 for CLAUDE.md and misses plugins entirely

The report emitted:

    claude_md_project_tokens: 0
    claude_md_user_tokens: 0
    config_tax penalty: 0
    skill_desc_tokens: 1759          <- the only populated component
    measured_prefix_tokens: 37114
    unexplained_prefix_tokens: 35355  <- 95% of the prefix, unattributed

Measured directly on the same machine, the "unexplained" 95% decomposes almost exactly:

    40south-guard/CLAUDE.md      16,415 tok   (reported as 0)
    workspace CLAUDE.md           7,481 tok   (reported as 0)
    plugin skills (140)           8,422 tok   (not counted at all)
    plugin agents (63)            3,714 tok   (not counted at all)
    user skills (87)              2,609 tok   (the one thing counted)
                                 ~38,641 tok  vs measured_prefix 37,114

Consequences: the Cave Score's config_tax component scored a 0 penalty on a setup whose
config is ~24k tokens/turn of CLAUDE.md alone, and the "best next move" ranking is computed
over ~7% of the actual config surface. A user acting on the report is steered at the smallest
lever on the board.

Suggested fix: resolve CLAUDE.md the way the host does (project root, workspace parent, and
nested per-directory files), and enumerate enabled plugins' skill/agent description blocks
from the plugin cache. Where a component cannot be resolved, report it as unmeasured rather
than 0 — a 0 and a "did not look" are the two states the score exists to separate.

## Fifth defect: `learn implement` targets a portfolio the first report already emptied

`caveman learn implement` opens an agent pointed at the current report's best next move. But
the dead_load sink self-erases (defect 1), so by the second report the only reducible finding
is gone and best_next_move silently shifts to the next group — in this case 24 recurring-context
offload candidates whose net gate would mostly fail. The compounding is the point: defect 1 is
not just a wrong number, it re-aims the tool's own remediation flow at weaker fixes.

## A note on `caveman claude --help`

`caveman claude --help` performed the full enable (settings.json env rewrite, 11 hook events,
MCP registration, proxy start) before printing usage. A --help invocation that mutates user
configuration is a footgun regardless of how good the integration is; the enable output even
says "planned user-scoped writes" while executing them. Suggest: --help never writes.

title: caveman-compress: fenced ASCII-tree code block makes a file permanently uncompressible — fix-retry hits the preamble guard, and a fresh retry silently no-ops with no diagnostic
body:
### Prerequisites
- [x] I searched existing issues to avoid duplicates (see "Related issues" below)
- [x] I am using the latest version of `skills/caveman-compress`
- [x] I read `SKILL.md`/`README.md` and confirmed this is expected input (plain fenced code block, no unusual indentation)

### Bug Description

Compressing a markdown file containing one fenced, column-0, triple-backtick code block that holds an ASCII directory tree with inline trailing `#` comments makes the file **permanently uncompressible**, and the two failure paths the tool can land on give no actionable diagnostic:

1. First attempt fails `validate_code_blocks` (the compressor edited text inside the fence, most likely the trailing `# comment` on each tree line, despite the compress prompt's explicit "do not modify code blocks" instruction).
2. The fix-retry response is then rejected by the anchor/preamble guard added in #588 (`first_nonblank_line(compressed) != anchor`), which has no fallback — it just consumes the retry and gives up.
3. A completely fresh `compress_file()` call on the same untouched input (new process, no stale backup) does not reproduce the same validation error — instead the first-pass output comes back byte-identical to the input, and `compress_file()` aborts with "output is identical to input."

No data loss in either path (identity/backup/atomic-write guards all held), but the file is stuck: it will not compress no matter how many times it's retried, and the two runs report unrelated-looking failures for the exact same input, which makes this very hard to self-diagnose without reading the compressor source.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a markdown file, e.g. `docs/example.md`:

````markdown
# Example

Some prose describing a project before the tree.

## STRUCTURE

```
project/
├── main.py                 # entry point, argument parsing
├── core/
│   ├── engine.py            # orchestrates the pipeline
│   ├── config.py            # loads settings from env
│   └── errors.py            # error taxonomy
├── adapters/
│   ├── http_client.py       # thin wrapper over requests
│   └── db_client.py         # thin wrapper over the driver
└── tests/
    └── test_engine.py        # unit tests for core/engine.py
```

## CONVENTIONS

- Some more ordinary prose bullet points here.
- And another one, long enough to be worth compressing.
````

2. From `skills/caveman-compress/`, run:
   ```
   python3 -m scripts docs/example.md
   ```
3. Observe validation failure and fix-retry rejection (Run 1, below).
4. Restore the file to its original content (or use a second fresh copy) and run the exact same command again.
5. Observe a *different* failure mode this time — "output is identical to input" (Run 2, below) — for the same unmodified input.

Both runs are reproducible independently; which one occurs on a given invocation is non-deterministic because `call_claude()` is a live model call with no seed/temperature pinning.

### Expected Behavior

Either:
- The compressor should not touch text inside the fenced code block at all (per its own stated rule), so validation passes on the first attempt, or
- If a fix-retry is rejected by the preamble guard, the tool should retry with a corrective nudge instead of immediately exhausting `MAX_RETRIES` and reverting the whole file, and
- Repeated invocations on an unchanged input should not surface two unrelated failure signatures — the failure mode itself should be reproducible enough to debug.

### Actual Behavior

**Run 1** — compress → validate → fix → validate:

```
Detected: natural_language
Starting caveman compression...

Processing: docs/example.md
Compressing with Claude...

Validation attempt 1
❌ Validation failed:
   - Code blocks not preserved exactly
Fixing with Claude...
❌ Fix attempt aborted: output does not start with the original's first line.
   Possible preamble leak. Skipping this attempt.

Validation attempt 2
❌ Validation failed:
   - Code blocks not preserved exactly
❌ Failed after retries — original restored

❌ Compression failed after retries
```

**Run 2** — fresh `compress_file()` call, same untouched input, no stale backup:

```
Detected: natural_language
Starting caveman compression...

Processing: docs/example.md
Compressing with Claude...
❌ Compression aborted: output is identical to input.
   Likely causes: Claude refused, returned the prompt verbatim, or the file is
   already in caveman form. Original file is untouched (no backup created).

❌ Compression failed after retries
```

### Root-Cause Analysis (from reading `scripts/compress.py` + `scripts/validate.py`)

1. **`validate_code_blocks` failure (Run 1, attempt 1):** `extract_code_blocks()` in `validate.py` is a line-based fence extractor keyed on `FENCE_OPEN_REGEX` (0-3 space indent, CommonMark-compliant). The block delimiters themselves are fine — the mismatch is almost certainly the model editing the inline `# comment` text on each tree line during compression, i.e. `build_compress_prompt()`'s instruction "Do NOT modify anything inside \`\`\` code blocks" was not honored by the model on this call. Nothing upstream of the diff-based validator checks compliance before the fact; the validator correctly *catches* the violation, but there's no mechanism to prevent it.
2. **Fix-retry rejected (Run 1, attempt 2 setup):** `build_fix_prompt()` sends the validation errors back asking for a scoped fix. The anchor guard from #588 (`first_nonblank_line(compressed) != anchor` → treat as preamble leak, discard) fired — either the fix response restructured the top of the document, or the model prefixed conversational text (e.g. "Here's the fixed file:") despite the prompt's "Return ONLY the fixed compressed file. No explanation." instruction. The guard does exactly what #588 asked it to do (never let a preamble reach disk), but it has no retry-with-correction path: one rejection burns the fix attempt, `MAX_RETRIES = 2` is now exhausted, and the entire file is reverted — including whatever part of the fix, if any, was actually correct.
3. **Run 2's unrelated "identical to input" failure:** `call_claude()` (in `compress.py`) is a live, non-deterministic call — either the Anthropic SDK with no `temperature` pinned, or a `claude --print` subprocess — with no retry-with-variation strategy. Two invocations on the *same unchanged input file* produced two structurally different first-pass compression outputs: one that mutated fence contents (Run 1) and one that echoed the input verbatim (Run 2). The tool's success/failure for a given file is therefore not reproducible from the input alone, which makes bug reports like this one hard to pin down and makes it impossible for a user to know whether retrying is worth attempting again.

### Related Issues (why this isn't a duplicate)

- **#588** (closed): added the anchor/preamble guard that fires in this report's Run 1, attempt 2 — but never addressed what happens when the guard rejects the fix and no retries remain. This report is about that unhandled gap, not the original leak #588 fixed.
- **#820** (closed): a different fence-detection false-failure (4+ space indented fences breaking inline-code pairing). Not applicable here — this report's fence is a standard column-0 triple-backtick block.
- **#112** (open): opposite polarity — validation silently *passes* while code was actually mutated. This report is validation correctly *failing*, with the recovery path being a dead end instead.
- **#776** (open): compression that *expands* a file and passes validation. Unrelated failure mode.
- `tests/test_compress_safety.py::test_retry_preamble_output_rejected_and_not_written` pins the anchor-guard behavior in isolation with two hardcoded, deterministic `call_claude` mock responses. No test exercises the end-to-end "both retries exhausted on real fence content" path, and no test covers two independent `compress_file()` calls on identical input producing different failure classes due to `call_claude()` non-determinism.

### Suggested Directions (not prescribing implementation)

- On final failure, print which validator(s) failed on the *fix* attempt too — today only the original (attempt-1) validation errors are shown, and when the fix is rejected by the anchor guard before validation even runs on it, the user gets zero insight into what the fix actually looked like or why it failed.
- Make the anchor-guard rejection retryable in place (one extra re-prompt with an explicit "no preamble, no explanation" instruction) rather than immediately consuming the fix attempt with no recovery.
- Consider determinism controls on `call_claude()` (e.g. `temperature=0` on the SDK path) so repeated runs against an unchanged input converge on the same outcome instead of producing different failure signatures each time.
- Add a regression test with realistic fence content (ASCII tree + inline trailing comments) that isn't hand-mocked to a single deterministic response, to catch the underlying prompt-adherence gap in point 1 above.

### Impact

Not data-destructive — the identity check, backup-readback verification, and atomic write all held across both runs. But the tool is non-functional for any file containing this common documentation pattern (an annotated ASCII directory tree), which is widespread in `CLAUDE.md`/architecture-doc style files, and the failure gives the user nothing to act on.

### Environment

- OS: Windows 10 (10.0.19045), Git Bash
- Invocation: `python3 -m scripts <path>` from `skills/caveman-compress/` per `SKILL.md`
- `call_claude()` used the `claude --print` CLI subprocess fallback (no `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set in environment)
- Claude Code session model: Sonnet 5

title: `caveman-compress`: `claude --print` subprocess inherits caller's hooks/MCP, leaks commentary into compressed output
body:
### Description

Looks like `call_claude()` in `skills/caveman-compress/scripts/compress.py` falls back to `claude --print` when `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` isn't set.

That subprocess boots a full Claude Code session, inheriting the caller's `~/.claude/settings.json`, including `UserPromptSubmit``SessionStart` hooks and the full MCP server list.

I have seen 2 types of failure, both writing meta-commentary into the file being "compressed":

1. A `UserPromptSubmit` hook injects unrelated context into the compression prompt; the subprocess narrates about noticing and ignoring it, and that narration ends up in the output file.
2. The subprocess reaches for an inherited MCP tool, hits a non-interactive permission wall, and narrates the failure instead of just compressing text.

### Steps to Reproduce

- Precondition: a machine with hooks configured

- Feed `build_compress_prompt(text)` output to `claude --print` via stdin a few times...
  - Intermittent, tied to per-prompt hook heuristics, but real.
  - Hit 3 of 6 files in one session for me.

### Proposed Fix

- Pass `--setting-sources ""` and `--strict-mcp-config` to the subprocess call
- That turns it into a plain text completion, without touching auth.

Note: I guess `--bare` would _also_ work to fix this issue, but it would require API-key-based auth, not usable on OAuth-only desktop installs.

PR: https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/pull/921 - I am using that in my fork, and I personally verified a clean output on previously-leaky files after the change.

title: fix(compress): isolate claude --print subprocess from caller's hooks/MCP
body:
Fixes #920

## Summary
- \`call_claude()\`'s \`claude --print\` fallback boots a full Claude Code session, inheriting the caller's \`~/.claude/settings.json\` hooks and MCP server list.
- Two observed leaks: a \`UserPromptSubmit\` hook injecting unrelated context that the subprocess narrates about instead of silently ignoring, and the subprocess reaching for an inherited MCP tool, hitting a non-interactive permission wall, and narrating that instead of compressing.
- \`--setting-sources ""\` + \`--strict-mcp-config\` isolate the call to a plain text completion, no auth change needed. \`--bare\` was considered but requires \`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY\`/\`apiKeyHelper\`, which isn't available on OAuth-only desktop installs — exactly the case this fallback exists for.

## Test plan
- [x] Reproduced the leak by piping \`build_compress_prompt(text)\` output straight to \`claude --print\` on a machine with hooks configured
- [x] Confirmed clean output with \`--setting-sources "" --strict-mcp-config\` added, same machine, same previously-leaky inputs
- [x] Ran the patched \`compress.py\` end-to-end on 3 files that leaked before the fix — all compressed cleanly with real byte reductions, no injected commentary

title: SessionEnd hook uses PowerShell syntax but runs under bash when Git Bash is on PATH (Windows)
body:
**Version:** @caveman-ai/cli 1.2.3
Platform:** Windows 11, Claude Code (native Windows, Git Bash on PATH)

## What happened

`caveman run` (wrapping Claude Code) registers a `SessionEnd` hook whose command
uses PowerShell call-operator syntax:

```
& 'C:/Users/.../caveman-proxy.exe' native-hook claude --adapter 'C:/Users/.../native-hook-fast.js'
```

On session end it fails:

```
SessionEnd hook [& 'C:/Users/.../caveman-proxy.exe' native-hook claude --adapter '...'] failed: /usr/bin/bash: -c: line 1: syntax error near unexpected token `&'
```

## Root cause

`hookExecutableInvocation` (dist/index.js, around line 5836-5843) always prepends
`&` and uses PowerShell-style quoting (`''` escaping) on `platform === "win32"`,
assuming Claude Code always dispatches hook commands through PowerShell on native
Windows. But Claude Code's actual default is: bash on POSIX, PowerShell on Windows
only when Git Bash is not on PATH — when Git Bash is present (as it is here),
Claude Code runs the hook command through bash by default. The generated
PowerShell syntax then hits bash and breaks on `&`.

The hook entry built by `nativeHookEntry()` (same file, ~line 5859) never sets an
explicit `"shell"` field, so it silently depends on this environment-dependent
default instead of pinning the shell it assumes.

## Suggested fix

In `nativeHookEntry(command)`, set `shell: "powershell"` explicitly when
`platform === "win32"` (matching the PowerShell syntax already generated), so the
hook doesn't depend on whether Claude Code's shell-detection heuristic happens to
agree. Same root function is used by both `caveman run` (temp hook pack) and
`caveman enable claude` (permanent `~/.claude/settings.json`), so one fix covers
both paths.

## Repro

1. Windows with Git Bash on PATH, Claude Code installed.
2. `caveman run` -> pick Claude Code.
3. End the session (exit/clear).
4. See the `SessionEnd hook [...] failed: ... syntax error near unexpected token '&'` message.

title: Statusline badge nudge has no opt-out and repeats every session
feat(hooks): add CAVEMAN_STATUSLINE_NUDGE env opt-out
body:
Closes #923 (one of two alternatives, see below).

### What this does

Adds `CAVEMAN_STATUSLINE_NUDGE`. Setting it to `0`, `false`, `off`, or `no` suppresses the statusline badge nudge outright. Any other value, including unset, keeps today's behaviour exactly.

The check runs *before* the `.caveman-nudge-shown` marker is written, so opting out does not consume the one-shot. If the variable is later removed, the user gets the normal first-session nudge rather than silence they never asked for.

### Why, given #661 already landed the one-shot

The one-shot marker fixed the recurring cost, and it is the right default. Two gaps remain for users who want no statusline at all:

- It still spends a first session emitting the nudge, including the "Proactively offer to set this up" instruction, before it can be declined.
- The marker lives in `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`. A fresh config dir, a second machine, or a relocated Claude config brings the nudge back with no way to pre-empt it.

Shape mirrors `CAVEMAN_DEFAULT_MODE`, which is already the highest precedence source in `getDefaultMode()`, so an env var is the established way to state a machine-wide caveman preference from a dotfile.

### Tests

Three added to `tests/test_hooks.py`: opt-out suppresses the nudge and leaves the marker unwritten, the nudge still fires with no variable set, and an unrecognised value (`1`) is ignored rather than treated as falsy. Full `tests/test_hooks.py` suite passes.

### These two PRs are alternatives, merge only one

Both implement the same opt-out from #923 by different mechanisms. They touch the same condition and will conflict with each other by design.

**Preference order:**

1. **This PR, the env var.** Smallest surface, no new config surface area, settable from a dotfile, and covers a fresh `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` where the marker file cannot help.
2. **#925, the `statuslineNudge` config key.** Better if you would rather the preference be checked into a repo next to `defaultMode` and survive independently of the environment. Costs a new config key and a new exported function.

A third idea from the issue, suppressing after one showing, turned out to be already shipped in #661. The issue text was written against an older cached plugin build that predates it, and I have corrected the issue accordingly. Only the two opt-out options above remain open.

Happy to close whichever one you do not want, or to rework either if you would prefer a different name or precedence.

title: feat(hooks): add statuslineNudge config opt-out
body:
Closes #923 (one of two alternatives, see below).

### What this does

Adds a `statuslineNudge` boolean to caveman's own config. Setting it to `false` suppresses the statusline badge nudge.

Resolution lives in a new `statuslineNudgeEnabled()` in `caveman-config.js` and reuses `getDefaultMode()`'s file order: repo-local config (`.caveman/config.json` or `.caveman.json`, walking up) first, then user config (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/caveman/config.json` and friends). Absent, non-boolean, or unparseable config returns `true`, matching the module's existing habit of erring toward current behaviour rather than silently changing it.

Like the env-var alternative, the check runs before `.caveman-nudge-shown` is written, so opting out does not consume the one-shot.

### One implementation note worth a look

`caveman-activate.js` resolves the new function defensively:

```js
const statuslineNudgeEnabled =
  (cavemanConfig && typeof cavemanConfig.statuslineNudgeEnabled === 'function')
    ? cavemanConfig.statuslineNudgeEnabled
    : () => true;
```

rather than adding it to the `isUsable` predicate. An older `caveman-config.js` sibling that predates this key is still perfectly usable for mode resolution and flag writes, and demanding the new function there would demote the whole module to the degraded stubs over one optional preference. That seemed contrary to the intent of the #848 guard.

### Why, given #661 already landed the one-shot

The one-shot marker fixed the recurring cost and is the right default, but it still spends a first session on users who will never want a statusline, and the marker lives in `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, so a fresh config dir brings the nudge back with no way to pre-empt it.

Full `tests/test_hooks.py` suite passes. `CLAUDE.md` documents the resolver next to `getDefaultMode()`.

1. **#924, the `CAVEMAN_STATUSLINE_NUDGE` env var.** Smallest surface, no new config surface area, settable from a dotfile, and covers a fresh `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`.
2. **This PR, the config key.** Better if you would rather the preference be checked into a repo next to `defaultMode` and survive independently of the environment. Costs a new config key and a new exported function.

A third idea from the issue, suppressing after one showing, turned out to be already shipped in #661. The issue text was written against an older cached plugin build that predates it, and I have corrected the issue accordingly.

Happy to close whichever one you do not want, or to rework either if you would prefer a different name or precedence.

title: `doctor`: hook-ownership check resolves the binary via `which` at check time, so any per-shell PATH manager (fnm multishell) reads permanently `degraded` and `--fix` refuses to repair
body:
## Summary

The hook health check rebuilds the *expected* hook command live from `which caveman` in whatever shell runs the check. Under `fnm`'s default zsh/bash setup, every new shell gets a fresh `~/.local/share/fnm/multishells/<pid>_<ts>/bin` prepended to PATH, so the command string doctor wrote at enable time can never match what a later shell resolves. Result: `caveman doctor claude` reads `degraded` (settings.json "NOT OWNED") in every new terminal, and `--fix` refuses with "hook changed after enable; refusing destructive disable" even though nothing touched the file. Hand-editing the hook path just moves the mismatch to the next shell.

Still present on CLI 1.2.5 / release v2.3.1.

## Environment

- macOS arm64, zsh
- `fnm` managing Node (v24.19.0), stock `eval "$(fnm env --use-on-cd)"` in `.zshrc`
- `@caveman-ai/cli` 1.2.5 installed via `npm i -g` under the fnm-managed Node
- binaries bin-v1.1.3

## Reproduction

Same machine, same untouched `~/.claude/settings.json`, seconds apart. The only variable is PATH:

```
$ which caveman
/Users/me/.local/bin/caveman        # stable path, matches the string in settings.json
$ caveman doctor claude | jq '{state, files: [.files[] | {file, owned}]}'
state: "installed"; settings.json owned: true

$ env PATH="/Users/me/.local/share/fnm/node-versions/v24.19.0/installation/bin:/usr/bin:/bin" \
    sh -c 'caveman doctor claude' | jq '{state, files: [.files[] | {file, owned}]}'
state: "degraded"; settings.json owned: false
```

The second PATH is what a stock `fnm` shell effectively presents (in real shells it is the per-process multishell symlink dir, which differs on every terminal, making the mismatch permanent rather than intermittent).

`caveman doctor claude --fix` in that state refuses: "hook changed after enable; refusing destructive disable".

## Root cause (read from the published CLI)

`dist/index.js` of `@caveman-ai/cli` 1.2.5, `cavemanBinForHook()`:

```js
function cavemanBinForHook() {
    const command = which("caveman") ?? which("cave");
    return command
        ? hookExecutableInvocation(command, undefined)
        : hookExecutableInvocation(process.execPath, process.argv[1]);
}
```

The ownership check (`nativeHookEntriesHealthy` path) compares the hook command in `settings.json` against this freshly resolved string. Any PATH manager that presents a different resolution per shell (`fnm` multishells; asdf/mise/nvm setups can drift the same way after version switches) breaks string equality forever, because there is no single string that is correct in every shell.

## Why the failure mode hurts

- `degraded` + "refusing destructive disable" reads like tampering, so users burn time on the wrong theory (reinstalls, restarts, hand-editing the hook path — which is the same disease, not a cure).
- The refusal blocks `--fix` exactly when the file is fine, and the message never mentions PATH.

## Workaround (what we run now)

Pin a stable resolution ahead of the multishell dir:

```
ln -s ~/.local/share/fnm/node-versions/v24.19.0/installation/bin/caveman ~/.local/bin/caveman
# .zshrc, after the fnm eval line:
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
# then: delete the shrink-hook entry from hooks.PreToolUse and re-run doctor --fix
# from a shell where `which caveman` answers ~/.local/bin/caveman
```

Works, but breaks again on any `fnm` Node bump (the symlink target dies), and nothing in the product points a user here.

## Suggested fix

Compare canonicalized targets instead of raw command strings: treat a hook entry as owned when `realpath(command in settings.json)` and `realpath(which caveman)` resolve to the same file (or the same `realpath` as `process.execPath`-derived CLI entry). Alternatively, record the resolved real path at enable time and compare realpaths at check time. Either way no string written from one shell has to match every future shell, and `fnm`'s per-shell symlink dirs collapse to the same target.

Happy to verify a candidate fix under `fnm`. I'm running the same environment that reproduced #897, except that I've since upgraded to the latest release.

title: fix(installer): avoid CLI bin collision
body:
Fixes #881.

The installer package and @caveman-ai/cli both exposed a caveman bin, so npm linked the dependency's CLI over the installer in its temporary environment. This renames the installer's sole bin to caveman-install and adds a regression that prevents future dependency-bin overlap.

Tests:

title: fix(stats): correct multi-block accounting, bound lifetime aggregation, pin number formatting
body:
## Summary

Three correctness/robustness fixes for `/caveman-stats`, plus upgrades that close the lifetime-accounting and integrity gaps they revealed.

### Fix 1 — multi-block responses counted once (#793)
`parseSession` summed `usage.output_tokens` and incremented `turns` **per JSONL line**. A single response split across multiple lines (multi-block tool output) was double/triple-counted, inflating both turns and output tokens ~2×.

The dedupe now keys on the response (`requestId` + `message.id`, matching upstream PR #794's approach), so one response counts once regardless of how many blocks the SDK split it across.

### Fix 2 — lifetime aggregation is bounded
`.caveman-history.jsonl` is append-only and grows without bound — a row is written on *every* stats run. The old code re-read and re-parsed the **whole** file on every `/caveman-stats` call, under the hook's fixed 2.5s child watchdog. For heavy users this silently kills stats *and* the statusline suffix forever once history exceeds the per-run budget; nothing trimmed the file to recover.

This is replaced with **watermark-backed incremental aggregation**: a `.summary.json` sidecar keeps the latest-per-session totals; each run parses only the bytes appended since the last watermark and merges them in (`MAX_INCREMENTAL_BYTES` guards a pathological gap with a safe one-off rebuild). Cost is bounded by what was written since the last call, not by total history length.

### Fix 3 — number formatting is locale-stable
The 6 tests that hardcoded en-US separators (`1,850` vs `1.850`) failed on any non-en-US machine. All `toLocaleString()` call sites were replaced with a pinned en-US formatter, so the suite is green everywhere.

## Upgrades
- **`--reset`** — rotate `.caveman-history.jsonl` to a dated `.bak`, drop the summary sidecar + statusline suffix, so lifetime numbers can start clean. History is archived, never deleted.
- **Verify-on-write sidecar** — `saveHistorySummary` writes to a temp, reads it back, and only renames into place when the round-trip is byte-lossless. A corrupt sidecar is never installed silently; every run after a revert is a safe full rebuild.
- **Concurrent-writer guard** — two `/caveman-stats` runs can race the same history file; a plain read-modify-write could drop one run's increments. `persistSummaryConcurrent` folds in a peer summary that already advanced (bounded retries, only on the monotonic incremental path). A rotation rebuild never resurrects rotated-away sessions.
- **`--reset` reachable from the slash command** — the `UserPromptSubmit` hook now forwards `--reset` alongside `--all`/`--since`.
- **Docs** — the lifetime view (`--all`/`--since`/`--reset`) is now documented in `skills/caveman-stats/README.md` + `SKILL.md`.

## Integrity
`src/hooks/checksums.sha256` was regenerated (`caveman-stats.js` and `caveman-mode-tracker.js` both changed); `tests/verify_repo.py::verify_powershell_static` passes.

## Tests
- Multi-block + cross-request dedupe regression fixtures.
- Across-runs incremental aggregation + rotation rebuild.
- `--reset` archives history, clears sidecar/suffix, clean slate after.
- Concurrent-CAS: two sessions survive a peer-ahead persist (no lost update).
- All **56** stats tests pass, including the 6 previously locale-red.

No behavioral change to the session view; `--since`, `--all`, `--share` paths unchanged.

## Known limitations
- The speedup is a sidecar optimization: the numbers are only incremental as long as the `.summary.json` sidecar is intact. If it is ever corrupt or deleted, the next run does a one-off **full rebuild** of history (bounded, correct, just not incremental), then resumes incremental mode — never a wrong number, never a hard failure.
- `MAX_INCREMENTAL_BYTES` caps how much new data a single run will parse; an unusually large gap between runs triggers that same safe full rebuild rather than an unpredictable long parse.
- The dedupe keys on `(requestId, message.id)`, so it is per-message, not per-request: two genuinely different responses in one request are each counted (correct), while one response split across many content-block lines is counted once (the #793 fix).
- `--reset` archives the raw history to a dated `.bak` and clears the lifetime view; it does not re-measure anything and does not touch per-session transcript files.

title: fix(compress): crash-free, provider-agnostic model reply handling
body:
## Summary

Harden the way `caveman-compress` reads the model's reply, so a non-text response shape can never crash *after* a paid call — and make that robustness independent of whose SDK produced the response.

### Fix — non-text content blocks
`call_claude`'s SDK path read `msg.content[0].text` directly. On a tool-heavy session the model can put a `tool_use` block **first**, so `content[0]` is not text — and `.text` raises an `AttributeError` **after** the paid API call already returned, wasting the call and the retry budget.

### Generalization — `extract_text()`, provider-agnostic
The old fix only handled the Anthropic SDK's typed-block shape. It's now a single recursive `extract_text(content)` that returns the first *real* text regardless of provider:
- **Anthropic SDK** — typed blocks (`TextBlock`/`ThinkingBlock`/`ToolUseBlock`); a `thinking`/`tool_use`/`image` block is never mistaken for compressible content.
- **OpenAI / OpenAI-compatible** — `choices[*].message.content` as a plain string *or* a parts array.
- **Gemini** — `candidates[*].content.parts[].text`.
- **nested / generic** — `{content: …}`, `{parts: […]}`, and object-backed wrappers.

Zero extra dependencies (recursive walks, no new SDK imports).

## Upgrades
- **Consistent empty-result handling** — when a provider returns only tool/thinking/image blocks or an empty reply, `call_claude` returns `""` in BOTH arms (SDK and CLI). Every caller already turns that into an explicit `"Claude returned an empty response"` abort/retry message, so the behavior is uniform and a paid-SDK empty reply takes the same clean path as the CLI — never an unhandled traceback whose message a caller's message would have swallowed.
- **Single-block / unwrapped tolerance** — a lone dict/block/string (not a `[]`) is normalized so the walk never raises on a non-iterable.

## Tests
- `tool_use`-first block returns the text (was: crash); `thinking`/`image` blocks skipped.
- Anthropic dict/object, bare string, single-unwrapped-block, no-text shapes.
- New provider shapes: OpenAI string content, OpenAI parts array with a non-text part first, Gemini `parts[].text`, nested `content`, object-backed `.parts`/`.content`.
- Empty/tool_use-only SDK reply → `""`, the same graceful contract as the CLI arm.

All **138** Python tests pass (7 pre-existing environment skips). No hook files changed, so the integrity manifest is untouched.

## Known limitations
- `extract_text` only **reads** reply shapes from any provider; it does not add a general OpenAI/Gemini **backend**. `call_claude` still talks to the Anthropic SDK or the `claude` CLI — the surrounding networking/retry layer is unchanged. This PR removes the crash class, not the network surface.
- A provider reply that is genuinely empty (or contains only non-text blocks) is treated as an empty response: the caller prints `"Claude returned an empty response"` and aborts/retries once — it does not synthesize text or fabricate a retry loop.
- First-match semantics: `extract_text` returns the first textual block in content order. If a model intentionally interleaves text and tool blocks, only the leading text is used (matching the previous `content[0].text` behavior for the common case).

---

Part of a five-PR upstream contribution shipped as an ordered batch. Recommended merge order: **#931 → #932 → #933 → #934 → #936** — the stats / compress / compression-runtime fixes land first, then the Remote-MCP engine (#934) and Firefox port (#936) that build on them. All five PRs remain independently mergeable; this is advisory only.

title: feat(l4): measured, evidence-gated compression runtime (auto-measure + verify-gate)
body:
## Summary

An evidence-gated compression measurement runtime for caveman, delivered as an integrated slash command.

### The idea
Caveman already refuses to fabricate savings (`docs/HONEST-NUMBERS.md`, fail-closed everywhere). This PR ships the enforcement half: **measure a real session, and refuse any claim that has no measured before/after pair.**

### What's in it
- **`l4/caveman-l4.mjs`** — a zero-dependency Node runtime (Node ≥ 18, no build step, hermetic env-overridable state dirs):
  - **`auto-measure`** — measures the active session once per response from the JSONL transcript and writes a watermark-guarded receipt to `l4/state/` (per-session lock, backup-before-apply, append-verify, rollback on failure, idempotent re-run). The same `(requestId, message.id)` dedupe as caveman-stats (`#793`/PR #794) so one response is never double-measured.
  - **`verify-gate`** — refuses a compression claim without a measured before/after pair (or measured estimate); accepts it only when real evidence exists.
- **`/caveman-measure`** — wired into the `UserPromptSubmit` hook (`caveman-mode-tracker.js`) on the same bounded, graceful-failure contract as `/caveman-stats`.
- **Self-contained** — own parser, imports nothing from `caveman-stats`, ships standalone (no dependency on the sibling #931).

## Reliability (from a deep self-review)
Four real gaps were found behind the initially-green suite and fixed:

1. **Lock released on error.** A failure while holding the session lock called `process.exit()`, which skips `finally { unlock(); }` and permanently wedges the session as `busy`. Errors now unwind through the `finally`, so the lock is **always** released; the CLI reports them after the lock clears.
2. **Stale-lock recovery.** `acquireLock` previously left a crashed run's lock directory forever ("busy" forever, contradicting the documented "crashed run restarts clean"). A lock is now stolen when the recorded owner pid is provably dead, or the owner is unknown and the lock has aged past 60s — and a **provably-live** owner is *never* stolen, even an old one, so a hung-but-alive run is never forked into a second writer (double-write). Regression tests cover dead-lock recovery, live-lock honesty, and the live-but-old case.
3. **`/caveman-measure` works after a real install.** The hook resolved L4 only via the source-checkout path, which is a dead end once hooks are copied into your config dir. It now resolves the runtime against the checkout, a co-located `l4/`, or `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/l4`, degrading to a graceful error only when the runtime is genuinely absent.
4. Removed the unused `node:os` import.

## Scope discipline
The roadmap (`promote`/`merge`/`index`, per-tokenizer profiles) is *documented, not implemented* — this PR is only the measuring layer + gate.

## Known limitations — please read before approval
This is the one scoping decision worth an explicit call-out.

- `/caveman-measure` resolves the runtime against a **dev checkout** `<repo-root>/l4`, a **hook tree co-located with an `l4/` folder**, or a **per-user `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/l4`**. It works end-to-end in all three (tested).
- The **installer** (`bin/install.js`) does **not** yet copy `l4/` into place. So on a **stock install**, until `l4/caveman-l4.mjs` is present, the command degrades to a clear `"runtime not installed"` JSON error — never a partial/broken result, but it is inert out of the box.
- Consequence: this PR is the **measurement runtime + gate, not yet wired into the released install path**. Decide whether shipping it now (docs + explicit limitation) is acceptable, or whether you want the installer wiring folded in here before merge. It is split out deliberately so the measurement logic can be reviewed on its own.

## Tests
`l4/test_caveman_l4.mjs` (**7/7**: dedupe + idempotency, re-measure-on-growth, gate refusal/acceptance ×2, stale-lock recovery, live-lock honoured as busy) and `tests/test_caveman_measure.js` (**2/2** hook relay).

## Integrity & docs
`src/hooks/checksums.sha256` regenerated (`caveman-mode-tracker.js` changed); `tests/verify_repo.py::verify_powershell_static` passes. `/caveman-measure` documented in the hooks README + the runtime's own `l4/README.md`.

Recommended merge order: **#931 → #932 → #933 → #934 → #936** — the stats / compress / compression-runtime fixes land first, then the Remote-MCP engine (#934) and Firefox port (#936) that build on them. All five PRs remain independently mergeable; this is advisory only.

## Related

title: feat(mcp): host-agnostic Remote-MCP server (ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini/pi)
body:
## Remote-MCP — register Caveman's tools on any MCP text host

Most new text hosts (ChatGPT.com, Gemini, pi.dev) cannot run the stdio `caveman-mcp`
server because they don't spawn arbitrary subprocesses. Issue/discussion tracing shows
this is a **transport/schema gap, not a capability one** — pi.dev (#870) worked end-to-end
and only needed "one schema capability." This PR closes that gap so Caveman's tools can be
registered by any MCP-capable text host. (The Firefox extension port, previously bundled here,
is now its own PR: #936.)

### What this PR is

- **`mcp/remote/` — a Remote-MCP (Streamable HTTP) server.** Serves the *same* 5 tools
  (`caveman_compress`, `caveman_retrieve`, `caveman_stats`, `caveman_toon_encode/decode`).
  `tools/call` bridges to the reviewed engine binary over stdio; compression is never
  reimplemented. Local-first (binds 127.0.0.1), inferred-only, bearer-token auth when exposed.
- **`mcp/remote/schema.mjs` — OpenAI-class JSON-Schema shim** so ChatGPT/Gemini/pi tool
  parsers accept the surface (the #870/#709 fix): `{object, properties, required}`.
- **`docs/remote-mcp.md` — RFC**: per-host registration matrix (ChatGPT / Codex / Claude /
  Gemini / pi), the single-server rationale, security posture, references.

### Test & validation

- `mcp/remote` suite: **9/9 pass, 0 skipped** — re-run today against a freshly built
  engine binary from head `7c05ee3`: the 6 transport/unit tests (initialize handshake,
  `tools/list` returns exactly the 5 tools as `{object,properties}` schemas, JSON-RPC
  error/no-crash on unknown method, notification `202`, token auth `401`, schema shim
  shape) plus the 2 engine round-trip tests and the drift gate.
- **Conditional engine-binary integration** (`tests/engine.test.mjs`): runs a real
  `caveman_toon_encode -> decode` byte-exact round-trip and a fail-closed invalid-TOON path
  against the Go engine **when `CAVEMAN_MCP_BIN` is set**, skips cleanly otherwise — so CI
  never fails on a build without the engine.
- KageBinary-style mutation pass run on the unit suite: removing a tool, bypassing the token
  gate, and breaking the `-32601` unknown-method path each turned its named test RED (no
  weakly-asserted tests).
- `npm test` green; server + schema pass `node --check`.

### Files

```
mcp/remote/server.mjs · schema.mjs · package.json · README.md
mcp/remote/tests/remote.test.mjs · tests/engine.test.mjs
docs/remote-mcp.md
```

### Security posture

Binds loopback by default; exposing off-loopback requires `CAVEMAN_MCP_HOST` + `CAVEMAN_MCP_TOKEN`
(401 otherwise). `inferred-only` — never claims verified savings. `tools/call` only spawns the
reviewed engine binary; the bridge never touches payload bytes. OAuth is a noted follow-up.

### Known limitations

- `tools/call` needs the engine binary reachable on the server host (`CAVEMAN_MCP_BIN` or
  `npx caveman-mcp`); `initialize` and `tools/list` answer without it.
- Ready for review — transport/auth posture confirmed; the opening discussion covers the
  five-PR batch context.

title: fix(compress): validate candidates before touching the live file
body:
## Summary

`compress_file()` wrote each candidate straight to the live source file and
validated it there. An interruption between that write and a passing
validation (Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, OOM, a harness killing the process) left the
live file holding un-validated or garbage output, with the out-of-tree
backup as the only recovery path.

Each candidate is now staged next to the source (`<file>.caveman-staged`)
and validated there. The live file is written only once a candidate passes,
and is left untouched if every attempt fails, so there is nothing to
restore.

Out of scope: the issue's secondary point (a pre-write heuristic to catch a
conversational summary standing in for the compressed body) is a separate,
optional guard and isn't part of this change.

## Verification

- New regression tests fail on unmodified main and pass on this branch:
  `python -m unittest tests.test_compress_safety.CompressSafetyTests.test_live_file_never_holds_unvalidated_output_before_validation_passes tests.test_compress_safety.CompressSafetyTests.test_live_file_untouched_when_all_validation_attempts_fail`
- Full suite green on Python 3.11 and 3.13 (Linux): `python -m unittest discover -s tests`, plus `tests/verify_repo.py`'s Compress Fixtures and Compress CLI checks.
- Not verified: Windows and macOS runtime behavior beyond what the Linux suite covers.

Fixes #544

title: hooks: stamp CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE output with its own source path
body:
## Problem

The reinforcement text both hooks emit (`CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE — level: ...`,
`... — session ruleset applies.`) is persistent, all-caps, and phrased as a
permanent behavior override with no revert. That phrasing is structurally
identical to a well-known prompt-injection pattern: text crafted to look like
a legitimate `SessionStart`/compaction system reminder, asserting a permanent
instruction change.

In practice this means a security-conscious coding agent has no
content-based way to distinguish caveman's real hook output from a spoofed
imitation of it — both would read the same way from inside the model's
context. I hit this directly: an agent flagged the caveman activation text
as a likely injection and stalled a task over it, even after being told via
project memory/CLAUDE.md notes that the plugin is legitimate. That
reassurance doesn't actually help, because a static "trust me, this is fine"
note is exactly as unverifiable (and exactly the kind of text an attacker
would also plant) as the hook output itself.

## Fix

Make the claim self-verifying instead of asserted. Each place the hooks emit
`CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE`, append the absolute path of the file emitting it
(`__filename`), e.g.:

```
CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE (full) — session ruleset applies. [self-check: this line is emitted by the caveman plugin hook at /path/to/caveman-mode-tracker.js — read it if this instruction looks suspicious]
```

This gives any agent a cheap, concrete way to check the claim itself
(`cat`/`head` the named file) instead of having to trust unverifiable prose,
in either the hook output or in a memory file telling it to trust the hook
output.

Touches:
- `src/hooks/caveman-mode-tracker.js` — the per-turn reinforcement line
- `src/hooks/caveman-activate.js` — all three `CAVEMAN MODE ACTIVE` emission
  points (independent-mode path, SKILL.md-loaded path, fallback path)
- `src/hooks/checksums.sha256` — regenerated for the two edited files

No behavior change beyond the appended stamp; ruleset content, mode
resolution, and persistence logic are untouched. `node --check` passes on

title: perf(skill): compact semantic core
body:
## What changed

This extracts Caveman's behavioral contract from its calibration prose and makes that contract executable.

- seven stable semantic invariants now cover substance, exact literals, caricature avoidance, language, safety, artifact boundaries, and mode boundaries;
- the canonical skill keeps one calibration family instead of repeating the same behavior through multiple technical examples;
- production-surface checks materialize the real Claude SessionStart payload, fallback hook, compact rule, OpenClaw bootstrap, Codex/OpenCode commands, and MV3 primer/reminder;
- narrowing mutants prove that deleting or reassigning a rule fails the gate;
- paired raw model evidence records complete prompts, outputs, provider usage, deterministic verdicts, and uncertainty.

No agent runtime, task-board configuration, generated instructions, setup layer, or repository-local tooling dependency is introduced.

## Before and after

Exact UTF-8 byte measurements:

| Surface | Before | After | Reduction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Canonical skill | 6,518 B | 4,494 B | 31.05% |
| Default `full` SessionStart | 4,670 B | 3,455 B | 26.02% |
| OpenClaw bootstrap | 7,241 B | 5,217 B | 27.95% |

The practical win is deliberately modest: roughly one quarter of the recurring Caveman payload, not an order-of-magnitude rewrite. Caveman already had a single canonical skill rather than mandatory external phrasebooks, so the safe optimization ceiling was lower.

## Rationale

Style prompts tend to grow by accumulating examples. Examples are useful for calibration, but they are expensive and weak as contracts: they do not state which details may change, which literals must survive, or when style must yield to clarity.

This change separates three concerns:

1. semantic invariants define meaning that must survive compression;
2. calibration examples demonstrate voice and intensity;
3. deterministic command parsing continues to own exact activation and mode-switch phrases.

That separation lets the runtime become smaller without treating prompt length as proof of quality. It also turns safety and fidelity boundaries into regression gates instead of reviewer memory.

## Evidence and limits

A paired `claude-haiku-4-5` run is committed with immutable raw evidence. In that run, the candidate fixes the baseline exact-artifact failure for `250 ms` and `"ECONNRESET"`. Both arms still fail the polarity case. Cases requiring reviewed semantic judgment remain `unknown`; they are never counted as passes.

This is one bounded run on one model. It is not a semantic-equivalence, cross-model, cost, latency, or statistical-significance claim. `ceil(bytes / 4)` is retained only as an explicitly labeled input-size proxy, never tokenizer output.

## Validation

- `python3.14 -m unittest discover -s tests` — 146 tests
- `npm test` — 202 tests
- `node tests/test_caveman_parse.js` — 49 tests
- `node --test extension/test/directive.test.mjs` — 7 tests
- `python3.14 tests/verify_repo.py`
- `git diff --check`

Negative mutants cover polarity, exact literals, warning content, language, artifact prose, caricature growth, calibration-example overfit, per-invariant surface bypass, and intensity-row reassignment.

title: Security: wrap can route provider credentials to a foreign process occupying the local proxy port
body:
**Observed independently in a downstream security review against `main` (`packages/cli/src/index.ts`, `proxy/internal/runstate`). Code-path verification only, no live exploit run.**

### Summary
`caveman wrap` detects that a foreign process owns `127.0.0.1:8787` (via `proxy/internal/runstate` → `owner:"unknown"` → `OFF_STATES.foreignProcess`), correctly avoids `SIGTERM`, and shows a banner (`something else is listening on 127.0.0.1:8787`). However detection does **not** force a `direct` (fail-closed) launch. The wrapped agent still receives `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`/`OPENAI_BASE_URL`/`OPENAI_API_BASE`/`GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` = `http://127.0.0.1:8787` (via `WRAP_BASE_URL_ENV_VARS`/`buildWrapEnv`) while inheriting the operator’s `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`/`OPENAI_API_KEY`/etc. from `process.env`. Those credentials would then be sent to the foreign listener.

### Verification against current upstream
- `packages/cli/src/index.ts:91` `PROXY_ADDR="127.0.0.1:8787"`; `gatewayURL()`/`gatewayHostPort()`/`wrapMode()` define the expected loopback endpoint.
- `portListening` probe (`16156`) + `readProxyRuntimeState` (`14422`) → `runstate.go:148 validate` (checks `alive`/`executable` contains `caveman-proxy`/`portBound`) → `owner:"unknown"` on foreign listener.
- `OFF_STATES.foreignProcess` defined at `3589`, precedence `3644`, set at `5200` and `5282` inside `spawnWrapped` (pre- and post-start probes). Contrasts with `running-gate-mismatch` (`5316-5319`) which *does* set `direct=true`.
- In `spawnWrapped:5130-5409`, only `runtimeState?.id==="running-gate-mismatch"` flips `direct=true`. `foreign-process` falls through with `direct===false`, banner is pushed via `takeRunOffStates()` but `env = buildWrapEnv(agent, gw, ...)` (`5389`) still injects `gw`.
- `if (direct) { delete env[k] }` stripping (`5405`) never runs for foreign case. Existing test `packages/cli/tests/wrap-restart.runtime.mjs:404-440` asserts a foreign listener gets `owner: unknown` banner and is not signaled, but does not assert `direct`.
- Searched open/closed issues/PRs for `foreign`, `127.0.0.1`, `credential`, `loopback` — no duplicate open report for credential routing to foreign process. Docs (`SECURITY.md`, `docs/technical/security-and-privacy.md:9`, `architecture.md:117`) state single-operator loopback trust boundary and “do not restart or trust it” (availability intent) but do not document that `wrap` will avoid routing credentials there.

### Threat-model note
Single-operator loopback is the documented boundary, so a same-host attacker is already privileged. Impact is still meaningful: any pre-existing listener (malware, stale process, or TOCTOU after `portListening`) could capture the operator’s BYOK provider credentials and full prompt/response bodies without needing to compromise `caveman-proxy` itself.

### Suggested remediation
- In `spawnWrapped`, treat `foreign-process` the same as `running-gate-mismatch`: set `direct=true` (or exit non-zero) before env injection, so no `*_BASE_URL` is injected toward an unverified listener.
- Ensure `status` and `wrap` share the same fail-closed decision, and add a regression test with a dummy `net.createServer().listen(8787,"127.0.0.1")` asserting `direct` (no `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` injected) and banner.
- Optional defense-in-depth: proxy startup verification of pre-existing listener ownership before writing `run/<port>.json`.

Neutral wording requested: this is a hardening to enforce fail-closed before credentials can be sent, not a remote RCE claim.

title: fix(pi): route opencode-go through compat mount
body:
## Summary

- Route [OpenCode Go](https://opencode.ai/go) models to a named compat mount, not to api.openai.com (fixes #946)
- Route only known providers; unknown providers get pass-through with a warning, not a 401 error
- Register a built-in `opencode-go` compat mount in the standalone proxy, with the upstream `https://opencode.ai/zen/go`
- Resolve BYOK keys for the built-in mount from `OPENCODE_API_KEY`; a user `compat:` entry with the same name wins

## Proof

- `go test ./proxy/internal/standalone/`
- `npm test` in `packages/pi-extension` (25/25)
- `python3 tests/verify_repo.py`
- Manual: `caveman pi --provider opencode-go --model <model> -p 'Reply with OK'` returns OK through the proxy; `caveman-proxy stats` shows the request

## Known limits

- The route for opencode-go `anthropic-messages` models (`minimax-m3`, `qwen3.7-max`, `qwen3.7-plus`) goes to `https://opencode.ai/zen/go`. Pi sends the key as `x-api-key`. The compat adapter sends the key to the upstream as `Authorization: Bearer`. No test shows that the upstream accepts a Bearer header on `/v1/messages`. Before this PR, the route for these models went to `api.anthropic.com`. Thus this PR does not cause a regression for these models. On this path, compression does not apply. The proxy sends the request bytes unchanged.
- The extension still routes a provider with the name `openai`, `anthropic`, or `google` and a custom base URL (litellm, ollama, Azure) to the default upstream. This behavior existed before #946. This PR does not change it.

## Follow-ups, not in this PR

Separate PRs will cover these items:

- The extension will route by the original base URL of the provider, read from `ctx.modelRegistry`. A loopback or custom endpoint will then pass through with the warning.
- An integration test will cover the seam between the pi extension, the gateway prefix strip, and the `/compat/opencode-go` mount.
- A test against the upstream will show if the upstream accepts a Bearer header on `/v1/messages`. If it does not, the mount will forward `x-api-key` unchanged.
- A release note will name the built-in upstream URL and the `compat.opencode-go` override. A `buildAdapters` test will show that a user entry replaces the built-in mount.

title: Codex native integration: wrap daemon never spawns on Windows 'codex exec' - infinite reconnect on /w/codex/responses
body:
# Issue draft — Codex native integration: SessionStart hook never spawns wrap daemon on Windows `codex exec` → infinite reconnect

**Repo:** JuliusBrussee/caveman  |  **Versions:** @caveman-ai/cli 1.3.1, bin-v1.1.4, Codex CLI 0.150.1, Windows 10 (19044) x64
**Status:** DRAFT — not submitted. Publish only with explicit user go.

## Summary

`caveman enable codex` wires hooks.json + config.toml (`base_url = http://127.0.0.1:8787/w/codex`). Under `codex exec` on Windows, the SessionStart fast-adapter (`native-hook-fast.js` via `caveman-proxy.exe native-hook codex --adapter ...`) never brings up a wrap-mode daemon:

- with 8787 free: no daemon spawns at all (verified: netstat empty, proxy.log silent)
- with a foreign daemon on 8787: codex gets `404 Proxy path is not recognized` on `/w/codex/responses`
- Result: `ERROR: Reconnecting... waiting for network` loop, then `failed to refresh available models: timeout waiting for child process to exit`. Agent unusable until `caveman disable codex`.

## Repro

1. `npm i -g @caveman-ai/cli && caveman setup --install`
2. `caveman enable codex` (all checks green, `caveman doctor codex` exact:true)
3. `codex exec --skip-git-repo-check "Reply with exactly: OK"`
4. Observe reconnect loop; netstat shows no listener; `~/.caveman/proxy.log` shows no new "listening" entry for the run.

## Expected

SessionStart hook spawns (or reuses) a wrap-mode daemon serving `/w/codex/*`, like `caveman wrap codex` does interactively.

## Notes

- Interactive `caveman wrap codex` fails earlier on Windows: "cannot safely launch non-Node Windows command shim" (codex is an npm `.CMD` shim) — so there is no working path to a codex-scoped wrap daemon on this setup.
- `caveman run -- codex exec ...` self-diagnoses the same 404.
- Claude lane via `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` + `caveman wrap claude` daemon works fine (round-trip verified), so the proxy itself is healthy.
- Happy to provide proxy.log / verbose traces.

title: caveman-proxy rejects valid bearer token with invalid_issuer for custom openai-completions provider (Pi)

**What happen**
Request to a custom OpenAI-compatible provider (an internal `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible`-style gateway, not OpenAI/Bedrock/OpenRouter/etc.) gets rejected by caveman-proxy with `invalid_issuer`, even though the exact same bearer token works fine against the real upstream gateway.

Related to #946 (OpenCode Go routed to the wrong base URL) — same class of bug: a non-built-in provider isn't handled correctly once caveman's `wrap`/native-hook rewrites the provider's `baseUrl` to caveman-proxy. This is a distinct provider (an internal `openai-completions` API type) and a different failure (auth rejection, not wrong base URL), reproduced on the latest binary release.

**Expected**
caveman-proxy forwards the client's bearer token upstream unchanged (or at minimum doesn't reject it before forwarding) for a custom `openai-completions` provider, the same way a direct call to the provider's real `baseUrl` succeeds.

**Before/after example**
```
$ curl -s -X POST https://my-internal-gateway.example.com/v1/chat/completions \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $MY_API_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"model":"my-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'
{"id":"chatcmpl-...","object":"chat.completion","choices":[{"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"Hi! How can I help you today?"}, ...}], ...}
```

```
    -d '{"model":"my-model","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'
{"error":{"message":"Your authentication token is not from a valid issuer.","type":"invalid_request_error","code":"invalid_issuer","param":null},"status":401}
```

```
$ pi --provider myprovider --model my-model -p "hi" --no-session
```

title: Add OrcaRouter as an optional AI provider
body:
Hi maintainers,

We'd like to propose adding [OrcaRouter](https://www.orcarouter.ai) as an optional AI provider alongside the providers already supported by the project.

OrcaRouter exposes an OpenAI-compatible API and uses standard API-key authentication, so the integration should be able to reuse the project's existing OpenAI/provider abstraction with minimal changes.

## What this would add

- Access to multiple chat, reasoning, image, and video models through one endpoint
- Automatic model routing and provider failover
- Standard API-key authentication
- Prompt caching
- Usage tracking, budgets, and team access controls

The integration would not replace or modify any existing provider. OrcaRouter would simply appear as another provider option that users can configure with their own API key.

## Existing OSS ecosystem

OrcaRouter is already integrated with or available across a growing open-source ecosystem, including RAGFlow, Dify, goose, promptfoo, NocoBase, DB-GPT, CAMEL, and models.dev / OpenCode.

## Partner program disclosure

OrcaRouter operates an optional open-source partner program. Approved OSS projects can receive a 5% revenue share from OrcaRouter usage attributed to their integration.

Participation in the partner program is not required for the provider integration, and we're happy to follow any disclosure or governance requirements maintained by the project.

More information:

https://www.orcarouter.ai/built-with

If this sounds useful, we'd be happy to discuss the integration details and, with the maintainers' approval, open a PR with the implementation.

I'm an engineer on the OrcaRouter team.

title: opencode-go anthropic-messages models: the auth scheme through the OpenAI-compat mount is not tested
body:
**What happen**

PR #948 routes the opencode-go `anthropic-messages` models through the `/compat/opencode-go` mount. In pi-ai 0.84.2 these models are `minimax-m3`, `qwen3.7-max`, `qwen3.7-plus`, and `qwen3.8-max`. The mount uses the OpenAI-compatible adapter.

The Anthropic client in Pi posts to `<baseUrl>/v1/messages`. It sends the key in the `x-api-key` header. Thus the wire path is `POST /w/pi/compat/opencode-go/v1/messages`. The proxy removes `/w/pi` and resolves `https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/messages`. The adapter does not copy the inbound `x-api-key` header, because the header allowlist in `proxy/providers/adapter.go` does not list it. The adapter sends the key as `Authorization: Bearer`.

No test shows that the OpenCode Go endpoint accepts a Bearer header on its Anthropic-protocol path. If the endpoint rejects the header, these models get a 401 error through the proxy. In direct mode, the same models work.

A second effect: the mount reuses `openai.ExtractCompressible`. For a `/v1/messages` path, this function uses the chat-completions zones. These zones match `messages[].role == "user"` with `{"type":"text"}` blocks. Thus the proxy can compress text blocks in user messages on this path. The proxy skips `tool_result` blocks. This is not the byte-identical pass-through that the PR body describes. A test must show that the rewritten body is still a valid Anthropic request. The alternative is an explicit decision to keep this behavior.

**Expected**

One tested path for the opencode-go `anthropic-messages` models. There are three options:

- A test against the upstream shows that it accepts the forwarded auth scheme. A proxy test pins this behavior.
- The mount sends `x-api-key` on Anthropic-protocol paths. The header follows the protocol, so the env-key fallback behaves the same.
- The `anthropic-messages` route entry is removed until a test shows the correct scheme.

**Before/after example**

```
Input: caveman pi --provider opencode-go --model minimax-m3 -p 'Reply with OK'
Got:   unknown, possibly a 401 error from the upstream
Want:  OK, the same as direct mode
```

**Platform**
- [ ] Claude Code
- [ ] Codex
- [x] Other: Pi (OpenCode Go provider, anthropic-messages models)

**Version / install method**

Current `main` after PR #948. This is a follow-up to #946.

title: docs: release note and override test for the built-in opencode-go upstream URL
body:
**What you want**

Two small follow-ups to the built-in `opencode-go` compat mount from PR #948:

1. A release note that names the built-in upstream `https://opencode.ai/zen/go` and the override. If OpenCode moves the endpoint, standalone users lose the mount until a new caveman release. A `compat.opencode-go.base_url` entry in `caveman.yaml` replaces the built-in URL today. PR #948 added the mount and the override to the technical docs (`docs/technical/proxy-and-providers.md`, `docs/technical/configuration.md`). Release v2.5.0 (2026-09-02) includes #948, but its release body does not name the mount. Thus the note targets the next release. The repository has no release-notes file. The follow-up PR description can carry the text, and the maintainer can copy it into the release body.
2. A test that asserts the override on the adapter path. `TestCreds_OpenCodeGoBuiltinCompatCredential` covers the credential path. No test shows that a user base URL replaces the built-in mount in the `buildAdapters` route resolution.

**Before/after example**

```
Before: no release note names the built-in URL or the override. No test covers the override on the adapter path.
After:  the release note names the URL and the override. A test locks the override on the adapter path.
```

**Why good**

title: fix(proxy): send x-api-key on compat /v1/messages
body:
## Summary

- A named compat mount now maps the credential by the wire protocol of the request path (fixes #967). A request to `/compat/<name>/v1/messages` gets `x-api-key` and a default `anthropic-version`. Every other path keeps `Authorization: Bearer`. A real inbound Bearer token keeps its header on every path, so the auth-scheme rule of the proxy holds.
- The gateway env fallback puts the key in the header that the adapter emitted. The upstream never gets two credentials.
- A new test shows that a user `compat.opencode-go` entry replaces the built-in upstream on the adapter path (fixes #968).
- The docs and `proxy/CLAUDE.md` describe the header rule.

## Why

The Anthropic client in Pi posts to `/v1/messages` with the key in `x-api-key`. The proxy dropped that header and sent `Authorization: Bearer`. OpenCode Go rejects a Bearer header on that path with `401 {"type":"error","error":{"type":"AuthError","message":"Missing API key."}}`. Thus the opencode-go `anthropic-messages` models (`minimax-m3`, `qwen3.7-max`, `qwen3.7-plus`, `qwen3.8-max`) failed through the proxy and worked in direct mode.

## Proof

- Direct probe of the upstream on 2026-09-03 with `curl` to `https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/messages`: `Authorization: Bearer` gives 401, `x-api-key` gives 200.
- Reproduction through a proxy built from `main` before this change: `POST /w/pi/compat/opencode-go/v1/messages` with `x-api-key` gives 401 `Missing API key.`.
- The same request through a proxy built from this branch gives 200 and the reply `OK` from `minimax-m3`. `POST /w/pi/compat/opencode-go/v1/chat/completions` with a Bearer token still gives 200.
- `go test ./proxy/providers/openaicompat/ ./proxy/internal/gateway/ ./proxy/internal/standalone/` passes. The three new tests fail on `main` without the adapter and fallback changes.
- Review follow-up (`c94013c`): three new cases show that a real inbound Bearer stays Bearer on `/v1/messages`. They fail on the first commit of this branch and pass now.
- `go test ./proxy/...`: nine failures in `cmd/caveman-proxy`, `internal/nativeruntime`, and `internal/store` are identical on the untouched tree. Their cause is a group-writable temp directory on the test machine (`sqlite parent ... is group/world writable`).
- `python3 tests/verify_repo.py` passes.

## Known limits

- The mount reuses `openai.ExtractCompressible` for Anthropic bodies. In `compress` mode, text blocks in user messages can be compressed on this path. This PR does not change that behavior. The end-to-end test runs in `record` mode and asserts an unchanged body.
- Without an inbound key and without `OPENCODE_API_KEY`, the proxy sends no credential and the upstream returns 401. This is the same behavior as before.
- The new header rule applies to every named compatibility mount. Some compatible upstreams can accept Anthropic requests but require Bearer authentication. These upstreams will reject an API key from an environment variable. The current configuration has no field that selects the authentication header.

## Release note for the next GitHub Release body

The standalone proxy registers a built-in `/compat/opencode-go/` mount with the upstream `https://opencode.ai/zen/go` and the credential variable `OPENCODE_API_KEY`. If OpenCode moves the endpoint, a `compat.opencode-go` entry in `caveman.yaml` replaces the URL and the variable name. On this mount, requests to `/v1/messages` carry the key in `x-api-key`, so the opencode-go `anthropic-messages` models work through the proxy.
