title: caveman-proxy pins deleted ccr.db WAL inode → `caveman retrieve` intermittently returns "recovery handle not found" mid-session
body:
## Summary

The long-lived `caveman-proxy` daemon opens `~/.caveman/ccr.db` (WAL mode) and holds it for the entire session. When the DB file is replaced on disk (new inode — e.g. after a config change, update, or a checkpoint that swaps files), the proxy keeps its file descriptors pointing at the **deleted** inode. Because WAL checkpoints only fully publish when the last reader/writer closes, and the always-on proxy never closes its orphaned handle, `caveman retrieve` (via `caveman-mcp` or `caveman-engine retrieve`) intermittently reads a snapshot that is missing recently-written recovery handles → returns:

```
retrieve: ccr: recovery handle not found
```

A full opencode restart kills the proxy; the next launch opens the current file and retrieve "works again for a while" — matching the user-visible symptom exactly.

## Environment

- OS: Linux (Ubuntu)
- CLI: `@caveman-ai/cli` 1.3.3, binary release `bin-v1.1.6`
- Host: opencode (native integration via `caveman enable opencode`)
- Proxy: `/home/USER/.caveman/bin/caveman-proxy`, listening 127.0.0.1:8787

## Evidence

Proxy holds deleted WAL/SHM inodes while the on-disk `ccr.db` is a different inode:

```
$ ls -l /proc/<proxy-pid>/fd | grep ccr
lrwx------ 10 -> /home/USER/.caveman/ccr.db-wal (deleted)
lrwx------ 11 -> /home/USER/.caveman/ccr.db-shm (deleted)
lrwx------  9 -> /home/USER/.caveman/ccr.db        (old inode 89173)

$ ls -li ~/.caveman/ccr.db
1220765 -rw------- ... ccr.db     ← current inode, different from proxy's
```

Store schema confirms handles are durable in WAL-mode SQLite:

```
$ sqlite3 ~/.caveman/ccr.db ".tables"
recoveries  typed_objects
```

Retrieve works after proxy restart (fresh proxy opens current inode, no `(deleted)` markers):

```
$ caveman tools retrieve ccr_<handle> "query"   # succeeds
```

## Root cause

`caveman-proxy` opens the CCR store once at startup and never re-opens it, while other writers (`caveman-mcp`, `caveman-engine`) open it by path per invocation. If the file is replaced underneath the proxy (atomic rename swap), the proxy's fds point to an orphaned inode. WAL checkpointing requires all readers to close; the proxy never does, so:

1. New handles written by `caveman-mcp` land in the WAL of the *current* file.
2. A `retrieve` racing the checkpoint (or opening the store at the wrong moment) can miss the handle.
3. The proxy's own writes may go into the orphaned inode, invisible to everyone else after restart.

## Expected behavior

One of:

- **(a)** `caveman-proxy` detects that `ccr.db` has been replaced (stat inode/mtime change) and re-opens it, or
- **(b)** `caveman-mcp`/`caveman-engine` force a WAL checkpoint (`PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`) after writing a recovery handle, so the handle is durable in the main DB file regardless of who else holds the WAL open, or
- **(c)** `caveman-proxy` exits when its session ends (e.g. via the host plugin's dispose hook) instead of pinning the store indefinitely.

## Workaround (local)

In the opencode native plugin's `dispose` hook, SIGTERM `caveman-proxy` when opencode exits. This forces a clean close + checkpoint; the next session's proxy opens the current file. Confirmed working locally, but it only helps at session boundary, not mid-session, and it lives in a generated file that gets overwritten on `caveman enable opencode`.

Happy to provide `strace`/logs or test a patch.

title: Redaction covers ghs_ but never gho_ (OAuth), ghu_ or ghr_ (App tokens)
body:
## What

Redaction covers GitHub App installation tokens (`ghs_`, fixed in #1003/#1005) but never covered OAuth access tokens (`gho_`), App user-to-server tokens (`ghu_`) or App refresh tokens (`ghr_`). All three are current, non-migrating GitHub token formats, so this is a live gap today, not a forward-looking one.

## Where

Four independent sites, same shape as the `ghs_` gap:

- `shared/platform/redact/redact.go`, `credentialPrefixRe`: has `ghp_` and now `ghs_`, but no `gho_`, `ghu_` or `ghr_`.
- `shared/platform/redact/payload.go`, the `credential-prefix-token` needle list: same omission, and it gates whether the regex pass runs at all.
- `proxy/internal/repointel/index.go`, `safeTerm`'s prefix denylist: same three missing.
- `packages/subagent-tax/lib/sink.mjs`: already has `gho_` (confirmed by testing the live regex), still missing `ghu_` and `ghr_`.

## Character class

Unlike `ghs_`, which is migrating to a stateless JWT, `gho_`, `ghu_` and `ghr_` are plain alphanumeric tokens with no dots or dashes, the same shape `ghp_` already uses. A `gho_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}`-style class (matching the neighbouring `ghp_[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}` convention) covers all three without the JWT-specific character class `ghs_` needed.

## Not affected

`shared/platform/redact/residual.go` reuses `credentialPrefixRe` rather than keeping its own list, so it needs no separate change.

title: fix(redact): recognize gho_/ghu_/ghr_ GitHub OAuth and App tokens
body:
Added `gho_`, `ghu_` and `ghr_` branches at the same four sites #1003 touched for `ghs_`. Unlike `ghs_`, these three are not migrating to a JWT shape, so they use the plain alphanumeric class the neighbouring `ghp_` pattern already uses, not the wider dotted class `ghs_` needed.

`sink.mjs` already had `gho_`, it was only missing `ghu_` and `ghr_`.

Added a fixture per token per site (split mid-token in source so push protection does not flag the fixtures), following the same pattern as the existing `ghs_` tests. The new test cases fail without the change and pass with it. Full `go test ./...` passes; the `subagent-tax` node suite passes in full (51/51). Did not run the full `pnpm -r build`/`pnpm -r test` across the other workspace packages, since this change touches only `subagent-tax` and its own suite already covers it end to end.

Fixes #1009

title: Invariant summary sheds facts without saying so
body:
summarizeElided drops entries until the summary fits summaryBudget, and renderInvariants joins whatever is left. Nothing records that anything went, so a trimmed `all ...` list is indistinguishable from a complete one.

Constants are shed 4th of 6 (invariants.go:379), which is the awkward part, since each one is a claim about every elided unit.

Repro is 120 log lines with 6 constant fields, then adding class-enumeration fields to put the budget under pressure:

    extra enums   constants still in the marker
    0             6/6
    1             5/6
    2             2/6
    3             1/6

Same marker shape every time, no sign of the drop.

Reading a field's absence as "wasn't constant" is most of what the marker is good for, so this is where it can mislead. A `; +N omitted` suffix would cover it. Can send a patch if useful.

title: daily triage 2026-09-07: OAuth/App token redaction, OpenCode session headers, silent invariant shedding, .mdc detection
body: ## Fixes | Issue(s) | Root cause | Hosts/OS affected | Test added | Supersedes | |---|---|---|---|---| | #1009 | `gho_`/`ghu_`/`ghr_` missing from four independent credential-prefix lists; only `ghp_`/`ghs_` were covered | All hosts — redaction is shared platform code (proxy, repointel index, subagent-tax sink) | `redact_test.go` (3 cases), `payload_test.go` (3 cases), `index_test.go`, `sink.test.mjs` | #1010 (adopted) | | #1006 | `Base.SanitizeAndMapHeaders` rebuilds upstream headers from a fixed allowlist with no `x-opencode-*`; the opencode-go override returned early on every non-`/v1/messages` path and never restored them | Pi → OpenCode Go through the proxy, all three routed paths (`/v1/messages`, `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`) | `openaicompat_test.go` (path matrix + negative + other-mount isolation), `standalone_test.go` (3 e2e cases) | #1007 (adopted) | | #1011 | `summarizeElided` sheds whole entries until the render fits `summaryBudget`; nothing recorded the drop, so a trimmed `all …` list was indistinguishable from a complete one | Engine compression markers — all hosts | `TestTrimmedSummaryDeclaresWhatItShed` | — | | #176 | `detect_file_type()` content-sniffs only EXTENSIONLESS files, so an extension on neither list returns `unknown`; `.mdc` was on neither | caveman-compress, all hosts (Cursor rule files) | `test_cursor_rule_mdc_is_natural_language` | #177 (same one-line change against the pre-cleanup path, no test) | Notes on the two larger ones: **#1011.** Constants shed 4th of six kinds, which is where the silence misleads: each constant is a claim about *every* elided unit, so reading a field's absence as "it wasn't constant" is most of what the marker is good for. The reporter's table reproduces exactly (6/6 → 5/6 → 2/6 → 1/6 constants as enumeration pressure rises, same marker shape throughout). This is the rule `enumerateField` already enforces one level down, where a partial value list is refused outright because "a list that looks complete and is not would let an agent conclude that a value it cannot see was never there". The notice is charged to the **same budget** as the facts, so both caps that govern a marker still hold exactly — the `invariantMaxBytes` ceiling and the rule that a summary never costs more than half the bytes it replaced. I first tried exempting it from the budget; that reads better in isolation but breaks both caps on a tight run, and a marker that stops shrinking what it stands in for is the one thing a marker may never do. Shed *priority* is unchanged — the existing order tests pin the same survivors, now stating the count they expect to be told about. An untrimmed summary renders byte-identically to before (nothing has shed on the first pass, so no notice is charged). **#1006.** I verified the sibling the issue flagged as unchecked: there is no separate `/w/opencode` provider mount. `/w/pi/` is the agent-workspace prefix, and `opencode-go` is the only entry in `builtinCompat`, so `a.prefix` is `/compat/opencode-go` and the gate is correct as written. Forwarding is scoped to that one mount, with a test asserting a second named mount receives none of the four headers. This ships in the Go proxy binary, so users need a new `bin-v*` release, not just a CLI bump. ## Triaged, not fixed - **#1008** (proxy pins deleted `ccr.db` WAL inode): partially reproduced the *mechanism* but not the *trigger*. I grepped every rename/remove in the repo — nothing in caveman replaces or deletes `ccr.db`; the only `os.Rename` in the proxy is proxy-log rotation (`main.go:979`). SQLite WAL checkpointing does not swap inodes either. So the replacement comes from outside caveman, and without knowing what does it I can't write an honest root-cause test. The issue offers three fixes (re-open on inode change / checkpoint after write / exit on session end) that trade differently on hot-path cost — that's a maintainer call. Asked the reporter for the specific trigger. - **#278** (caveman deletes existing code comments): real gap, not reproducible as a test. SKILL.md line 90 covers *writing* normal prose in comments but says nothing about *preserving* existing ones. A deterministic test can't be written for a prose rule, and a static assertion that the rule string exists would be circular. Proposed wording under "Needs maintainer decision". - **#705** (marketplace sync fails in Claude Desktop): cannot reproduce — no Claude Desktop here. `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` and `plugin.json` both parse and match the documented shape. The reporter themselves later suspects a different root cause. PR #540 (add `version`) is plausible but unverified as the fix; shipping it as one would be a guess. - **#575** (CJK ARTICLES): reproduced the mechanism — `/\b(?:a|an|the)\s+(?=[a-z])/gi` is case-insensitive in its lookahead, so `a LLM 模型` → `LLM 模型`. But whether an English article inside Chinese text is filler or semantic is a linguistic design decision about compression aggressiveness, not a defect with one right answer. PR #576 exists; verdict below. - **#991 / #994** (retire the unsourced 0.65 COMPRESSION constant): squarely inside "never change a savings or token-reduction number" — maintainer's call, not mine. ## Contributor PRs reviewed - **#1010** by @AmirF194 — **adopted**, cherry-picked with authorship preserved. Covers all four sites; I independently grepped for `ghp_` repo-wide and found no fifth. `residual.go` correctly needs no change (it reuses `credentialPrefixRe`). Test fixtures are split mid-token so push protection never sees a contiguous literal — a nice touch. - **#1007** by @zsltg — **adopted**, cherry-picked with authorship preserved. Gating on adapter identity rather than URL path is the more robust choice (the workspace prefix can't confuse it). Verified the `/w/opencode` concern raised in the issue is a non-issue. - **#1003** by @AmirF194 (`ghs_`) — **superseded by #1005**, already merged 2026-09-06. Nothing left to do; safe to close. - **#1000, #998, #980** — **superseded by #1005** (shrink parentheticals, compress block order, gemini install hang all landed there). Safe to close. - **#177** by @GunnarAK — **superseded**. Correct diagnosis and correct one-line change, but against `caveman-compress/scripts/detect.py`, which moved to `skills/` in the cleanup, so it no longer applies. Reimplemented at the current path with a test; credited as co-author. - **#576** by @lg320531124 — **needs a maintainer decision, not changes.** The code change is sound and minimal. The question is whether skipping ARTICLES on any CJK character is the right policy. - **#540** (add `version` to `plugin.json`) — low risk and probably worth taking on its own merits, but I could not verify it fixes #705, so I did not fold it in as a fix. ## Needs maintainer decision 1. **#1008 fix shape.** Re-open on inode change (a stat per operation on a hot path), checkpoint after every handle write (write amplification), or tie proxy lifetime to the session (the reporter's local workaround, session-boundary only). I'd lean toward detecting and re-opening, but it's a real cost/robustness trade on a daemon path. 2. **#278 SKILL.md rule.** Proposed addition: *"Compression apply to your own prose only. Never delete, shorten, or reword existing comments, docs, or code in files you edit — caveman style never touch content already on disk."* Behavioral, unverifiable in `tests/`, so I did not ship it unasked. 3. **#576 / #575 policy.** Should the shrinker be CJK-aware at all? Skipping ARTICLES whenever any CJK codepoint is present is coarse (it disables the rule for a mostly-English doc with one Chinese word) but it is safe in the direction that matters. 4. **#991 / #994** — the 0.65 constant. Numbers are off-limits to this run by design. ## Housekeeping spotted, not touched - `proxy/internal/store/learn_digest_test.go` is not `gofmt`-clean on main (pre-existing, unrelated to this diff). - `skills/caveman-compress/README.md`'s extension table omits `.markdown`, which *is* in `COMPRESSIBLE_EXTENSIONS`. I added `.mdc` (my change) but left the pre-existing `.markdown` gap alone to keep the diff minimal. - `node scripts/test-windows-compat.mjs` fails at its final TS step with `TS2688: Cannot find type definition file for 'node'` — I confirmed this reproduces identically on a pristine `origin/main` worktree here, so it's a missing-`node_modules` environment gap, not a regression. Every check before that step passes. ## Verification `npm test` (279 pass) · `node --test tests/*.js` (13 pass) · `python -m unittest discover -s tests` (137 pass) · `python tests/verify_repo.py` (all checks) · `go test ./engine/... ./proxy/... ./shared/...` (all pass). Every fix was confirmed red first: the two adopted PRs had their test files applied against unmodified source to watch them fail for the right reason before the source change was cherry-picked. No changes to `plugins/caveman/**`, `dist/**`, `packages/agent/**`, `packages/create-caveman-agent/**`, or `browse/**`. No `src/hooks/` changes, so `checksums.sha256` is untouched. No benchmark, savings, or token-reduction numbers changed. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) https://claude.ai/code/session_01HM6EY9cQzRPuVaaSGh3pSi --- _Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code/session_01HM6EY9cQzRPuVaaSGh3pSi)_ ---

title: fix(init): honor force when refreshing rules
body:
Running `caveman-init --force` on an already initialized Cursor, Windsurf, or Cline repository reports `skipped-already-installed` and leaves stale rules in place. The sentinel check returns before the force-overwrite branch, despite the documented refresh behavior.

Honor `--force` when checking the sentinel. Regression tests exercise all three targets through the CLI, verifying that default runs preserve existing content, `--force --dry-run` reports an overwrite without writing, and `--force` restores the current rule and frontmatter.

Validation on macOS (Node v24.18.0):
- `node tests/test_caveman_init.js`: 15 passed. The three new cases failed before the fix.
- `npm test`: 279 passed.
- `node --check src/tools/caveman-init.js` and `git diff --check`: passed.

Changes are limited to the MIT initializer and its tests.

title: fix(hooks): reduce per-turn reinforcement when a compression plugin conflicts
body:
Re-ports the conflict-detection behavior from #577 against current HEAD. That branch predated the per-session (#599/#601) and level-aware (#975) refactors and can't be cherry-picked as-is, but the settings.json read and plugin-name detection still apply unchanged.

When settings.json's `installed_plugins` or `permissions` names a known compression plugin (ponytail, grill-me, grilling), the per-turn reminder in `caveman-mode-tracker.js` now reduces to a one-liner instead of restating the full ruleset. Plugin list is taken from #577's body; I haven't independently verified those are the only compression plugins caveman users pair it with.

Added tests in `test_mode_tracker.py` for the reduced/full/unrelated-plugin/malformed-settings paths. The ponytail and permissions-key cases fail on main.

title: daily triage 2026-09-08→09-14: Codex api-key route missing /v1 (and the conformance stub that hid it), think.shrink ignored by the native install, uninstall stranding the Claude route, Codex approval rules broken by the shrink rewrite, ccr.db POSIX lock loss, plugin version identity, RepositoryMap dedup, compat-mount wire dialect, opencode mode log
body:
Seven triage runs on one branch (2026-09-08 through 09-14), per the one-open-PR rule. Run 7 (today) adds the three rows at the top of the table and the **Run 7** sections below; everything else is unchanged from the previous body and kept for the record.

> Run 7 is three clusters, all of them the same shape: **a switch, a route or an uninstall that the code half-implemented, and a test that made the other half look fine.** The sharpest is #1045 — the conformance harness drives every agent profile through the real proxy binary and has been green the whole time, because its Codex stub appended `/v1/responses` to whatever `base_url` it found and quietly supplied the segment the config had left out. Real Codex never does that. Every api-key Codex session has been 404ing before one request reached OpenAI, and the harness built to catch exactly this could not see it.
>
> Two of the three contributor PRs are adopted with a gap closed; #1050's `think.shrink` fix is correct and left the rewrite live on precisely the machines that asked for it off, because `enable` merges into the host's live file.

## Fixes

| Issue(s) | Root cause | Hosts/OS affected | Test added | Supersedes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| #1049 | Every native writer passed a literal `true` for `includeShrink`, so `enable` / `doctor --fix` / `repairNativeAgent` reinstated the `shrink-hook` PreToolUse entry whatever `think.shrink` said — and honoring the switch only on the entries we ADD still merged a pre-existing entry straight through, leaving the rewrite live and the fresh install born `degraded` | Claude Code, Codex, Gemini native installs — all OS | 2 in `packages/cli/tests/native-enable.runtime.mjs` on top of the 2 adopted | #1050 (adopted) |
| #1040 | `--uninstall` never withdrew the CLI-owned `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` route, and the delegation that now does only fires while the `caveman` CLI is still on PATH — with no word to the user when it isn't | Claude Code (route), every native agent (journal) — all OS | 2 in `tests/installer/uninstall-safety.test.mjs` on top of the 2 adopted | #1042 (adopted) |
| #1045 (bug 1) | Codex's OpenAI-Responses client appends `/responses` onto `base_url` itself; the CLI wrote `…/w/codex`, so the proxy got `/responses`, which its closed route allowlist does not hold. The conformance harness modelled the client as appending `/v1/responses` and so ran green against the broken config | Codex api-key sessions — all OS | conformance stub corrected + 3 cases across `codex-subscription-wrap`, `native-enable`, and a new `proxy/internal/gateway/codex_native_route_test.go` | #1047 (route half adopted) |

### Run 7 — #1045: the harness that could not see it

@g0GobliN filed two bugs in one report and both are real. Bug 1 is the one fixed here, and its evidence is already complete in the issue: `base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8787/w/codex"`, Codex's client appends `/responses`, the proxy 404s with `cave_route_not_found`, and `/w/codex/v1/responses` routes. I confirmed the proxy half from the other side before touching anything — `proxy/providers/openai/openai.go` declares `Routes: ["/v1/chat/completions", "/v1/responses", …]` and `Base.MatchRoute` treats every route without a trailing slash as **exact**, deliberately (`"Treating all routes as prefixes made /v1/responses-anything … valid proxy surfaces, violating the gateway's closed route allowlist"`). So `/responses` was never going to match, and aider already routes `/w/aider/openai/v1` for exactly this reason.

**The part worth your attention is why CI was green.** `tests/agent-compression-conformance.runtime.mjs` is not a mock — it builds `caveman-proxy` from source, runs it, and drives every shipped agent profile through it end to end. It is the test designed to catch a broken route. Its Codex stub read `base_url` out of the generated `config.toml` and then appended a hardcoded `"/v1/responses"`:

```js
} else if (profile.wire_protocol === "openai-responses") {
  path = "/v1/responses";
```

Against the old `base_url` of `…/w/codex` that composes to `/w/codex/v1/responses` — the correct path — so the harness exercised a URL no real user could produce. The stub was supplying the missing segment on Codex's behalf. Real Codex appends the bare verb, always, the same way it does against `api.openai.com`; the `openai-chat` branch three lines down already encodes that rule (`…endsWith("/v1") ? "/chat/completions" : "/v1/chat/completions"`).

The stub now appends `/responses`. That turns the harness into the guard it was meant to be, which I verified by mutation rather than assertion — reverting the route constant alone brings the reporter's error back through the real proxy binary:

```
codex: HTTP 404: {"error":{"type":"cave_gateway_error","code":"cave_route_not_found", …}}
```

Codex is the only `openai-responses` profile in the registry, so no other agent's conformance run changes.

The route itself now lives in one constant. Three places have to agree about it — the provider TOML, the install journal's `owned.route`, and `nativeIntegrationStatus`'s `expectedRoute` — and a route only some of them know reads as permanently `degraded`. Two narrower guards pin each end of the contract, because the two spellings live in different languages and nothing else fails when they drift: a CLI assertion that what Codex concatenates equals the path the proxy serves, and a new Go test that `/w/codex/responses` does **not** match the openai adapter while `/w/codex/v1/responses` does.

**Existing installs.** Everyone who ran `caveman enable codex` on an api key has the old route on disk. They do not silently stay broken and they do not silently look healthy: a third test pins that such an install reads `state: degraded`, `components.routing: false`, `repair: "caveman doctor codex --fix"`, and that `--fix` writes the `/v1` route and returns the install to `installed`. Mutation-tested.

**Bug 2 is not fixed and is not the same bug.** The 401 `Missing scopes: api.responses.write` is a ChatGPT-plan OAuth token being forwarded to the platform API. The proxy already has the right destination — `/chatgpt/` is a separate mux handler targeting `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex` (`proxy/internal/gateway/chatgpt.go:23`) — so nothing is missing from the proxy. What happened is that `config.toml` bakes the auth lane in at install time and `codex login` flips it afterwards without touching the file. That drift is **already detected**: `nativeIntegrationStatus` recomputes `expectedRoute` from `detectCodexWrapAuthMode()` at read time, and `doctor codex` reports `routing: false` with the repair command (pinned by an existing test, "doctor reports Codex routing degraded when auth lane changes"). So `caveman doctor codex --fix` fixes bug 2 today.

@g0GobliN's PR adds a self-heal for it: `repairNativeAgent("codex")` from inside the SessionStart hook when routing is degraded. I did **not** adopt that half, and the reason is not that the instinct is wrong. It rewrites the user's `~/.codex/config.toml`, takes the integration lock, and restores-then-reapplies journal files, all inside a host hook on a budget — and it does it without the user having asked. Whether Caveman may silently rewrite a host config from a hook is a policy call, item I below; a `--fix` that has to be typed is at least a decision someone made.

### Run 7 — #1049: honoring a switch only for what you add

@brandonwie's report is precise enough to act on as written, down to the line numbers, and the mechanism is exactly as described: `nativeHooksDocument(agentId, true, …)` at three call sites, with `think.shrink` read only by the ephemeral launcher. Reproduced both spellings against the built CLI before reading @L4XB's #1050 — `think.shrink=false` and `CAVEMAN_SHRINK=0` each yield `shrink-hook` in `~/.claude/settings.json`.

The motivating detail in the report is worth repeating because it is not hypothetical: they run their own `rtk hook claude` shell-command rewriter, Claude Code executes only one `updatedInput` among parallel PreToolUse hooks, and Caveman's entry silently displaces theirs. Removing it by hand held until `doctor --fix`, which the CLI itself recommends.

**#1050 is the right fix and I adopted it** — one reader (`nativeShrinkEnabled()`) so the writers and the health check that judges them cannot disagree, with `removeNativeHookEntries` deliberately left at literal `true` so `disable` still withdraws an entry an earlier install wrote. Their reasoning about which call sites keep the superset is correct and I kept both comments.

**What it misses is that `enable` merges into the host's live file.** `nativeHooksDocument` filters the *lifecycle* entries out of `base` before re-adding them, but the shrink block only ran under `if (includeShrink)`. With the switch off that block is skipped entirely, so a `shrink-hook` entry already sitting in `base` is never touched — and it is sitting there for anyone who used the standalone installer, or any caveman old enough to predate the switch. Reproduced:

```
fresh `caveman enable claude`, think.shrink=false, pre-existing standalone entry
  exit 0
  shrink-hook survived into the new install: true
  doctor state right after install: degraded
```

Exit 0, still rewriting, and born `degraded` — because `nativeHookEntriesHealthy` rejects a managed entry the expected document lacks. The switch reports success and changes nothing for exactly the population that set it.

The fix is to let the replace-not-accumulate rule the function already documents reach our own path: with the switch off, every managed shrink entry is withdrawn rather than merged through. This is not a claim on anyone else's hooks — `managedHookIdentity` returns `"shrink-hook"` only for a caveman executable invoked with exactly that one argument, so the reporter's `rtk hook claude` is untouched, which the new test pins alongside `disable` still restoring the host file it found, stale entry and all. Verified idempotent in both directions with a third-party hook and unrelated `env` present.

**Second half of the same report.** The gate in `enableNative` pointed a user at bare `caveman doctor <agent>`, which prints JSON containing `"state": "degraded"` and nothing that says how to leave it. Following that line lands you in a loop. It names `--fix` now, which is also the value the doctor's own `repair` field has carried all along.

### Run 7 — #1040: the delegation only fires while the CLI is still there

@ralph-oei did the work here: they traced the route to `~/.caveman/integrations/claude.json`, established that `previous_route` is `null` so nothing needs restoring, and pointed out that neither uninstall doc mentions the route at all. @AmirF194's #1042 is the right answer — hand it to `caveman disable --all` rather than re-deriving journal restoration inside `bin/install.js` — and I adopted both commits, including the Windows shim fix in the second.

Confirmed the delegation actually does the job rather than trusting the fixture (their test uses a recording stub): `enable claude` writes the route and the journal, `disable claude` removes the journal and restores `settings.json` to its pre-install state, which in a clean fixture means the file is gone again.

**The gap is the branch nobody tests.** `hasCmd('caveman')` guards the call, so a user who ran `npm uninstall -g @caveman-ai/cli` first — or whose `disable --all` failed — keeps the route, keeps the Remote Control breakage of #947, and the uninstall output says nothing. That silence is the reporter's entire experience; they only found the cause by editing `settings.json` by hand.

`disable` removes the journal it restored from, so a journal still present after the delegation is exact evidence that a route is still installed. That is a precise signal, not a heuristic: it cannot fire on a user's own `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` export, which the second new test pins. `remainingNativeIntegrations()` only reads, honors `CAVEMAN_HOME` the way the CLI does, and returns empty on any filesystem error, so an unreadable home can never fail an uninstall. Skipped under `--dry-run`, where nothing was disabled and the journals are expected to still be there.

Docs half, which the issue asks for by name: both uninstall sections now list the native route among what is removed, state that `--uninstall` runs **before** `npm uninstall -g`, and give the recovery for having done it the other way round.

### Run 6 — #1037: the README was right and nothing implemented it

The reporter filed a clean bug: with Caveman's Codex integration on, a command already covered by `prefix_rule(pattern=["git", "add"], decision="allow")` is rewritten and Codex asks for approval again. @AmirF194 found the mechanism the same day in #1039 — `shrinkHook()`'s dispatch folds Codex's tool names in with Bash and emits the Claude-shaped `permissionDecision:"allow"` + `updatedInput`.

I reproduced it against the built CLI before reading their fix, and the output is the reporter's paste with one extra fact in it:


### Run 5 — #1008: the reporter found the symptom, @andrebrait found the cause, and it is worse than either said

The issue reads as an inode-replacement race: the proxy pins a deleted `ccr.db`, so writes land somewhere nobody reads. The evidence in it is excellent — `ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd` showing `ccr.db-wal (deleted)` and `ccr.db-shm (deleted)` next to a live `ccr.db` on a different inode. That listing is the whole case, but not for the reason it was filed under.

**Nothing replaces the file.** `secureSQLiteFile` tightens permissions on `ccr.db`, `-wal` and `-shm` by opening each `O_RDWR` and closing it. POSIX record locks have the footgun that closing *any* descriptor for a file releases *every* lock the process holds on that inode, no matter which descriptor took them — and SQLite's unix VFS has no idea an unrelated `os.OpenFile` in the same process just did that. `openWithBudget` calls it at `store_sqlite.go:184`, **after** `sql.Open` and the schema migration, so the connection is live and holding its WAL lock when the lock is thrown away. Every store, every open, self-inflicted.

A long-lived `caveman-proxy` therefore spends its whole life holding a WAL connection without the lock that announces it as a live reader. The next short-lived `caveman-mcp` or `caveman-engine` open decides it is the last connection, checkpoints, and unlinks the WAL and SHM the proxy is still writing into. Hence `(deleted)`, hence `recovery handle not found`, hence "works again for a while" after a restart.

I reproduced it before reading the fix, and the isolation is worth recording because it explains why this survived review for so long:

| open/close performed on | foreign process can unlink the live WAL? |
|---|---|
| `ccr.db` alone | no |
| `-wal` alone | no |
| `-shm` alone | no |
| **all three, as `PrepareSQLitePathCanonical` does** | **yes** |

Any single one of those is survivable — SQLite still holds enough of the lock set elsewhere to block the checkpoint. Only the full sweep opens the window, which is exactly what the production path does and exactly what a narrower test would have missed. In my first end-to-end run the writer's post-sweep `Put` went into the orphaned inode and a *fresh* reader then failed with `disk I/O error (522)`, so the damage is not limited to missing handles.

**The adopted fix is @andrebrait's and it is the right one.** Chmod without ever opening the inode for I/O: on Linux an `O_PATH` descriptor (which Linux deliberately skips `locks_remove_posix` for on close) plus `fchmodat2(AT_EMPTY_PATH)`, with a chmod through the pinned `/proc/self/fd` link for older kernels; native no-follow `fchmodat` elsewhere; handle-based validation retained on Windows, where locks are per-handle and the original approach was never wrong. Creation moves to a temp file plus an atomic `os.Link`, so no descriptor is closed after the name is publishable. Cherry-picked with authorship preserved.

Verified load-bearing rather than trusted: reverting `chmodSQLiteFile` to an ordinary descriptor turns all three of their scenarios red with `ccr: recovery handle not found` — the issue's exact string.

**What I added: the fallback branch was untested, and it is the one most users take.** Every CI runner has `fchmodat2` (Linux 6.6+), so the procfs fallback never executed in a single test — while being the branch that ships to every pre-6.6 kernel still in support: RHEL 9 on 5.14, Debian 12 and Amazon Linux 2023 on 6.1. `fchmodat2` now sits behind a seam so a test can force the `EOPNOTSUPP` those kernels return, and the whole open/close-peer regression runs through the fallback, plus two narrower cases pinning that it still tightens the mode it exists to tighten and still refuses a symlinked path. The seam asserts the real syscall works before replacing it, so a future breakage of the primary path cannot hide behind a green fallback test. Both mutation-tested: an ordinary descriptor in the fallback fails with `recovery handle not found`, a silent no-op fails the mode assertion at `-rw-r--r--`.

**Sibling stores checked, per the one-guard-in-the-shared-function rule.** `mem/store.go` goes through the same `ccr.PrepareSQLitePathCanonical` and is fixed by the shared helper. `proxy/internal/store/store.go:328` uses a path-based `os.Chmod`, which opens nothing and so never had the bug — weaker against a symlinked path, but not this defect, and not something to change inside a lock fix. No JS host is affected: the hook flag writes in `safeWriteFlag` are ordinary files with no record locks.

**Not adopted: #1034's second commit.** The Pi elision verification is a capability-negotiation change across `packages/pi-extension` with a much wider blast radius than a triage run should take on. Left for the maintainer — item A below.

**One reviewer finding on the adopted commit, which I could not verify here.** `createSQLiteFile` now creates via `os.CreateTemp` + `os.Link`, and any link error other than `EEXIST` propagates as a hard failure. A `~/.caveman` on exFAT or a CIFS mount without hardlink support would therefore fail store creation outright, where the old `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` open succeeded. Narrow, but it is a *new* failure mode; a fallback on non-`EEXIST` link errors would close it. I did not patch it because I have no such filesystem here to write a failing test against, and this routine does not ship fixes it cannot test.

### #1023 — the adopted fix was right about the bug and short of it in two places

@AmirF194 diagnosed this correctly and their reproduction is honest work: they read their own `ccr.db`, found `RepositoryMap` at 21 rows over 4 distinct `content_hash` values and 272 MB of a 279 MB file, and confirmed the cleanup by hand. I cherry-picked their commit with authorship preserved and extended it on two points their tests could not see.

**The dedup key was too narrow.** It matched on `(object_type, source, repository_state, content_hash)`. `repository_state` is *itself* part of the object ID and advances on every commit, while the repository map is a structural index most commits leave byte-identical — so one long session over a large repo still re-stored the whole map once per commit, with no second session anywhere in the picture. `content_hash` is `sha256(data)`, verified against the bytes in `prepareObject`, so an equal hash already means byte-equal content and no other column needs to agree. I measured both halves before and after:

| Three identical 200 KB maps | `origin/main` | #1025 as sent | this branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| across three sessions | 600 KB | **200 KB** | 200 KB |
| across three commits, one session | 600 KB | 600 KB | **200 KB** |

**`ListSessionObjects` deadlocked.** `resolveObjectData` issued its lookup *inside* the open `rows` cursor. The store runs on one serialized connection (`SetMaxOpenConns(1)`, `store_sqlite.go:166`), so that nested query waits forever for the connection the cursor itself is holding. Not a slow path — a hang, and on a path that matters: `transitionAfterCompaction` walks `ListSessionObjects` on every compaction, and the receipt builder unmarshals a map's `Data` to count repository files. Any session whose map deduped against an earlier one would hang the proxy there. The cursor is now drained and closed before anything is resolved, which is what `Summary()` in the same file already does for the same reason. `GetObject` and `FindTaskDecision` were never exposed: `QueryRow.Scan` closes its rows before resolution runs.

I found this only because I wrote a test for the reader path; the PR's own tests exercise `GetObject`, which is the one shape that cannot hit it.

Dedup stays scoped to `RepositoryMap`, which was the right call in the original and I kept it: `FindTaskDecision` runs `json_extract` over the `data` column, so a `TaskDecision` stored as a pointer would silently stop being findable. Their test pinning that other types keep a full copy per session is kept.

**One thing for you, not a blocker.** A pointer row is `data=''` plus `data_ref=<id>` on disk (verified). A *downgrade* to a binary without this change would read those rows as an empty repository map — degraded, not corrupt, and self-healing since the map is rebuilt. Existing duplicate rows are also not retro-collapsed; the reporter's 267 MB → 63 MB still needs their manual delete + `VACUUM` once. Worth a line in release notes if this ships in a patch.

### #1026 — the reporter's own correlation is the proof, and it is not what they thought

@sebastianrueckerai's capture is unusually good, and the theory in the issue ("the provider's payload shape flip-flops between calls") is the one part that is wrong — in a way that makes the real cause visible. The tell is the line they lead with: every `provider_complete` row has `cache_status` `hit`/`miss`, every `provider_malformed` row has `unknown`.

`cacheStatusFor()` returns `unknown` when `Malformed` is set, so that correlation is not evidence about cache parsing — it is the *same* fact reported twice. What actually separates the two populations is whether the prompt cache was warm. `mergeSnakeUsage` computes `totalInput = rawInput` for `openai_compatible` (inclusive semantics), then flags `cacheTotal > totalInput` as malformed. An Anthropic-protocol upstream reports `input_tokens` *excluding* cache reads, so a warm response is `36` input against a `1280` cache read — a contradiction under OpenAI rules, and not one under Anthropic rules. Nothing flip-flops; cold requests parse and warm ones do not.

That also explains the reproduction they found puzzling: hand-rolled curl probes are small and cold and "usually parse `provider_complete`", while a real `claude -p` carries a cached system prompt and tool catalog and lands `provider_malformed`. Claude Code traffic is warm almost always, which is the 92%.

I verified the adopted fix is load-bearing rather than trusting the tests: deleting the `Base.UsageProvider` override turns the warm-cache and non-stream cases red with `Malformed:true CacheStatus:unknown` — the reporter's signature exactly.

**On the design, since it is an unusual amount of machinery for an accounting bug.** Auto-detecting the dialect from the path is available — `SanitizeAndMapHeaders` already does exactly that to choose `x-api-key` over Bearer — and I think declining it is correct here. Guessing wrong in the other direction (an upstream that really is OpenAI-inclusive) would silently *inflate* input tokens rather than decline to count them, and this repo's whole posture is that a number it cannot stand behind is not reported. Opt-in config keeps the failure honest. My one change: `anthropicWireZones` carried its own copy of the Messages path set, so I routed it through `anthropicMessagesPath` and added a table test asserting the header rule and the zone rule answer identically for every path shape — a mount that sends Anthropic auth headers while compressing under OpenAI zone rules is a bug waiting for the first person to add a Messages sub-path. Verified load-bearing by growing one side alone.

**Both halves ship together on purpose.** The zone change looks like scope creep next to an accounting fix, but the accounting fix is what makes these requests compression-eligible in the first place — that is the reporter's headline. Turning compression on for a mount while leaving it the wrong zone grammar is worse than leaving it off, and both are behind a flag no existing install sets, so the blast radius on current users is zero.

It needs an eval run. It also lands on the line flagged in item 6 below as already grammatically broken and awaiting your call.

There is a real argument for it — CLAUDE.md notes every `skills/*/` description "competes for activation on ordinary work" — but the tradeoff is exactly the one only you can price, and it is unverifiable here without evals.

- **#1020**, **#1017 / #864**, **#403**, **#574**, **#278**, **#575/#576**, **#991/#994**: unchanged from previous runs; details preserved in the sections below.

### #1020 in detail — eligible-with-zero-tokens is the documented shape of a substitution turn

The reporter's counters are real and their method is careful, but `compression_tokens_before` cannot answer the question they are asking it. Accounting is once-per-message by design: a block compressed on an earlier turn is re-emitted from the prefix cache on every later turn and **re-books nothing**, because claiming it again would inflate one message's delta into a per-turn saving. That is pinned by `TestPrefixSubstitutionOnlyTurnClaimsNoTokens`: a substitution-only turn is eligible, rewrites the bytes, discloses a recovery handle, and records `before = 0`. That is their table, line for line.

The cache is the reason this bites print mode hardest. `prefix_replacements` is keyed on `sha256(scope + original bytes)` alone — no session, no process, no auth mode — and it is a durable table in `~/.caveman/caveman.db`. The reporter ran the same three files five times. After whichever run compressed those `tool_result` blocks first, every later run is a pure substitution, forever, across processes. Run E being a control for `--settings` does not control for that.

So the open question is not "why is print mode skipped" but "were these requests compressed at all", and one field settles it: **`recovery_handle` on the print-mode rows**. Non-empty → the bytes were compressed and this is accounting, not a gap. Empty on every row → a real gap, and then `optimization_ids` says which stage dropped it.

### #1017 / #864 in detail — one scanner, two findings, and only one of them is noise

#864 (Snyk `W007` on `caveman`/`caveman-compress`) is a heuristic firing on "preserve code blocks and exact error strings verbatim". That is an instruction *not to corrupt* a stack trace during stylistic compression, and reading it as forced secret echo is the scanner over-reaching.

#1017 is not that. It flags **`caveman-setup`**, which #864's scan did not even list — and that skill's actual job is to take a `CAVE_API_KEY`, write it into the repo's env file, and re-point every LLM callsite at a gateway base URL. A scanner calling that high-risk is describing what the skill does. The honest answer to the reporter is not "false positive".

The part that needs you is upstream of the finding. `skills/` is auto-discovered wholesale, and `npx skills add JuliusBrussee/caveman --all` installs the whole tree. A user who wanted "talk like caveman" is offered a skill that can rewire their app's LLM traffic to a hosted gateway and handle its secret. That is the same question as #374, arriving through a security scanner instead of a preference. (Note: **#1035 is no longer part of this cluster** — see Run 6.)

May Caveman rewrite a host config from inside a hook?** #1047 proposes calling `repairNativeAgent("codex")` from the SessionStart hook whenever routing reads degraded, which fixes bug 2 of #1045 without the user doing anything. Nothing in this branch writes that value.

Adversarial pass on today's diff (`f191803..8bc01d6`).

**Path resolution.** No `../` chain and no `__dirname` join anywhere in the diff. The one runtime path construction is `remainingNativeIntegrations()`, which builds an absolute path from `CAVEMAN_HOME` or `os.homedir()` and so resolves identically at all three installed depths; nothing here is a hook file resolved at runtime.

**Referenced but not shipped.** One new file, `proxy/internal/gateway/codex_native_route_test.go` — a Go test, never shipped. No installer file list, npm `files` array or plugin layout is involved. `remainingNativeIntegrations` is a function inside the existing `bin/install.js`, not a new module.

title: browse: caveman-browse installs no signal handler — SIGTERM orphans its Chrome and leaks the temp profile dir (same defect as #742)
body:
**What happen**

`caveman-browse` releases its Chrome process and its temp profile directory only from the deferred `Close` calls in `main()`. `main()` registers no signal handler, so the SIGTERM an MCP host sends at session teardown kills the process outright: Chrome survives, reparented to PID 1, and the `caveman-browse-*` directory under `$TMPDIR` is never removed.

`browse/cmd/caveman-browse/main.go`:

```go
driver, err := browse.NewCDPDriver(context.Background(), browse.CDPOptions{...})
...
defer driver.Close()   // kills Chrome and does os.RemoveAll(tmpProfile)
...
srv := mcp.NewServer("caveman-browse", browse.BrowserTools(session), logger)
if err := srv.Serve(os.Stdin, os.Stdout); err != nil { ... }
```

`signal.Notify` appears nowhere in `browse/`. The stdin-EOF path is correct: `mcp.Server.Serve` returns `nil` on `io.EOF`, the defers run, and cleanup happens. Only the signal path leaks.

This is the same defect #742 fixed for `caveman-shrink`, in the browse driver.

**Expected**

SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP should run the same cleanup as stdin EOF: close Chrome, remove the temp profile directory.

**Repro**

```sh
BIN=~/.caveman/bin/caveman-browse

# leaks: killed by signal
CAVEMAN_BROWSE_EPHEMERAL=1 "$BIN" < <(sleep 60) >/dev/null 2>&1 &
SRV=$!
# wait for Chrome to appear, then:
CH=$(pgrep -P $SRV -f "Google Chrome" | head -1)
kill -TERM $SRV
ps -o ppid= -p $CH               # 1  -> orphaned, still running
ls -d "$TMPDIR"caveman-browse-*  # its profile directory is still there

# clean, for contrast: stdin EOF
CAVEMAN_BROWSE_EPHEMERAL=1 "$BIN" < /dev/null >/dev/null 2>&1 &
# server exits 0, Chrome exits, its profile directory is removed
```

Measured impact on one machine: 24 orphaned Chrome instances holding 8.9 GB of RAM, and 32 stale profile directories holding 3.3 GB of disk, accumulated at roughly 5 per day.

**Platform**
- [x] Claude Code

**Version / install method**

Plugin `caveman@caveman` at `df2ccd85c94e`, binary release `bin-v1.1.4`, installed from the marketplace. macOS 26.6.2 (Darwin 25.6.0), Chrome 152.0.7977.77.

**Suggested fix**

Mirror the shape #742 landed in `src/mcp-servers/caveman-shrink/index.js`: in `main()`, `signal.Notify` on SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP and run the same cleanup before exiting.

As a host-side workaround until then, a wrapper that owns the child's stdin and closes it on those signals is enough, since the EOF path already cleans up correctly.

title: fix(browse): close Chrome and remove temp profile dir on SIGTERM/SIGINT/SIGHUP
body:
Fixes #1016.

`main()` never called `signal.Notify`, so an MCP host's SIGTERM at session
teardown killed `caveman-browse` before its deferred `driver.Close()` and
`store.Close()` ran. Only the stdin-EOF path (`srv.Serve` returning `nil` on
`io.EOF`) reached those defers, so a signal-driven shutdown orphaned Chrome
and left its temp profile directory on disk. Same shape as #742/#985, ported
to the browse driver's Go binary.

`srv.Serve(os.Stdin, os.Stdout)` blocks reading stdin until EOF, so it can't
be interrupted directly. The fix runs it on its own goroutine behind a new
`runUntilSignal(ctx, srv, in, out)`, with `ctx` from
`signal.NotifyContext(..., os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM, syscall.SIGHUP)`.
On a signal, `ctx.Done()` wins the `select` and `runUntilSignal` returns
`nil` without waiting for `Serve`, so `main` returns normally and its
deferred `Close` calls run.

Verification (Docker, `golang:1.26`, matching `go.mod`):
- Added `TestRunUntilSignalReturnsOnContextDoneWithoutWaitingForServe`, which
  drives an unclosed `io.Pipe` reader (blocks forever, like stdin with no
  EOF) through an already-canceled `ctx` and asserts a prompt return instead
  of an indefinite block; it does not compile before this change, since
  `runUntilSignal` is new. `TestRunUntilSignalReturnsServeError` pins the
  unchanged EOF path.
- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `go test ./...` (the repo's own `go`
  CI job) all pass.
- I couldn't run the issue's own live repro (checking the orphaned Chrome
  process's PPID and the leftover profile directory), since this environment
  has no real Chrome binary; the tests above exercise the same control-flow
  defect without one.

title: print mode (`claude -p`): eligible subscription requests never reach the engine, while interactive sessions compress normally
body:
**What happen**

On Claude Code **subscription (OAuth)**, compression works in an **interactive** session but never engages for **print mode** (`claude -p`). Print-mode requests are counted and marked `requests_eligible_for_compression`, yet `compression_tokens_before` does not advance at all — the engine is handed nothing.

This is downstream of #908 / #929. That fix landed: subscription requests *are* eligible now, and `recovery_via_mcp` is true. The next step is where it stops.

**Environment**

- macOS 26.5.1, arm64
- `@caveman-ai/cli` 1.3.3, `binary_release` bin-v1.1.6
- Claude Code 2.1.266
- Claude Pro/Max OAuth, no API key — `auth_mode_accounting: {"subscription": N}` on every request
- `think.mode = compress` (default), `execute.mcp = auto` (default)
- `caveman status` → `no off-states — everything the layer can do is on`

Preflight, all green:

```
~/.caveman/run/8787.json  {"mode":"compress","owner":"wrap","recovery_via_mcp":true}
~/.caveman/mcp/claude.json {"tool":"caveman_retrieve","command":"~/.caveman/bin/caveman-mcp","args":[]}
claude mcp list           caveman: ~/.caveman/bin/caveman-mcp - ✔ Connected
```

**Interactive session: compression works**

Over one long interactive session, lifetime counters moved:

```
compression_tokens_before   543 → 11741
compression_tokens_after    535 → 10046
compression_tokens_saved      8 →  1695     (~14.4%)
```

**Print mode: zero, five runs**

Identical workload each time — read three files totalling ~250KB (~60k tokens) with the Read tool, then summarise one line each, 7–9 turns. Deltas taken by snapshotting `caveman stats` before and after each run:

| run | extra flags | Δrequests | Δeligible | Δbefore | Δsaved |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | `--settings` ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto | 16 | 10 | 0 | 0 |
| B | `--settings` ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=0 | 12 | 7 | 0 | 0 |
| C | `--settings` ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto | 15 | 10 | 0 | 0 |
| D | `--settings` ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=0 | 16 | 9 | 0 | 0 |
| E | none — inherits normal config | 18 | 10 | 0 | 0 |

Run E is the control: no `--settings` override at all, so the flag is not the variable. `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH` is not the variable either — with it set to `0` the caveman MCP tool schemas are in-band in the request rather than deferred, and the result is unchanged.

Across all five, ~77 requests and ~46 of them eligible produced `Δcompression_tokens_before = 0`. Meanwhile the same proxy, same config, same machine compressed 11,198 tokens of interactive traffic.

**Repro**

```bash
snapshot() { caveman stats; }
B=$(snapshot)
claude -p 'Read these three files in full: <three large files>. Then reply with
exactly one line per file. Use only the Read tool.' --allowed-tools Read
sleep 6
A=$(snapshot)
jq -n --argjson b "$B" --argjson a "$A" \
  '{requests:($a.requests-$b.requests),
    eligible:($a.requests_eligible_for_compression-$b.requests_eligible_for_compression),
    before:($a.compression_tokens_before-$b.compression_tokens_before),
    saved:($a.compression_tokens_saved-$b.compression_tokens_saved)}'
```

Deltas matter here — `compression_tokens_before` is a lifetime counter, so reading it raw after a fresh session shows the same stale number and looks like "no change" in every arm.

**Hypothesis, unverified**

#929 proves recovery per request from the `caveman_retrieve` tool carried in the request. I have not confirmed whether a `claude -p` session presents its MCP tool list to the provider identically to an interactive one. If print mode differs there, the per-request recovery proof would fail while eligibility — computed earlier — still passes, which matches exactly what the counters show.

**Not a problem**

Two things I checked that turned out fine, in case they save someone else the work:

- Routing through the proxy costs no prompt-cache hits. Same workload alternated proxy vs direct, provider-reported usage: hit rate 69.8% proxy vs 69.2% direct, cost within $0.001, latency within noise. `cache_bust_requests` advancing does not correspond to lost cache reads.
- The `PreToolUse` shrink hook works normally in print mode; this is specific to the engine path.

title: RepositoryMap typed_objects not deduped by content_hash — unbounded ccr.db growth
body:
## What happened

\`ccr.db\`'s \`typed_objects\` table has a \`content_hash\` column that most \`object_type\`s use correctly for dedup — e.g. on my db, \`DiffSnapshot\` had 68 rows / 68 distinct hashes, \`TaskContract\` 89/89 (expected, those legitimately differ each snapshot).

\`RepositoryMap\` doesn't dedup: 21 rows collapsed to only 4 distinct \`content_hash\` values. On a large monorepo each map snapshot is ~13MB, and it's re-inserted on every write with no existing-hash check. This alone accounted for 272MB of a 279MB db file.

macOS also flagged the proxy process itself for excessive disk writes (2.15GB over ~10.7h, spindump attached below) while this was happening — consistent with repeatedly re-writing the same large blob.

## Repro / evidence

\`\`\`sql
SELECT object_type, COUNT(*), SUM(length(data)), COUNT(DISTINCT content_hash)
FROM typed_objects GROUP BY object_type ORDER BY 3 DESC;
\`\`\`

\`\`\`
RepositoryMap|21|272704238|4
DiffSnapshot|68|3277388|68
TaskDecision|1252|602642|1252
...
\`\`\`

After manually deleting duplicate \`RepositoryMap\` rows (keeping newest per \`content_hash\`) and running \`VACUUM\`: 267MB -> 63MB.

## Suspected cause

Insert path for \`RepositoryMap\` skips the existing-hash lookup that other object types go through before writing a new row.

## Side note (separate concern, same session)

Running \`VACUUM\` on \`ccr.db\` while \`caveman-proxy\` (mode \`record\`) had it open killed the running proxy silently (no crash report, just stopped listening on 8787) — timestamps of the last \`native-events.jsonl\` entry and the \`ccr.db\` mtime from the VACUUM lined up to the second. Might be worth the proxy holding its own connection more defensively, or checkpointing/WAL-friendly maintenance instead of requiring an external VACUUM to reclaim space at all — which circles back to the main ask here: dedup on write so this never needs manual cleanup.

## Environment

- macOS 26.5.2, arm64e
- caveman CLI (npm \`@caveman-ai\`)

title: fix: fixed reply-language instruction wins over dominant-language match
body:
## Summary
`main`'s current "preserve dominant language" rule in `skills/caveman/SKILL.md` already stops the old few-shot Portuguese/Spanish example tokens from leaking into a reply — the original repro in #812. But it doesn't say what should happen when a user or project instruction *fixes* the reply language outright (e.g. a `CLAUDE.md` that says "always respond in French"). As worded, dominant-language matching could still override that fixed instruction, which is the actual "Expected" behavior #812 asks for.

This adds the missing precedence clause: a fixed-language instruction always wins; dominant-language matching only applies when no such instruction exists.

Fixes #812

## Test plan
This is a one-clause wording addition to the always-on prompt in `skills/caveman/SKILL.md` (the MIT-licensed source of truth per CONTRIBUTING/CLAUDE.md — didn't touch the CI-synced copies). No code changed, so no `go test`/`pnpm test` applies. Verified by re-reading the rule against #812's Before/After example: with the new clause, a fixed-language project instruction is explicitly stated to override dominant-language detection, closing the gap the issue reported.

title: fix(ccr): dedupe RepositoryMap payloads across sessions
body:
`PutObject` computes a typed object's ID from `Type + SessionID + Source + RepositoryState + ContentHash`, so `ON CONFLICT(object_id) DO NOTHING` only dedups within one session. A `RepositoryMap` object gets a fresh `SessionID` every session (it's rebuilt from scratch each time), but its `ContentHash` repeats whenever the underlying repository state hasn't changed since the last session. The result: an unchanged repo stores a full copy of the same ~MB-scale map on every session, growing `ccr.db` without bound.

I confirmed this is specific to `RepositoryMap`, not a missing lookup that every type shares: forcing `TaskDecision` through the same two-session scenario with matching content shows the same non-dedup, because there is no per-type content lookup at all, only the ID-collision check above. Other types legitimately produce different content per session even when it happens to match, so applying the same shortcut to all of them would be wrong (the second test below pins that boundary).

Fix: when a `RepositoryMap` put finds an existing row with the same `(source, repository_state, content_hash)` from any session, store a small row that references that row's data (`data_ref`) instead of writing another full copy. `GetObject`/`ListSessionObjects`/`FindTaskDecision` resolve the reference transparently, so every caller still sees the exact original bytes and each session still gets its own `object_id` (session-scoped listing is unaffected). Nothing in the table is ever deleted or the `data`/`data_ref` columns ever updated after insert, so a referenced row can't later be pointed at a row that becomes a pointer itself.

The new schema column needed a migration (`ALTER TABLE typed_objects ADD COLUMN data_ref ...`), and adding it exposed a real bug in that pattern under concurrent processes: `mem/cmd/cavemem`'s own `TestConcurrentRememberSubprocesses` (24 subprocesses opening the same fresh db) failed with `duplicate column name: data_ref` two out of five runs, because the PRAGMA-check-then-ALTER sequence isn't atomic across processes sharing one file. Fixed by treating that specific error as "another process already added it" rather than a real failure.

Verification:
- New regression test: two sessions putting the same repository map grow storage by roughly 2x the payload size before this change and roughly 0x after, and both sessions still read back the exact bytes.
- A second new test locks the scope: two sessions putting the same `TaskDecision` content still store two full copies, so that type must keep its own per-session data.
- `go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test ./...` (whole module, matches the `go` CI job) is green, including `mem/cmd/cavemem`'s concurrent-subprocess test run 5 times in a row after the migration fix.
- Opened a database written by the previous schema directly and confirmed it opens cleanly under the new code with its existing rows read back unchanged.

I only ran this in Linux containers, so I can't speak to the `macos` and `windows` CI legs specifically, though nothing here is filesystem- or OS-dependent.

title: provider_malformed usage accounting on a Z.AI compat mount (Claude Code traffic): zero requests compression-eligible
body:
**Environment**

- caveman-proxy `bin-v1.1.6` (per `.bin-manifest.json`); `caveman-proxy version` prints `dev`; Linux x86_64
- Self-configured compat mount: `/compat/zai` -> `https://api.z.ai/api/anthropic` (GLM coding plan, Anthropic-compatible endpoint); mode `compress`
- Client: Claude Code, all model aliases mapped to `glm-5.3` / `glm-5.3-flash`

**Symptom**

`caveman-proxy stats` after ~2,500 requests in one day:

```json
"token_accounting": {"provider_complete": 74, "provider_malformed": 2361, "unavailable": 122},
"compression_tokens_before": 0,
"compression_tokens_saved": 0,
"requests_eligible_for_compression": 0,
"compression_token_count_basis": "unavailable"
```

92% of responses classify `provider_malformed`, so no provider token arithmetic runs and nothing becomes compression-eligible on this mount.

**What the upstream returns (captured through the proxy)**

Non-streaming, final usage block:

```json
"usage": {"input_tokens": 19, "output_tokens": 3, "cache_read_input_tokens": 0,
          "server_tool_use": {"web_search_requests": 0}, "service_tier": "standard"}
```

Streaming `message_start` (input count zero, no cache fields):

```json
data: {"type": "message_start", "message": {"id": "...", "usage": {"input_tokens": 0, "output_tokens": 0}}}
```

Streaming `message_delta` carries the real usage (`input_tokens: 19`), again without `cache_creation_input_tokens`.

Deviations from the Anthropic usage contract:

1. `message_start.usage.input_tokens` is always 0.
2. `cache_creation_input_tokens` never appears in any usage block.
3. Extra nonstandard fields are present (`server_tool_use`, `service_tier`).
4. The shape is inconsistent between calls (see reproduction).

**Correlation in the `requests` table**

- Every `provider_complete` row has `cache_status` `hit` or `miss` (72/72 streamed, same pattern non-streamed).
- Every `provider_malformed` row has `cache_status` `unknown` (1,795/1,795 streamed).

So the completeness verdict appears to hang on cache-field parsing, which this provider emits only sometimes.

**Reproduction**

- Hand-rolled curl requests through the mount (small ones, and a 340 KB streamed response with thinking, tools and `anthropic-beta` headers) usually parse `provider_complete`.
- A real one-shot `claude -p "say ok"` through the mount: 337 KB request, valid 922-byte response, classified `provider_malformed`.
- Two near-identical back-to-back curl probes (same body, seconds apart): one `provider_complete` / `miss`, the next `provider_malformed` / `unknown`. The provider's payload shape itself flip-flops between calls.

**Ask**

Lenient usage accounting for compat mounts, or a per-mount flag for it: treat a missing `cache_creation_input_tokens` as 0, take input tokens from the final usage block when `message_start` reports zeros, and ignore unknown extra fields — so a mount that is Anthropic-shaped-but-not-exact can still account tokens. Happy to test a build against real traffic and report the malformed rate before/after.

title: fix(proxy): parse compat-mount usage with a configurable provider dialect
body:
Fixes #1026.

## Root cause

Named compat mounts are built with `Provider: "openai_compatible"`, so usage
accounting runs through the shared OpenAI-shape parser. An upstream that
answers the Anthropic Messages wire shape on such a mount reports
`input_tokens` **exclusive** of cache reads/writes. The OpenAI-shape parser
treats `input_tokens` as cache-inclusive, so every cache-warm response trips
the cache-total-over-input contradiction check in `mergeSnakeUsage` and
classifies `provider_malformed` with `cache_status: unknown`. The verdict
flips with cache temperature because only warm rows carry a nonzero cache
read — which is why the issue's back-to-back identical probes alternated
complete/malformed.

Captured on the reporting mount (Z.AI GLM, before this change):

- cache-cold: `{"input_tokens":1316,"output_tokens":16,"cache_read_input_tokens":0,...}` → `provider_complete` / `miss`
- cache-warm, same body seconds later: `{"input_tokens":36,"output_tokens":4,"cache_read_input_tokens":1280,"server_tool_use":{"web_search_requests":0},"service_tier":"standard"}` → `provider_malformed` / `unknown`

The other three deviations from the issue were already handled and are now
pinned by tests: `message_start` zeros merge away against the final usage
block, a missing `cache_creation_input_tokens` counts as 0, and the extra
`server_tool_use` / `service_tier` fields are ignored.

## Change

New per-mount option `compat.<name>.usage_dialect` (default empty = shared
OpenAI-shape parser, behavior unchanged for every existing mount and
first-party adapter). `"anthropic"` keys the mount's usage parser to Anthropic
semantics. The dialect changes usage parsing only — routing, header mapping,
telemetry provider, and pricing keep the mount's `openai_compatible`
identity. Unknown dialect values fail config load instead of silently
reverting to the misreading parser.

Plumbed as `Base.UsageProvider` (empty keeps `Provider`), consumed by
`ParseUsage` and `NewUsageScanner`. Documented in
`docs/technical/configuration.md`.

## Tests

Captured-shape tests at the scanner level (warm cache hit, cold cache miss,
non-stream), the default-off verdict (unchanged malformed classification
without the opt-in), config parsing and validation, and the standalone
wiring. Full Go suite: 68/68 packages pass. A mutation check (dialect mapping
neutered) fails the warm tests with exactly the reported symptom, so the
tests catch the regression they guard against.

## Verification on the reporting mount

Before (2,705 rows, official bin-v1.1.6): 2,478 `provider_malformed` (91.6%),
`cache_status unknown` on every malformed row; 100 `provider_complete`
(75 `hit` / 25 `miss`); 122 `unavailable`.

After this build + `usage_dialect: anthropic` (33-minute window of live
Claude Code traffic, 45 requests, stream and non-stream):

- 45/45 `provider_complete` (100%), all `cache_status hit`, 0 malformed,
  0 unavailable
- token arithmetic now matches the wire: `input_tokens` 1316 = 36 fresh +
  1280 cached on the probe bodies
- probe matrix (2× stream, 2× non-stream, cache-cold then warm): 4/4
  `provider_complete` / `hit`
- cumulative `provider_malformed` counter stopped growing at the restart;
  the last malformed row was written by the old process 0.1 s before the new
  one started listening

`requests_eligible_for_compression` stays 0 on this mount and is NOT caused
by the usage misclassification: eligibility is gated by the compression
recovery path (`mcpRecoveryAvailable` — the caveman MCP retrieve tool or
wrap-verified recovery), which this client does not provide. That is a
separate mechanism this PR does not change.
