title: fix(stats): price rule overhead at the cache rate before net verdict
body:
`/caveman-stats` tells users on long agentic sessions to turn caveman off when the bill says caveman is saving them money.

`deriveNet()` subtracts the rules' input tokens (1,250 × turns) from the output tokens saved, as if both cost the same per token. They don't:

- every model in `MODEL_OUTPUT_PRICE_PER_M` bills input at 1/5 of its output rate;
- the rules ride the cached prefix, so after the first turn a Claude Code session reads them from cache at 0.1× the input rate.

Real session (Opus 5, 35 turns, every response a cache hit):

```
Est. tokens saved:     25,242 (~65% of output)
Est. rule overhead:    43,750 (input, ~1,250/turn over 35 turns)
Est. net:              -18,508 (caveman cost more than it saved for this workload — consider turning it off)
```

At billed rates that session saved about $0.63 of output and the rules cost about $0.03 of cached input. The lifetime view has the same problem: my `--all` shows `Est. net: -47,003 … consider turning it off` across sessions that were all net savings.

This goes in the same direction as docs/HONEST-NUMBERS.md ("Provider-billed A/B totals outrank output-only estimates"). The stats line was the one place that compared the two buckets 1:1.

## Approach

- `inputCostMultiplier(usage)` prices one input token of each response at that response's own logged mix: uncached 1×, cache write 1.25× (5m) / 2× (1h), cache read 0.1×. `parseSession` stores it per message.
- `ruleOverheadUsd()` sums 1,250 × multiplier × input price over the turns. Input price = output price × 0.2.
- `netLines()` adds `Est. net (USD)` when the model has a known price. The turn-it-off advice follows the USD net when there is one. When the token net is negative but the USD net is positive, the token line keeps its number and is relabelled `raw token count — the rules are mostly cached input, billed far below output; see USD net`.
- History rows gain `est_rule_overhead_usd` (omitted when the model is unpriced). The lifetime view shows a USD net only when every netted row carries the field, so the token and USD nets always describe the same sessions.

Every uncertain input is resolved so the rules look more expensive, never cheaper:

- a cache write with no TTL split is priced at the 1h rate (2×);
- Fable 5.1's 0.025× read rate is not used (0.1× everywhere);
- a response with no input breakdown is priced as fully uncached;
- the rules sit at the front of the prompt, the part most likely to be cached, yet each turn is priced at its average input token.

Unchanged: the token overhead and net lines (same numbers), `CAVEMAN_RULE_OVERHEAD_TOKENS`, and all output for unpriced or unknown models. The #145 regime (short, uncached replies) still reports a loss on both lines.

After (same 35-turn shape, test fixture):

```
Est. rule overhead:    43,750 (input, ~1,250/turn over 35 turns)
Est. net:              -18,530 (raw token count — the rules are mostly cached input, billed far below output; see USD net)
Est. net (USD):        +$0.603 (rules priced at this session's input mix, ~0.13× input rate)
```

## Testing

Six tests added to tests/test_caveman_stats.js. The first three below fail against unpatched main:

- cached 35-turn Opus 5 session: token net negative, USD net positive, no turn-it-off advice
- uncached single turn (#145): still negative on both lines, advice kept
- `inputCostMultiplier`: uncached / read / 5m / 1h / missing-TTL / empty usage
- history row carries `est_rule_overhead_usd` and the lifetime view nets it
- regression guards: no USD line for an unpriced model; no lifetime USD line when a netted row predates the field

Local runs: `tests/test_caveman_stats.js` 61/61, every `tests/*.js` file passes, `node --test tests/installer/*.test.mjs tests/hooks/*.test.mjs` 279/279, `python -m unittest discover -s tests` 137 OK, `tests/verify_repo.py` passes. `src/hooks/checksums.sha256` is regenerated for `caveman-stats.js`.

The stats SKILL.md and README each gain one sentence about the USD line. The hand-committed `plugins/caveman/skills/caveman-stats/SKILL.md` copy is left untouched.

title: test(agent): SIGKILL escalation test races worker startup
body:
**What happen**

The test `sandbox timeout waits for stubborn worker close after SIGKILL escalation` fails on loaded CI runners. It failed on PR #1015 in the `engine-ci` job `typescript`. The PR changes no file under `packages/agent/`. The same test failed earlier on PR #974, which changed only markdown.

The test asserts an elapsed-time window:

```js
assert.equal(elapsed >= 1_200 && elapsed < 3_000, true);
```

The failed job reported 1050 ms, below the 1200 ms floor. The assertions for `result.text === "terminated"` and `cave_sandbox_timeout` passed.

- Failed job: https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/actions/runs/34450460971/job/102784780302
- Commit: `18ec31ccc1cf0d220b162312a1a2eebf05d7ca23`, run attempt 1, no rerun

**Expected**

The test proves that the runtime sends SIGTERM, escalates to SIGKILL after 250 ms, and waits for child close. The proof must not depend on worker startup time.

**Before/after example**

Got (CI, Node 22):

```text
not ok 290 - sandbox timeout waits for stubborn worker close after SIGKILL escalation
  duration_ms: 1050.442215
  Expected values to be strictly equal:

  false !== true

  packages/agent/tests/framework.runtime.mjs:5850:10
```

Want: the test passes on every runner, or fails only when the runtime does not escalate to SIGKILL or does not wait for close.

**Likely mechanism**

- The fixture tool `ignore_timeout` sets `timeoutMs: 1_000` and installs `process.on("SIGTERM", ...)` only inside `execute()` ([fixture](https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/blob/18ec31ccc1cf0d220b162312a1a2eebf05d7ca23/packages/agent/tests/fixtures/sandbox-agent.mjs#L157)).
- The runtime starts the deadline before `spawn` ([runtime.ts#L4755](https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/blob/18ec31ccc1cf0d220b162312a1a2eebf05d7ca23/packages/agent/src/runtime.ts#L4755)). On timeout it sends SIGTERM and schedules SIGKILL 250 ms later ([runtime.ts#L4791](https://github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/blob/18ec31ccc1cf0d220b162312a1a2eebf05d7ca23/packages/agent/src/runtime.ts#L4791)).
- If worker startup consumes the deadline, SIGTERM arrives before the handler exists. The worker exits at once. The SIGKILL timer never fires. `elapsed` lands near 1000 ms.

This is the likely cause, not the proven one. `terminalError ??= error` keeps the first error, so it masks every exit cause after the abort. The runtime settles on `close`, not `exit`, so a process that exited just before the abort but closed after it is masked too. The passing assertions prove only that the close handler did not settle before the abort and that close came inside the 250 ms window. No runtime channel exposes worker readiness or the terminating signal.

An isolated probe with the same 1000 ms deadline and 250 ms escalation reproduces the mechanism (Linux, Node 24.8.0):

| Handler installed | Exit signal | Elapsed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before deadline | SIGKILL | 1320 ms |
| After deadline | SIGTERM | 1059 ms |

**Proposed fix**

1. Add a package-internal sandbox lifecycle observer to `executeSandboxedTool`: stderr chunks as they arrive, each signal sent, and close with code and signal. Do not re-export it from `src/index.ts`. Do not change the deadline or the `terminalError` semantics.
2. Make the fixture signal readiness. After it installs the SIGTERM handler, it writes one marker line to stderr. The worker runs under `unshare --net`, so loopback is not available; stderr is an inherited descriptor and the parent already receives it live.
3. Gate the escalation test on that marker. Give the tool a long `timeoutMs`, abort through `RunOptions.signal` when the marker arrives, then assert the ordered sequence SIGTERM → SIGKILL → close(SIGKILL) → run rejection. Prove that the rejection settled after close with a sequence counter, not wall-clock.
4. Add a separate startup-timeout test with a tiny `timeoutMs`. There, a prompt SIGTERM exit is correct.
5. Remove the elapsed-time assertion. Keep a bounded test timeout.

Lowering the 1200 ms floor lets the test pass without SIGKILL. Raising `timeoutMs` only moves the race threshold.

**Ownership**

`CLAUDE.md` routes Agent SDK work to `caveman-agent-sdk`. `engine-ci` runs the copy in this repository, so the fix must land here too. A PR with the readiness-gated test is in preparation.

**Related**

- #1015 — PR where the failure was observed; a comment proposes fake-clock or event assertions
- #974 — earlier failure of the same test on a markdown-only PR
- #995 — SIGKILL escalation for MCP shrink; does not change this test
- #942 — MCP subprocess timeouts; closed, does not address this test

**Platform**
- [x] Other: `packages/agent` test suite, `engine-ci` job `typescript`

**Version / install method**
- Commit `18ec31ccc1cf0d220b162312a1a2eebf05d7ca23`
- CI: Node 22, ubuntu runner

title: test(agent): gate SIGKILL escalation on readiness
body:
Fixes #1030.

The test `sandbox timeout waits for stubborn worker close after SIGKILL escalation` fails on loaded CI runners. It failed on #1015 and #974, which changed no file under `packages/agent/`. This PR removes the startup race from the test and replaces its wall-clock assertion with an event-order proof.

## Fixes

| Issue(s) | Root cause | Hosts/OS affected | Test added | Supersedes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| #1030 (seen on #1015, #974) | The fixture installed its SIGTERM handler inside `execute()`. The runtime starts the deadline before `spawn`. When startup consumed the deadline, SIGTERM arrived before the handler existed. The worker exited at once, the SIGKILL timer never fired, and `elapsed` fell below the 1200 ms floor. | `packages/agent` test suite, engine-ci job `typescript`, all OS | `sandbox abort waits for stubborn worker close after SIGKILL escalation` and `sandbox timeout during worker startup settles the run` in `tests/framework.runtime.mjs` | — |

## Change

- `src/runtime.ts`: adds a package-internal sandbox lifecycle observer. `executeSandboxedTool` reports each stderr chunk as it arrives, each signal it sends, and the child close event before the result settles. `src/index.ts` does not re-export the setter, so the public API does not change. An observer exception cannot change the tool outcome. The deadline, `terminate`, and `terminalError` semantics do not change.
- `tests/fixtures/sandbox-agent.mjs`: `ignore_timeout` writes one stderr marker after it installs the handler and uses a 10 s timeout. A new `startup_timeout` tool has a 1 ms deadline and no handler.
- `tests/framework.runtime.mjs`: the escalation test waits for the marker, aborts the run through `RunOptions.signal`, and asserts the order SIGTERM → SIGKILL → close(SIGKILL) → run rejection with a sequence counter. The startup-timeout test proves that a deadline during startup reaches the model context and settles the run.

The old floor of 1200 ms cannot be lowered without losing SIGKILL coverage. A longer `timeoutMs` alone only moves the race threshold.

## Verification

- `pnpm test` in `packages/agent`, in a privileged `node:22` container where user namespaces work: `tests 319 / pass 319 / fail 0`.
- The two new tests, 10 runs in a loop: `pass 2 / fail 0` on each run.
- Race proof: with `await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1_500))` inserted before the handler install, the escalation test still passes. The old test could not pass with that delay. The delay is not in the commit.
- `python3 tests/verify_repo.py`: all checks pass.
- Hosts with `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1` cannot run the `unshare`-based sandbox tests. Those tests fail there before and after this change with `Operation not permitted`.

## Ownership

## Validation

title: fix: preserve recovery-store locks and verify elisions
body:
## Problem

Native tool output could advertise a newly stored `ccr://` handle that a separate MCP reader immediately rejected as unknown. A long-lived producer still held an unlinked WAL/SHM pair while readers used newly created sidecars for the same database.

The cause is `secureSQLiteFile`: opening and closing an ordinary descriptor for the database or SHM file drops **all POSIX record locks held by that process on the inode**, including SQLite's locks. Both post-open permission checks and preparing a path already open elsewhere in the same process could therefore let a short-lived reader unlink a live writer's sidecars.

## Changes

Two separately reviewable, DCO-signed commits:

1. **Preserve SQLite locks while securing files.** Linux uses an inode-validated `O_PATH` descriptor and `fchmodat`, with a pinned procfs fallback for older kernels. Other Unix platforms use native no-follow chmod; Windows retains handle-based validation. Newly created files are closed before atomic, no-overwrite publication. Existing permission, symlink and inode checks remain in place. The shared helper also covers memory-store callers.
2. **Verify recovery before publishing Pi elisions.** The existing session recovery client verifies the advertised handle, exact byte length and SHA-256. A capability-gated `verify_only` mode on `caveman_retrieve` returns metadata without consuming the recovery delivery ledger. Missing, malformed, mismatched, old or unavailable recovery retains the original output, including non-text blocks.

No provider/OAuth routing changes, dependency additions, live-database migration code, or generated bundles are included.

## Reproduction and regression coverage

The storage regression keeps a writer open, opens and closes subprocess readers, then writes new objects and verifies both old and new originals from fresh readers. It also covers repeated same-process opens and direct path preparation. An independent reproduction failed with an unknown handle before this fix and recovered byte-identical content afterward.

Publication regressions cover missing/conflicting/malformed references, wrong proof hashes and lengths, older companions, failed/timed-out verification, preserved non-text output, and verification followed by the model's first full retrieval.

## Verification

On this PR branch, rebased onto current upstream `main`:

- `go build ./...` — passed
- `go vet ./...` — passed
- `go test ./...` — 68 packages passed; 4 have no tests
- `pnpm --filter @caveman-ai/pi test` — build/typecheck and all 38 tests passed

Additional verification of the same fixes before rebasing:

- Race-detector run of the cross-process locking regression passed.
- Forced `fchmodat2` failures using `strace -f -e inject=fchmodat2:error=ENOSYS`; the real older-Linux fallback passed both the independent reproduction and focused CCR permission/locking tests.
- CCR tests cross-compiled for Darwin/arm64 and Windows/amd64 (not runtime-tested locally).
- Deployed and exercised through installed OMP tools against a shared live producer: exact recovery at startup, after session replacement, and after consumer restart. An unavailable recovery store retained the original output. The formerly stranded handle became recoverable, and live SQLite integrity checks passed.

## Compatibility notes

Older MCP companions do not support non-consuming verification, so the updated Pi extension conservatively retains original output until the companion is upgraded. Availability verification is a publication-time check, not a promise against later deletion. This prevents new lock loss; it does not automatically repair already-diverged or corrupted databases.

title: feat(omp): add native extension lifecycle and package entry
body:
## Summary
Add a separately typed native OMP entry to @caveman-ai/pi while retaining the Pi entry and shared gateway/native-hook protocol. Keep session-owned recovery, routing and prompt context in one runtime with serialized, generation-safe lifecycle transitions.

- OMP prompt arrays preserve existing blocks; session switch/tree/branch invalidates old asynchronous work and renews per-session recovery.
- Provider overrides are removed and selected models restored to direct endpoints on closure. OMP has no model_select extension event, so routing is revalidated at before_agent_start; Pi retains its existing model_select handling.
- Compress only successful supported read/bash results; preserve error, recovery, mutation/custom-tool and non-text output behavior.
- Build and publish separate Pi/OMP entries, explicit manifest metadata, optional host peers and a package license notice.

## Related work / scope
Related installer proposal:#782. This is runtime-package lifecycle support, not another installer change. Separate from my recovery-store PR#1034: no recovery-store publication or locking changes here, and no running Caveman deployment was changed.

## Verification
- npm test: TypeScript/build and39 protocol/provider/recovery/runtime/integration tests pass.
- npm run test:omp: built manifest-selected native entry lifecycle regression passes (disposable MCP processes and HTTP fixture).
- Real OMP loader/ExtensionRunner/AgentSession: native Core policy delivered on ordinary prompt, fresh steer and promoted follow-up using isolated disposable gateway/native-hook/MCP protocol fixtures and a scripted model response. No live daemon or external model service accessed.
- npm package preview includes both built entries, README and LICENSE.

Tested OMP18.1.17 integration SHA6aef0e8ad51b3bc5ea7a5f2a255c3d48e4c5af72. The version string alone does not establish that published builds include external-input/queued-startup fixes. OMP's current project-trust compatibility API is not a sandbox.

AI-assisted implementation, independently reviewed for contract conformance, lifecycle correctness/hostile input, test honesty and unnecessary complexity. Commits carry DCO sign-off.

## Subagents

OMP rebinds every extension into each subagent session (task tool, eval `agent()`, `/tan` clones). Without this section's changes the runtime treated each of those as a full Caveman session: a new session in telemetry and proxy revival on `SessionStart`, an autopilot spawn on `SessionEnd`, Core injection plus `UserPromptSubmit` on every prompt, and `Stop` on every turn, all under the subagent's own id.

Requires OMP 18.5.1 or newer, the first release whose extension context carries `ctx.agent` (`{ kind: "main" | "sub", id, name, depth }`, can1357/oh-my-pi#13314). Older OMP has no `ctx.agent`; every session there keeps the previous behavior.

For a subagent (`ctx.agent?.kind === "sub"`):

- **Identity.** Every native-hook call sends the main session's id as `session_id`, so the runtime sees one session. The hook input also carries `agent_id` (`ctx.agent.id`) and `agent_type` (`ctx.agent.name`); the Caveman CLI does not read them yet. The id comes from the subagent's own session file, `ctx.sessionManager.getSessionFile()`, by layout: OMP names a top-level session file `<timestamp>_<id>.jsonl` and writes every session it spawns (task subagents, `/tan` clones, advisors) to `<that file minus .jsonl>/<agentId>.jsonl`, one directory deeper per nesting level. The runtime climbs to the top-level stem and reads the `id` in that file's header line. If the file is missing or unreadable (OMP persists lazily), it uses the id in the file name. If OMP exposes no file for the subagent, or the path is outside this layout, the subagent keeps its own session id. The header's `parentSession` is deliberately not used: it is a path for task subagents but a session id for `/tan` clones.
- **Lifecycle.** Start sends `SubagentStart`; shutdown or navigation away sends `SubagentStop`. A subagent never sends `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit` or `Stop`. `ModelBefore`/`ModelAfter`, `PreToolUse` and tool-result shrinking keep working with the same ids.
- **No compaction events.** A subagent sends neither `PreCompact` nor `PostCompact`. The runtime keys compaction state by session id, so under the main session's id a subagent compacting its own context would demote the main session's whole evidence store.
- **Routing gate.** The CLI prints nothing for `SubagentStart`, so its response is not used as the reachability signal. A subagent goes straight to the run-state and recovery gate and routes through a live proxy exactly like its parent. It prints no direct-mode or pass-through notice (the main session already did) and does not run the 3 x 300 ms retry loop when no run-state file exists, since `SubagentStart` starts no proxy.

**Behavior change: Core is no longer injected into subagents.** A subagent receives only the `additionalContext` that `SubagentStart` returns (none today). This matches Claude Code, where `SessionStart` context does not reach subagents.

The Pi entry (`index.ts`), main sessions and sessions without `ctx.agent` are unchanged. `shrinkToolResult` now takes the hook ids object instead of a session id string.

Known limit: OMP routes an advisor's tool calls through the advising session's `tool_call`/`tool_result` handlers with a `sub` identity. Those calls stay attributed to the advising session, without `agent_id`.

Tests added in `runtime.runtime.mjs` cover: `SubagentStart` with the main session's id and agent fields and no `SessionStart`; `SubagentStop` instead of `SessionEnd` (shutdown and navigation); no `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `PreCompact` or `PostCompact` from a subagent while a main session still sends them; only `SubagentStart` context reaching a subagent; an unchanged main session with and without `ctx.agent`; a `/tan` clone whose header `parentSession` is an id; session-id resolution for two-level nesting, absent intermediate and root files, an unreadable root, a non-session or id-less header, and the 64 KiB header cap; the own-id fallback; no notices and no retry sleeps for a subagent; and the gate opening for a subagent against a live run-state. `omp.runtime.test.ts` repeats the lifecycle through the built `dist/omp.mjs` with the real hook subprocess, a live run-state and a real recovery child.

title: fix(codex): stop rewriting shell commands for Codex, breaks saved approval rules
body:
Confirmed the mechanism. `shrinkHook()`'s dispatch treats `exec_command`/`shell`/`shell_command` (Codex) as another Bash-shaped tool and emits the same `permissionDecision: "allow"` + `updatedInput` shape. The function's own top comment never actually lists Codex among the harnesses it rewrites for, so this looks like Codex got folded in without the output branch being adjusted for it.

That rewrite is exactly what breaks your `prefix_rule`: it changes the command text Codex sees.

```
git add -A                          # what your rule matches
caveman shrink -- git add -A        # what shrinkHook actually sent Codex
```

This PR just stops rewriting for Codex tool events, same as any command the function already declines to touch, so the original command reaches Codex unmodified and your existing rule applies.

I don't have a live Codex to check the full round trip, so this is verified at the hook boundary only: `exec_command`/`shell`/`shell_command` now get no rewrite at all (empty stdout, same no-op the function already uses for anything it won't touch). title: npx --uninstall leaves the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL route in ~/.claude/settings.json, so Remote Control stays broken after uninstall
body:
**What happen**

`caveman setup --install` writes a persistent route into the user-scoped Claude Code settings:

```json
"env": {
  "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "http://127.0.0.1:8787/w/claude",
  "_CLAUDE_CODE_ASSUME_FIRST_PARTY_BASE_URL": "1"
}
```

The integration record at `~/.caveman/integrations/claude.json` owns exactly this: `owned.route = http://127.0.0.1:8787/w/claude`, `owned.assume_first_party = "1"`, `previous_route = null`.

As already documented in #947 and in `docs/technical/agent-wrapping.md` (section "Claude Code Remote Control"), this route makes Claude Code Remote Control unavailable. To get Remote Control back I uninstalled Caveman with the command both uninstall sections document:

```bash
npx -y github:JuliusBrussee/caveman -- --uninstall
```

After that, both env keys were still in `~/.claude/settings.json`, and Remote Control stayed broken. It only came back after I removed `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and `_CLAUDE_CODE_ASSUME_FIRST_PARTY_BASE_URL` from `settings.json` by hand.

**Why it happens (docs)**

- `INSTALL.md#uninstall` lists what `--uninstall` removes (hook entries, hook files, plugins, mode state) and what it does not remove. The env route written by `caveman setup --install` / `caveman enable claude` is in neither list.
- `docs/technical/install-and-update.md#uninstall` gives the same `npx … --uninstall` plus `npm uninstall -g @caveman-ai/cli`, and neither touches `settings.json` env.
- The only place that mentions `caveman disable claude` is the Remote Control section of `agent-wrapping.md`, which a user following the uninstall docs will not read.

So a user who uninstalls exactly as documented keeps a dead (or still-proxied) `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, and keeps the Remote Control breakage from #947, with nothing in the uninstall output pointing at the cause.

**Expected**

One of:

1. `--uninstall` also removes the CLI-owned route. The integration record already knows the owned keys and that `previous_route` was `null`, so there is nothing to restore, only two keys to delete.
2. Or the uninstall sections in `INSTALL.md` and `install-and-update.md` say to run `caveman disable claude` (or `caveman setup --agent-native claude --remove`) before `--uninstall` / `npm uninstall -g`, and `--uninstall` warns when it finds a Caveman route still in `settings.json`.

Separately, it would help if the install docs (not only `agent-wrapping.md`) mention up front that native routing disables Claude Code Remote Control.

**Before/after example**

```
Input:  npm install -g @caveman-ai/cli && caveman setup --install
        npx -y github:JuliusBrussee/caveman -- --uninstall
        claude remote-control
Got:    ~/.claude/settings.json env still contains ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787/w/claude
        and _CLAUDE_CODE_ASSUME_FIRST_PARTY_BASE_URL=1; Remote Control stays unavailable (#947)
Want:   both keys removed (previous_route was null), Remote Control available again
```

I did not test whether `caveman disable claude` removes the keys correctly; this report is about the documented uninstall path.

**Platform**
- [x] Claude Code
- [ ] Codex
- [ ] Other: ___

**Version / install method**

- `@caveman-ai/cli` 1.3.3 (`binary_release: bin-v1.1.6`), installed via `npm install -g @caveman-ai/cli`, then `caveman setup --install`
- Integration `pack_version` 2.2.0
- Claude Code 2.1.269 at install time, 2.1.270 now

title: fix(hooks): repair win32 junction handling in the flag write/delete guards
body:
## Symptom

Caveman mode drifts back to verbose prose mid-session on Windows machines where `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` (or `~/.claude`) is a directory junction to another drive — a common setup for anyone who keeps their home directory on a small system drive.

Two independent mechanisms both fail through the junction and compound into that symptom:

1. The per-turn reinforcement in `caveman-mode-tracker.js` is gated on a flag file that `safeWriteFlag` refuses to write, because its win32 symlink-parent check compares the resolved junction target against `os.homedir()` — the wrong proxy, since a junctioned config dir resolves to a realpath on a different drive with no home-directory prefix at all.
2. Even when the flag *can* be written elsewhere, `writeSessionMode`'s legacy-mirror cleanup deletes it with a bare `fs.unlinkSync`, which happily follows the same junction `safeWriteFlag` just refused to write through — so the one case where the write guard is doing its job is also the case where the delete path bypasses it and the file can never come back.

The SessionStart injection (`caveman-activate.js`) is not blocked by either bug — its own comment already explains why the per-turn reminder matters as much as it does:

> ```
> // 2. Emit full caveman ruleset, filtered to the active intensity level.
> //    The old 2-sentence summary was too weak — models drifted back to verbose
> //    mid-conversation, especially after context compression pruned it away.
> //    Full rules with examples anchor behavior much more reliably.
> ```
> — `src/hooks/caveman-activate.js:326-328`

That comment is upstream's own evidence for why this matters: the SessionStart ruleset is exactly what gets pruned by context compaction, and the per-turn reminder is the only thing that re-anchors behavior between SessionStart events. When the flag it depends on can never be written (or is destroyed and can't be recreated) on a junctioned config dir, that reinforcement silently stops firing for the rest of the session.

## Fixes (two commits, each independent)

1. **`fix(hooks): safeWriteFlag win32 guard uses writable-parent check, not home-prefix`** — replaces the `startsWith(homedir)` check with `fs.accessSync(dir, fs.constants.W_OK)`, testing what the guard actually cares about (can the current user write here) instead of a path shape that a junction breaks.
2. **`fix(hooks): guard the legacy flag delete path the same way its write path is guarded`** — adds `safeDeleteFlag`, mirroring `safeWriteFlag`'s junction-resolve + ownership/writable + no-symlink-target checks, and routes `writeSessionMode`'s legacy-mirror deletion through it instead of a bare `unlinkSync`. Before this, any prompt matching "stop caveman" / "normal mode" could destroy the flag through a junction even where the write path (correctly) refuses to touch it.

## A third defect that turned out to already be fixed

The original diagnosis (done against a plugin-cache install pinned at `655b7d9`) also found a SKILL.md-path off-by-one in `caveman-activate.js` — `path.join(__dirname, '..', 'skills', ...)` needing a second `'..'`. Checking current `main` before opening this PR: that one is already fixed, via #591 (`6d71b9e`, merged as `4520554`) — `skillPathCandidates()` in `caveman-config.js` now tries the correct two-levels-up path first and only falls back to the one-level-up path for the standalone-hook-install layout where it's actually correct. No action needed here; noted for the record since the branch this PR is based on is well past `655b7d9`.

## Testing

- `node --check` on the modified file.
- `node --test tests/hooks/caveman-config.test.mjs` — 24/25 pass; the one failure (`gcSessionStore refuses to follow a symlink out of the sessions dir`, `EPERM` creating a symlink without elevated privileges) reproduces identically on unmodified `main` in a separate worktree — pre-existing Windows-environment limitation, not a regression.
- `node tests/test_mode_tracker_stdin.js` — 17/18 pass; the one failure (`brevity trigger ("be brief") activates caveman at the default mode`, expects `full` got `ultra`) also reproduces identically on unmodified `main` in a separate worktree — a pre-existing environment leak (a repo-local `.caveman` config being picked up from an ancestor directory), not caused by this change.
- `src/hooks/checksums.sha256` regenerated for `caveman-config.js` in both commits, per the repo's own hook-integrity manifest.

title: fix(install): disable native agent integrations on uninstall
body:
`caveman enable claude` writes ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL (and the MCP entry) straight into settings.json and journals the previous value at ~/.caveman/integrations/claude.json so `caveman disable` can put it back. uninstall() never reads that journal, only the hook-based install state, so those keys survive `--uninstall` verbatim and Remote Control stays routed at a proxy that's gone.

Rather than re-implementing the journal restore in JS, uninstall() now shells out to `caveman disable --all` when the CLI is on PATH, before the hook cleanup runs. That restores every native agent (claude, codex, gemini, ...) in one call through the same code `caveman disable` already uses, and it's a no-op when nothing was ever enabled natively.

One gap this doesn't close: if `caveman` itself was already removed from PATH before `--uninstall` runs, there's nothing to shell out to and the journal is left alone. Same blind spot `claude plugin uninstall`/`gemini extensions uninstall` already have for their own missing binaries.

Added a test that stubs `caveman` and asserts uninstall calls `disable --all` (and that install itself never touches it). It fails on main, since nothing invokes the binary today. Ran the full `npm test` suite before and after: same 16 pre-existing failures on unrelated profile-scope tests either way, 261 passing plus the 2 new ones.

Fixes #1040

title: fix: move native-core.md out of pi's skills scan
body:
## Problem

When caveman is installed as a [pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono) package, pi collects every **direct `.md` child of the package's `skills/` directory** as a skill candidate (`SKILL.md` files from subdirectories, plus loose root-level `.md` files). `skills/native-core.md` is the native pack build source — consumed by `skills/compile.mjs` via `native_pack.core_source`, not a skill, and has no frontmatter — so pi warns `description is required` for it under the **[Skill conflicts]** banner on every launch.

## Fix

- Move `skills/native-core.md` → `skills/native/native-core.md`. pi only reads `SKILL.md` files from subdirectories, so the subdirectory is invisible to it.
- Relax the `native_pack.core_source` validator in `skills/compile.mjs` to allow subdirectory paths (still rejects `..` and absolute paths).
- Regenerate the compiled packs.

Instructions are embedded in the generated artifacts (`native-pack.generated.json`, `native-pack.generated.ts`, `skills/generated/*/pack.json`), so no consumer reads the source file at runtime.

## Verification

- `node skills/compile.mjs` passes; regenerated artifacts differ only in the `source` field.
- pi skill loader on a machine with this package installed: **34 skills, 0 diagnostics** (previously 1 warning).
- `packages/cli` native-enable test suite: same result before and after this change (pre-existing environment failures unrelated to this PR).

title: evals: isolate runs from local config, per-language prompts, pt-BR snapshot
body:
## What

Three changes to `evals/`, all MIT-side, no CI impact (no workflow reads the snapshot).

1. **Isolation.** `llm_run.py` called `claude -p` with the user's settings, hooks, CLAUDE.md, skills and MCP servers loaded. Measured with a probe prompt on my machine: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` was present in the *baseline* arm. Anyone with a "be terse" rule in their CLAUDE.md (or a hook/plugin that injects style rules) was measuring that in every arm. Every call now passes `--setting-sources "" --disable-slash-commands --tools "" --strict-mcp-config --no-session-persistence`. `--bare` would be simpler but it skips keychain reads and cannot authenticate.

2. **`--system-prompt-file`.** On Windows `shutil.which("claude")` resolves to `claude.CMD`; cmd.exe re-parses the multi-line SKILL.md argument (quotes, backticks, `&`) and the skill arm dies with `Input must be provided either through stdin or as a prompt argument when using --print`. The baseline and terse arms pass because their prompts are one short line, so the failure only shows up on the arm that matters. A temp file sidesteps every shell.

3. **Per-language prompts.** `CAVEMAN_EVAL_LANG=pt` reads `prompts/pt.txt`, uses a translated terse control (`Responda de forma concisa.`) and writes `snapshots/results.pt.json`. `CAVEMAN_EVAL_SKILLS=caveman` limits the run to named skills (20 skills × 10 prompts is a lot of calls for a language snapshot). English keeps its file names, so nothing that reads `results.json` changes.

## Why a Portuguese snapshot

SKILL.md promises "compress the style, not the language", and the rules are written against English function words (a/an/the, just/really/basically). Whether that transfers to a language with gendered articles and a different filler vocabulary was unmeasured; #812 reports language drift. This gives it a number.

## First pt-BR result (haiku-4-5, 10 prompts, single run)

| Arm | Tokens | vs baseline |
|---|---|---|
| baseline (no system prompt) | 3192 | — |
| terse control (`Responda de forma concisa.`) | 3096 | +3% |
| caveman | 2460 | +23% |

caveman on top of the terse control: **median +19%**, mean +19%, stdev 34%, range −43%..+69%. Same noise profile as the English snapshot: one prompt got longer, one got 69% shorter.

Language drift: zero English function words (`the/is/are/because/with/your`) in any of the 30 Portuguese replies, all three arms. With the current SKILL.md and haiku, the PT/ES leak in #812 did not reproduce.

## How to reproduce

```bash
CAVEMAN_EVAL_LANG=pt CAVEMAN_EVAL_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5 CAVEMAN_EVAL_SKILLS=caveman uv run python evals/llm_run.py
CAVEMAN_EVAL_LANG=pt uv run --with tiktoken python evals/measure.py
```

The English snapshot was **not** regenerated; it still carries `caveman-cn`/`caveman-es` arms that no longer exist as skills. Happy to refresh it in a follow-up if wanted, but that is a separate diff.

title: Codex integration (pack v2.2.0): base_url missing /v1, and chatgpt-auth tokens sent to platform API cause 401 missing scope api.responses.write
body:
**Versions:** caveman CLI 1.3.3, binary_release bin-v1.1.6, caveman-proxy running dev build on 127.0.0.1:8787. codex-cli 0.154.0. Codex integration pack_version 2.2.0.

**Bug 1 — wrong base_url written by the codex integration installer**

`caveman <agent> codex` (or whatever installs the integration) writes this to `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[model_providers.caveman]
base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8787/w/codex"
wire_api = "responses"
```

Codex's OpenAI-Responses client appends `/responses` directly to `base_url`, producing `http://127.0.0.1:8787/w/codex/responses`. The proxy doesn't recognize that path and 404s:

```
{"error":{"type":"cave_gateway_error","code":"cave_route_not_found","message":"Proxy path is not recognized."}}
```

Confirmed via direct curl: `/w/codex/responses` → 404 `cave_route_not_found`, `/w/codex/v1/responses` → routes correctly (gets a real upstream response). So `base_url` should be written as `http://127.0.0.1:8787/w/codex/v1` (matching the `/v1` the client expects to already be present, same convention as OpenAI's own base_url).

**Bug 2 — chatgpt-auth (OAuth) sessions get forwarded to the platform API and rejected**

After fixing base_url locally, requests reach the proxy and get forwarded upstream, but fail with:

```
401 Unauthorized: You have insufficient permissions for this operation. Missing scopes: api.responses.write.
url: http://127.0.0.1:8787/w/codex/v1/responses
```

`~/.codex/auth.json` has `auth_mode: "chatgpt"` (ChatGPT-plan OAuth login via `codex login`, tokens under `.tokens.access_token`, no `OPENAI_API_KEY`). It looks like the proxy is forwarding this ChatGPT session token straight to `api.openai.com/v1/responses` (the platform API), which requires `api.responses.write` — a scope ChatGPT-plan OAuth tokens don't carry (the codex login OAuth flow only requests `openid profile email offline_access api.connectors.read api.connectors.invoke`).

Reproduced with a fresh `codex login` (ruled out stale token) — same error both times.

**Workaround confirmed:** disabling the caveman `model_provider` override in `~/.codex/config.toml` (so Codex talks to OpenAI directly, provider `openai`) works immediately with the same ChatGPT login — confirming the OAuth session itself is fine, and the issue is specifically in how the proxy forwards `auth_mode: chatgpt` sessions.

**Suggested fix:** when `auth_mode` is `chatgpt`, the proxy should forward to the ChatGPT backend endpoint (e.g. `chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses`) instead of `api.openai.com/v1/responses`, same as native Codex does — rather than treating the OAuth access_token as if it were a platform API key.

**Bonus (non-blocking):** `GET /w/codex/v1/models` also 404s with `Proxy path is not recognized` — Codex logs this as an ERROR on every `codex exec` (background model-list refresh), doesn't block the session but is noisy.

title: Fix codex native/wrap route missing /v1; auto-repair stale auth-mode routing
body:
Fixes #1045.

**Bug 1: api-key route missing `/v1`**

`codexCavemanProviderToml` writes `base_url = ".../w/codex"` for api-key-mode codex sessions (both native install and ephemeral `wrap`). Codex's Responses client appends `/responses` directly onto that, giving `.../w/codex/responses` — but the proxy's own route table (`proxy/providers/openai/openai.go`) only matches `/v1/responses` (or `/openai/v1/responses`), never a bare `/responses`. Every api-key codex request 404'd with `cave_route_not_found` before reaching OpenAI.

Fixed by appending `/v1`, same as the existing `/w/aider/openai/v1` convention. Updated the two other places that construct/compare this route (`codexNativeMutations`, `nativeIntegrationStatus`) so install and `doctor` drift-checking stay consistent, plus the one test that hardcoded the old string.

**Bug 2: native install goes stale when auth mode changes**

`detectCodexWrapAuthMode()` is checked once, at install time, and baked into `config.toml`. If someone runs `codex login` afterward (switching from api-key to ChatGPT-subscription auth, or vice versa), nothing re-checks it — `caveman doctor codex` correctly reports `degraded`, but only if you think to run it. Added a small self-repair in the codex `SessionStart` hook: if status comes back degraded, it just runs the same repair `doctor codex --fix` does, instead of leaving a silent 401 waiting for the next session.

**Testing**

- `tsc --noEmit` clean.
- `node --test tests/codex-subscription-wrap.runtime.mjs tests/native-enable.runtime.mjs`: 38/39 pass — the 1 failure (`doctor reports Codex routing degraded when auth lane changes`) reproduces identically on unpatched `main`, so it's pre-existing and unrelated to this change.
- Verified end-to-end against a real Codex CLI session (both api-key-shaped and ChatGPT-subscription-shaped `auth.json`), confirming the route the proxy now receives actually resolves instead of 404ing.

title: codex: self-heal stale auth-lane routing after login
body:

Rebased onto current `main` after #1055. The original `/v1` route-fix half is intentionally dropped here because `main` already carries `CODEX_API_KEY_ROUTE` via #1015.

What remains in this PR:

This repairs stale `config.toml` routing after `codex login` switches between API-key and ChatGPT/subscription auth. title: fix: preserve Windows commands when shrink hook cannot identify the shell
body:
Windows coding hosts can report PowerShell commands as `tool_name: Bash` with only a `command` field. The shrink hook currently prepends a quoted executable path using Bash syntax; PowerShell treats it as a string and fails with `Unexpected token shrink`, blocking ordinary commands such as `git diff`.

Preserve commands on Windows when the hook cannot identify the execution shell. POSIX rewriting is unchanged, and explicit manual compression remains available. This applies the automatic-by-default-safe rule in `packages/cli/AGENTS.md`: optional compression must not change command execution semantics.

Validation: CLI build passed. Targeted shrink-hook tests passed 17 with four POSIX rewrite tests skipped on Windows. Regression cases exercise five host tool names, filenames with spaces, a successful diff, and a failing Git command through real PowerShell, preserving output and exit status. The formerly failing command also passed through an actual Windows Codex tool invocation after applying the guard. The full CLI suite was not run.

title: Native install always adds shrink-hook; think.shrink=false is not honored by enable/doctor --fix
body:
## Summary

`caveman enable <agent>`, `caveman doctor <agent> --fix` and `repairNativeAgent` always write the `caveman shrink-hook` PreToolUse entry into the agent's settings, regardless of the `think.shrink` config value. The only place `think.shrink` / `CAVEMAN_SHRINK` is consulted is the ephemeral launcher plugin (`caveman claude`), so there is no persistent way to run the native integration without the command-output rewrite.

## Where

`packages/cli/src/index.ts` (v1.3.3):

- `nativeMutationsFor` for Claude: `nativeHooksDocument("claude", true, settings)` — `includeShrink` is the literal `true` (around line 6932). Same for Gemini (`:7002`) and Codex (`:7391`).
- `nativeHooksDocument` (`:6434`) appends `${cavemanBinForHook()} shrink-hook` whenever `includeShrink` is true, with replace-not-accumulate semantics, so a manually removed entry comes back on the next repair.
- `think.shrink` is read into `noShrink` (`:3507`) and used only at `:5458` for `buildClaudeEphemeralPlugin`.

## Why it matters

Claude Code runs every matching PreToolUse hook in parallel and executes only one `updatedInput`. A user who already has a shell-command rewriter (in my case an `rtk hook claude` wrapper) gets it silently displaced by `shrink-hook`. On Codex, every `updatedInput` must carry `permissionDecision: "allow"`, so `shrink-hook` also widens the permission grant to everything on its allowlist (`gh`, `docker`, `kubectl`, `git push`, ...).

Removing the entry by hand works until `caveman doctor <agent> --fix` — which `caveman doctor` itself recommends as soon as the install is `degraded` — restores it. The only stable workaround today is `caveman disable <agent>`, which drops the lifecycle hooks and Core injection as well.

## Proposed fix

Have the native writer honor the persisted config: `nativeHooksDocument(agent, cfg.shrink, ...)` (or an explicit `--no-shrink` on `enable` / `doctor --fix` that is recorded in the integration journal), so `caveman config set think.shrink false` (or `CAVEMAN_SHRINK=0`) yields a native install with lifecycle hooks but no command rewrite, and repairs keep that choice.

## Repro

```bash
caveman config set think.shrink false   # or CAVEMAN_SHRINK=0
caveman enable claude
grep -c shrink-hook ~/.claude/settings.json   # expect 0, get 1
```

Related: #1037 (Codex re-prompt after the shrink rewrite) is a consequence of the same grant.

title: fix(cli): honor think.shrink in the native install, not just the launcher
body:
Closes #1049.

## What was wrong

`nativeMutationsFor` passed a literal `true` for `includeShrink` on all three native agents, so `caveman enable <agent>`, `caveman doctor <agent> --fix` and `repairNativeAgent` wrote the `shrink-hook` PreToolUse entry regardless of `think.shrink`. The only reader of that config (or `CAVEMAN_SHRINK`) was `buildClaudeEphemeralPlugin`, i.e. `caveman claude`. A hand-removed entry held until the next repair — and `caveman doctor` recommends that repair as soon as the install reads `degraded`.

The issue spells out why it is not just a preference: Claude Code runs every matching PreToolUse hook in parallel and applies **one** `updatedInput`, so an existing shell rewriter is silently displaced; on Codex every `updatedInput` must carry `permissionDecision: "allow"`, so the entry also widens the grant to everything on its allowlist.

## What changed

One helper reads the persisted value, and four call sites use it:

- `claudeNativeMutations`, `geminiNativeMutations`, `codexNativeMutations` — the three writers.
- **`nativeHookEntriesHealthy`** — the same helper, deliberately. Without it `doctor` keeps calling a correctly shrink-less install `degraded` and keeps recommending the `--fix` that used to reinstate the entry. That loop is most of the reported pain, and fixing only the writers would leave it in place.

Two sites keep the literal `true`, each with a comment saying why:

| site | why |
| --- | --- |
| `assertNativeHooksShape` | only reads event **names** to refuse a non-array; the superset is the safer set to check |
| `removeNativeHookEntries` | `disable` must withdraw an entry an earlier install wrote, whatever the config says now |

## What I wrote and then removed

A purge branch in `nativeHooksDocument` that dropped an already-present managed `shrink-hook` entry when the switch is off. It reads like the missing half of "replace, never accumulate" — but **no test could distinguish it**: `doctor --fix` rebuilds the document from the pre-install baseline, so the entry is never in `base` on that path, and the health check plus the repair already converge without it. I removed it rather than ship code no cell exercises. Happy to bring it back if you know a path that reaches it.

## Behaviour after this change

```
caveman enable claude                      # shrink-hook present (unchanged)
caveman config set think.shrink false
caveman doctor claude                      # degraded — honest: the install no longer matches the config
caveman doctor claude --fix                # entry removed, route + lifecycle hooks + Core kept
caveman doctor claude                      # installed
caveman doctor claude --fix                # no-op, not a reinstatement
```

`caveman enable claude` refuses while the install is degraded (pre-existing behaviour, and it names `doctor claude` in the message), so `--fix` is the route. The env form works the same and needs no repair because there is nothing to converge from:

```
CAVEMAN_SHRINK=0 caveman enable claude     # shrink-hook never written
```

## Tests

`packages/cli/tests/native-enable.runtime.mjs`, two cells, both starting from an accept control that proves the entry IS written with the rewrite on:

1. the persisted `think.shrink: false` path end to end — degraded → `--fix` → entry gone, `native-hook claude` and `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` intact → `installed` → a second `--fix` is a no-op → flipping back on restores it;
2. the `CAVEMAN_SHRINK=0` env form.

| mutation | red |
| --- | --- |
| writers back to the literal `true` (i.e. `main` today) | both new cells |
| health check back to the literal `true` | the persisted-config cell |

```
node --test tests/native-enable.runtime.mjs    34 pass, 0 fail
tsc --noEmit -p packages/cli/tsconfig.json     clean
```

One unrelated cell in the wider `pnpm test` run fails on this machine for a locale reason (`provider tokens 1.200 input` vs the expected `1,200`) — `de_DE` number grouping, present with or without this branch.

title: fix(cli): caveman enable <agent> doesn't start the local proxy it just wired config to
body:
Fixes #1051.

`caveman enable codex` writes config.toml to route Codex through the local caveman-proxy, but never starts or checks that the proxy is running. If nothing's listening yet (fresh install, reboot, or just running `enable` before ever launching through `caveman <agent>`), every Codex session after that hits a dead endpoint. The "stream disconnected before completion" error in #1051. The `caveman <agent>` shortcut already pre-starts the proxy after enabling; `enable` on its own never got that safety net.

Fix: best-effort, synchronous, fire-and-forget proxy spawn right after the config write succeeds. Not a reuse of `startWrapProxy`'s readiness-poll that loop's timer isn't `unref()`'d, so awaiting it would add up to a 2s hang to every `enable` call.

Verified: `pnpm lint` clean; `native-enable.runtime.mjs` 32/32 pass under WSL2 (fixtures don't run on native Windows, unrelated to this change); manual before/after on Windows confirms the proxy is spawned with the fix and isn't without it.

title: Codex Desktop ChatGPT Responses requests omit tools; standalone subscription compression cannot prove MCP recovery
body:
**Observed:**

- Actual HTTP Responses payloads are valid JSON and reach Caveman.
- Payload sizes commonly 300–650 KB.
- `caveman_retrieve` is callable from the Codex agent.
- But the provider-bound Responses JSON has no top-level `tools` member at all.
- `tool_choice:"auto"` is present, but `tools` is absent.
- Consequently request-scoped inspection sees zero `tools` and cannot see `caveman_retrieve`.
- `requests_eligible_for_compression` remains zero across hundreds of requests.

v2.5 release notes say standalone proxies prove recovery from the request's own tool list. Current Codex Desktop appears to keep its local/MCP tool registry out of the provider request, so this proof mechanism cannot succeed.

**Suggested direction:**
Allow Codex-native recovery proof based on a securely verified local MCP registration/session receipt rather than requiring the provider-bound tools array.

title: daily triage 2026-09-15: shrink compound-word corruption, win32 junction flag guards, codex enable proxy spawn
body:
Six fixes across three clusters. Every suite in the run book is green at HEAD, on top of a merge of current `main`.

> **Note on this run:** the container's `origin/main` ref was stale (`15581d1`) relative to the checked-out tip (`4df4b03`), so the branch was cut from an old base. `main` has since been merged in and every suite re-run against the merged tree. Three triage verdicts changed as a result and have been corrected on their threads (#575, #576, #1047) — details below.

## Fixes

| Issue(s) | Root cause | Hosts/OS affected | Test added | Supersedes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none (found during triage) | `\b` treats `-` as a word boundary, so a filler/hedge/pleasantry spelled as one component of a hyphenated compound matched and was stripped: `just-in-time` → `-in-time` | every host — `compressDescriptionsInPlace` rewrites MCP tool descriptions on `tools/list` | `tests/test_mcp_shrink.js` — 7 compounds + a "standalone words still dropped" guard | — |
| — | `safeWriteFlag`'s no-getuid branch required the resolved symlink target to sit under `os.homedir()`; a win32 directory junction resolves to another drive with no such prefix, so writes through a junctioned `~/.claude` were refused | Windows, junctioned `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` | `tests/test_symlink_flag.js` — reachable on POSIX by dropping `process.getuid` | #1041 |
| — | `writeSessionMode` cleared the legacy mirror with a bare `fs.unlinkSync`, which follows a symlinked parent that `safeWriteFlag` refuses to write through | all POSIX; win32 junctions | behavioural test (needs privileges, skips otherwise) + a source audit that holds on every runner | #1041 |
| — | `appendFlag` carries a byte-identical copy of the same home-prefix guard — the sibling #1041 missed. Left the lifetime stats log (`.caveman-history.jsonl`) silently dead on the same machines | Windows, junctioned `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` | `tests/test_symlink_flag.js` | — |
| #1051 | `caveman enable` writes the route into `config.toml` but never starts the proxy it just pointed at; the native SessionStart revive only fires after the host approves hooks, so a fresh Codex session hits a dead endpoint | Codex (all OS) | `packages/cli/tests/native-enable.runtime.mjs` — verified it fails without the source change | #1052 |
| — | Two defects in that adopted startup, caught by Devin Review: it ignored `opts.noProxy` (every other spawn site gates on it), and it sat inside the fresh-install-only callback, so a repeat `enable` — exactly what someone does when the route is dead — started nothing | Codex + every native agent, all OS | two regression tests, both verified to fail without the change | — |
| none (found during triage) | `agent-shortcut` fixtures spread `process.env` and strip only `CAVE_GATEWAY_URL`/`CAVE_TRANSFORM_IDS`/`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, so an exported `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` reaches the stub and reads as an injected value. Two "must not inject" tests fail on any such machine | contributors with a gateway configured — i.e. caveman's own users | fixes the two existing tests; scoped after verifying the other 7 suites referencing the var pass untouched | — |

### Merge resolution

One conflict, in `src/mcp-servers/caveman-shrink/compress.js`: `main`'s `5506ba8` added the CJK byte-identical short-circuit for #575 while this branch changed the same regex block. Resolved by re-applying the boundary patch onto `main`'s file, so both hold and are orthogonal — the CJK guard short-circuits before the regexes ever run, and the boundary change only affects the pure-English path. Verified:

```
"Enable just-in-time compilation" -> "Enable just-in-time compilation"   (compound intact)
"这是一个 a LLM 模型"              -> "这是一个 a LLM 模型"                (byte-identical)
"This is just a maybe wrong value" -> "This is wrong value"              (standalone fillers still dropped)
```

### Review round (Devin Review, 4 findings — all answered)

Two were real and are fixed in `ebbe417` (`noProxy` gate; repeat-`enable` revival), each with a regression test proven to fail without it. Two are answered on their threads rather than patched:

- **aider excluded from proxy startup** — not an oversight. `packages/cli/CLAUDE.md` records the same exclusion for the agent shortcut ("not aider, whose hookless native install could never start the proxy"), and aider is the one native agent installed with no MCP binary, so the recovery flag here would stamp `CAVEMAN_RECOVERY=mcp` onto a proxy with no `caveman_retrieve` tool behind it. The dead route predates this PR; aider is left exactly as it was. Devin's alternative — stop writing a persistent route for aider at all — looks like the better long-term answer and is in "needs decision" below.
- **win32 junction security** — the judgement call below.

### One judgement call worth your eyes

Both junction fixes replace the home-prefix check with `fs.accessSync(dir, W_OK)`, which on Windows is a weak test. I adopted it because **the check it replaces was not a security boundary either**: an attacker who can plant a junction at `~/.claude` can equally point it at another directory *inside* the home dir and satisfy `startsWith(homedir)`. It constrained where a redirect lands, not whether one happens — while breaking the cross-drive junction it was documented as allowing. The precondition also already implies worse: that directory is where caveman's installer writes `settings.json` hook commands, so anyone holding that access has code execution by a shorter route. The guards doing real work are untouched (`O_NOFOLLOW`, `0600`, target-must-be-a-directory, flag-must-not-be-a-symlink).

If you want strictness back, the principled version isn't a path-prefix test — resolve the junction **once at install time** and record the realpath in the install journal, so the trust decision happens where a human is present rather than on every hook invocation under a 5s budget. Happy to do that as a follow-up.

## Triaged, not fixed

- **#575** (CJK articles): **already fixed on `main`** by `5506ba8` — verified all four reported rows now pass through byte-identical. My first comment on that issue said otherwise; it was written pre-merge and has been corrected on the thread. Looks closeable.
- **#1053** (Codex Desktop omits `tools`): not reproduced — needs Codex Desktop + a ChatGPT subscription. The ask (accept a local MCP registration receipt as recovery proof) is a proof-model change, your call.
- **#1035** (Enterprise marketplace scan), **#1017**, **#864** (Snyk `W007`): one cluster, all three scanners flagging the same thing — SKILL.md instructing the model to preserve code, commands and exact error strings verbatim. That is caveman's core contract, so this is a policy question rather than a bug. Not touched.
- **#403** (caveman-stats on Gemini): root cause confirmed by reading the source — `caveman-stats.js` defaults to `~/.claude` and walks a Claude-shaped `projects/*.jsonl`. Real, but a new host backend is more than a triage slot — and CLAUDE.md already says Gemini should use its native `/stats`, so a backend may not be the wanted shape. PR #563 is adjacent.
- **#278** (comments deleted from edited code): plausible and serious, but not reproducible deterministically here, and the fix is SKILL.md wording whose efficacy I cannot verify. `SKILL.md:90` already says persisted artefacts get normal prose; it never says *don't delete existing comments*. Suggest adding that explicitly — flagging rather than guessing at your voice.
- **#186** (Cowork), **#312** (Gemini "Void tasks"), **#725**, **#523**: not reproducible in this environment (need the respective hosts).
- **#733**, **#727**, **#991**, **#716**, **#703**: savings/benchmark numbers — out of scope for this run by standing rule. Not touched.
- **agent-drift #976, #977, #978, #979, #988, #989, #990, #1021, #1054**: nine bot issues, one per agent, no duplicates. Mechanical pin bumps, but the pin *is* the assertion that `agent-conformance.yml` passed at that version, and that workflow installs nine upstream agents and builds the Go proxy. Bumping them here would assert verification I did not perform. Left for a conformance run. Not commented on (bot issues).

title: fix(shrink): finish the shutdown sequence when the upstream ignores stdin EOF
body:
Follow-up to #995, which you asked for as its own PR: the stdin-EOF orphan I reported there but deliberately left out.

## The bug

`caveman-shrink` is an MCP **client** to the upstream it spawns, so teardown is the sequence the spec gives that client ([lifecycle, Shutdown > stdio](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/lifecycle#stdio)):

> 1. First, closing the input stream to the child process (the server)
> 2. Waiting for the server to exit, or sending `SIGTERM` if the server does not exit within a reasonable time
> 3. Sending `SIGKILL` if the server does not exit within a reasonable time after `SIGTERM`

`endInput()` does step 1 and stops there. #995 added steps 2 and 3, but only behind `process.on(SIGTERM|SIGINT|SIGHUP)`, which is the path where the host signals us. Closing our stdin is the *first* thing a host does to shut an stdio server down, and on Windows it is the only thing: the comment at `index.js:108` already says teardown there "goes through the stdin EOF", and that is exactly the path with nothing behind it.

So an upstream that does not exit on EOF keeps itself and the wrapper alive, and the host waits on both.

## Repro, against current main (4df4b03)

An upstream that ignores EOF and would honour a signal if one ever arrived:

```js
// stubborn-server.js
process.stdin.resume();
process.stdin.on('end', () => { /* deliberately ignored */ });
setInterval(() => {}, 1000000);
```

Spawn the wrapper around it, close the wrapper's stdin, wait 10s:

```
$ node repro.js src/mcp-servers/caveman-shrink/index.js
client closed the wrapper stdin
STILL ALIVE after 10000ms - wrapper hung, upstream orphaned
```

Same repro on this branch:

```
client closed the wrapper stdin
wrapper exited after 2844ms  code=143 signal=null
```

800ms to the EOF, one 2s grace, then SIGTERM. This upstream does not trap it, so the SIGKILL step was not needed. 143 is `128 + SIGTERM` through the existing `onClose` contract, and it is accurate: that upstream did not shut down on its own.

## The change

`closeInput()` passes the EOF on, then arms the same grace period and falls into the existing `forward('SIGTERM')`, which already escalates to SIGKILL. Same constant, same escalation, reached from either entry point.

`forward` moves out of the returned object literal to a named function so `closeInput` can call it without `this` inside a timer callback. The body is unchanged apart from folding the two `exitCode/signalCode` checks into a shared `upstreamGone()`.

## Nothing is signalled on the normal path

A server that exits on EOF fires `close`, which clears the wait before anything is sent. Measured end to end against a server that answers `tools/list` and exits on EOF:

| | main | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| exit | 452ms, code 0, no signal | 448ms, code 0, no signal |
| response | compressed identically | compressed identically |

## Tests

34 pass, 0 fail (28 on main). The six new ones use the injected timers from #995, so they stay synchronous.

Each was checked against a broken variant rather than taken on trust:

| mutant | caught by |
|---|---|
| EOF arms no wait at all | escalates EOF through SIGTERM to SIGKILL; a repeated EOF does not arm a second wait |
| EOF signals immediately instead of waiting | does not signal an upstream that exits on EOF (+3 more) |
| `onClose` leaves the EOF wait armed | close clears a pending EOF wait |
| EOF is never passed on to the upstream | passes client EOF on to the upstream; EOF on an already-exited upstream arms nothing |
| the repeat guard is dropped | a repeated EOF does not arm a second wait |
| a wait is armed for an already-dead upstream | EOF on an already-exited upstream arms nothing |
| the escalation goes straight to SIGKILL | escalates EOF through SIGTERM to SIGKILL |

No mutant survived, and the detector itself reports nothing against the unmutated file.

`npm test` is unchanged by this: 351 pass on both main and the branch, and the same 11 installer tests fail on both (one symlink case, nine `powershell.exe` manifest cases, one `pwsh.exe` case). None of them are in caveman-shrink, and the two failure lists are byte-identical.

## Limits, unchanged from #995

The escalation still reaches the direct child only. An upstream that is really a launcher can leave the server running as a descendant holding the inherited stdout pipe, which also keeps `close` from firing. Owning the whole process tree is the larger change you and I both described on #995 and it is not attempted here.

Also: `tests/test_mcp_shrink.js` is touched by #1055, but its hunk is at line 113 in the compress tests and mine start at 360, so the two merge without a conflict.

title: Bedrock cache-points optimizer corrupts integers >2^53 anywhere else in the request body
body:
## What

`ApplyProviderNativeTransforms` in the Bedrock adapter's cache-points optimizer decodes the whole request body into `map[string]any`, mutates the map to add one `cachePoint`/`cache_control` marker, then re-marshals the entire document with `json.Marshal`. Go decodes untyped JSON numbers into `float64`, which only represents integers exactly up to 2^53 (9007199254740992). Any integer literal anywhere else in the body at or above that bound is silently rounded to the nearest representable double on the way back out, with no error and no signal.

A tool-result payload carrying a large id, a snowflake, a timestamp, or a monetary amount in cents has nothing to do with the cache marker being injected, but gets corrupted whenever the optimizer fires.

## Where

`proxy/providers/bedrock/cache_points.go`: `ApplyProviderNativeTransforms` decodes at line 53-54 (`json.Unmarshal(data, &root)`), the `injectConverseCachePoint`/`injectAnthropicCacheControl` helpers mutate the decoded map, and line 75 (`json.Marshal(root)`) re-marshals the whole document.

The rest of the codebase already avoids this: `proxy/providers/anthropic/cache_breakpoints.go`'s `injectBreakpointRaw` and `proxy/providers/openai/cache_key.go` decode only to make decisions, then splice the marker into the original byte slice via `proxy/providers/jsonsplice`, leaving every other byte untouched. `cache_points.go` has no splice attempt at all.

## Repro

```go
var root map[string]any
json.Unmarshal([]byte(`{"amount_cents":9007199254740993}`), &root)
out, _ := json.Marshal(root)
// out == `{"amount_cents":9007199254740992}`
```

Against the actual adapter method: a Converse request with a stable `system` prefix (so the optimizer fires) and a `toolResult` containing `amount_cents: 9007199254740993` comes back with `amount_cents: 9007199254740992` in the bytes that get signed and sent to Bedrock.

## Scope

Requires the operator to have the `bedrock-cache-points` optimizer enabled (off by default) and PAYG Converse/Invoke traffic on a cache-eligible Claude-on-Bedrock model with a stable tools/system prefix. Any deployment that does enable it (its documented purpose) is exposed on every matching request that happens to carry a >2^53 integer anywhere in its body, which is plausible for agentic tool-call traffic.

title: fix(bedrock): splice cache markers instead of decode-remarshal
body:
Fixes #1057

## Root cause

`ApplyProviderNativeTransforms` decoded the request into `map[string]any`, mutated the map to add a cache marker, then re-marshaled the whole document. Go decodes untyped JSON numbers into `float64`, exact only up to 2^53, so any larger integer anywhere else in the body (a tool-result id, a timestamp) was silently rounded on the way out.

## Fix

Splice the marker into the original bytes instead, matching the pattern `proxy/providers/anthropic/cache_breakpoints.go` and `proxy/providers/openai/cache_key.go` already use via the `jsonsplice` package. `jsonsplice` had no array-append primitive (only `AppendObjectFields`, for inserting fields into an object), needed here because both injection paths append a whole new `cachePoint` element rather than augmenting an existing one, so this adds `AppendArrayElements` alongside it.

## Verified

- Added a regression test that asserts a >2^53 integer survives byte-for-byte, for both the Converse and Invoke injection paths. Without this fix, it fails.
- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `go test ./...` all pass across the full repo, run in a golang:1.26-bookworm container.
- `gofmt -l` is clean on every changed file.
- I have not run this against the Windows or macOS legs directly; the change is plain `encoding/json` and `jsonsplice`, no OS-specific paths.

title: repointel's 500-symbol cap doesn't hold across sibling declarations in the CGO_ENABLED=0 build
body:
scanSymbols in symbols_nocgo.go tries to enforce the package's own 500-symbol-per-file cap by returning `len(out) < 500` from the ast.Inspect callback. That return value only controls whether Inspect recurses into that node's own children, it says nothing about later siblings. Top-level func/type declarations in a Go file are siblings in file.Decls, so once the cap trips inside one declaration, returning false only stops the rest of that declaration: every subsequent top-level decl in the file is still visited and appended.

A Go file with 600 top-level funcs comes back with 600 symbols under this build, not 500. symbols_cgo.go doesn't have this bug, it checks len(*out) >= 500 at the top of every recursive call before appending. build-release-binaries.mjs always sets CGO_ENABLED=0, so it's the broken nocgo path every shipped binary actually runs. Bites hardest on generated or vendored Go with lots of top-level declarations: protobuf stubs, mockgen output, big const tables.

title: fix(repointel): recheck the 500-symbol cap before every append, not after
body:
Fixes #1059

scanSymbols in symbols_nocgo.go checked the 500-symbol cap with `return len(out) < 500` from the ast.Inspect callback. That return value only prunes descent into the current node's own children, not later siblings, and top-level func and type decls in a Go file are siblings in file.Decls: once the cap is hit inside one declaration, returning false only skips the rest of that one, every later top-level decl still gets visited and appended. symbols_cgo.go already gets this right, checking len(*out) >= 500 before appending, and it's the nocgo variant that every shipped release binary actually runs (build-release-binaries.mjs always sets CGO_ENABLED=0).

Moved the check to the top of the closure, same shape as the cgo file.

Test builds a source string with 600 top-level funcs and asserts scanSymbols caps at 500: red on main, green here. Ran it under CGO_ENABLED=0 since that's the tag this file needs. The repo's `go test ./...` CI job links symbols_cgo.go by default, which was already correct, so this file isn't otherwise exercised under the build config that actually ships.

title: middleware: revoked scope tombstones are never reclaimed, wedging the shared capacity cap
body:
Revoking a session (`sessions/delete`) writes a tombstone that `Expire` can never reclaim, so revocation traffic alone can permanently exhaust the shared 100,000-row / 64MB capacity cap across every principal using the store.

`Delete` marks a revoked scope by setting `expires_at=0` (`proxy/internal/store/middleware.go`, `MiddlewareTx.Delete`). `Expire`'s reclaim query only ever selects rows where `expires_at>0 AND expires_at<=now` (`middlewareExpire`'s `dead` selection and its final scope-row delete). A row with `expires_at=0` can never satisfy `expires_at>0`, so a revoked scope's row, and the choice rows `purge()` leaves behind with their payload zeroed but the row intact, are never selected by any of `Expire`'s statements. They sit forever.

This is the same class of bug `c41b81f` fixed for elapsed scopes (an unreachable reclaim branch wedging the row cap), but for the other trigger: revocation, which is the protocol's own normal way to end a session early, needs no elapsed timer and no malformed input.

Reproduced against a real `Store`/`MiddlewareTx` (no mocks) on HEAD `4df4b03`:

```go
s, _ := store.Open(path, nil)
s.InitMiddleware(ctx)
s.WithMiddleware(ctx, func(tx *store.MiddlewareTx) error {
	tx.SaveScope(store.MiddlewareScope{ID: "s", Authority: "auth", Manifest: []byte("[]"), ExpiresAt: 1 << 40})
	return nil
})
s.WithMiddleware(ctx, func(tx *store.MiddlewareTx) error { return tx.Delete("auth") })
// 50 Expire() passes at an arbitrarily far-future time
for i := 0; i < 50; i++ {
	s.WithMiddleware(ctx, func(tx *store.MiddlewareTx) error { return tx.Expire(1 << 62) })
}
scope, err := ... tx.Scope("s") // still returns the row, err == nil, unchanged
```

The row survives every `Expire` call regardless of how far into the future `now` is. Filling a store past the row cap with only revoked scopes (no elapsed ones) reproduces `SaveScope` returning `ErrMiddlewareCapacity` forever, with no `Expire` pass ever draining it.

Go 1.26, `go test ./proxy/internal/store/...` at HEAD `4df4b03ba538751131d24415c59a1fad0d8c2c18`.

title: fix(middleware): reclaim a revoked scope's tombstone after its own grace period
body:
Fixes #1064.

`Delete` marks a revoked scope with `expires_at=0`, and `Expire`'s reclaim query only ever selects `expires_at>0` rows. A revoked scope's row, and the choice rows `purge()` leaves behind with a zeroed payload, can never be selected, so every `sessions/delete` call leaves one permanent row against the shared capacity cap. This is the same wedge `c41b81f` fixed for elapsed scopes, for the trigger that fix didn't cover.

`Delete` now records the revocation time as `-now` instead of the bare `0`. `Expire` treats any `expires_at<=0` as immediately payload-dead (same schedule as an elapsed scope, so choices/plans/an authority's dropped credit reclaim right away) and its final scope-row delete reclaims a revoked row once `-expires_at` is past one `MiddlewareGraceSeconds` window, mirroring the elapsed-scope tombstone exactly. `previousPlan` and `Grant`, the two readers of the old `expires_at==0` sentinel, move to `expires_at<=0` so a scope still answers "deleted" for the whole grace window, never earlier.

Verification (Go 1.26, Docker, HEAD `4df4b03`):
- New `TestMiddlewareRevocationTombstoneSurvivesGraceThenReclaims`: with the old `Delete`/`Expire` the tombstone never leaves the store; with this change it survives one tick short of grace and is gone exactly at the deadline.
- New `TestMiddlewareExpiryReclaimsCapacityFromRevokedScopes` mirrors the repo's own elapsed-scope capacity test with revoked scopes as the sole trigger: seeds past the 100,000-row cap with `expires_at<=0` rows only, confirms admission stays capped, then confirms `Expire` drains the store to empty and admission recovers.
- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `go test ./...` all pass repo-wide; a coverage run of `go test ./proxy/internal/store/... ./proxy/internal/middleware/...` confirms every changed line is exercised.
- Not run under coverage instrumentation: `TestMiddlewareAcceptanceTwentyTurnsAcrossProcesses` re-execs the test binary as a subprocess and fails whenever `-coverprofile` is enabled, a pre-existing interaction with this repo's own test that has nothing to do with this change. I measured coverage with that one test skipped instead.

A related, smaller gap I did not fix: an authority whose only scope was ever revoked (never elapsed) still keeps its `middleware_originals` credit row forever, since the drop for that row was never wired to a grace window at all. Flagging it rather than folding it into this diff.

title: trial: all-zero report when native routing is active; the trial's proxy never receives traffic and RecordPayload drops local labels
body:
**What happen**

On a native install, `caveman trial` produces a report with every counter at zero, even though the agent ran fine and the proxy was recording the whole time.

Report: Requests 0, Input tokens 0, Output tokens 0, Total cost $0.0000, Modeled dollar delta $0.0000. Usage Origins and Plan/Quota Windows both say nothing was imported. The one optimizer row comes back `insufficient_data`.

Nothing errored. The trial exited 0, and 29 requests were recorded during its window. They just went to a different proxy than the one the trial was reading.

Local evidence:

```
sqlite> SELECT * FROM trial_runs;
trial_mu38xdz3|claude|claude|2026-09-15T22:31:13Z|2026-09-15T22:36:09Z|0|

sqlite> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM requests
   ...> WHERE ts >= '2026-09-15 22:31:13' AND ts <= '2026-09-15 22:36:09';
29

sqlite> SELECT DISTINCT label FROM requests;
local

sqlite> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM trial_payloads;
0
```

29 requests inside the trial window, all labelled `local`, zero payloads captured.

What I think is happening:

The trial starts its own proxy on its own port with a trial label (`packages/cli/src/index.ts:15503`):

```js
env: { ...process.env, CAVEMAN_LISTEN: listen,
       CAVEMAN_LABEL: `trial:${trialID}`, CAVEMAN_MODE: "record" },
```

In my run that was `127.0.0.1:40873`, which shows up in `proxy.log` at the trial's start time. But Claude Code went to `127.0.0.1:8787` instead, the persistent listener from the native install, because `settings.json` pins `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and that beats whatever the trial injects into the child.

The 8787 proxy has no `CAVEMAN_LABEL`, so `labelOrDefault(rc.Label, "local")` labels everything `local`. And `RecordPayload` (`proxy/internal/store/trial_store.go:43`) drops anything without a `trial:` prefix:

```go
trialID := strings.TrimPrefix(label, "trial:")
if trialID == "" || trialID == label {
    return
}
```

So `trial_payloads` stays empty, the replay optimizer has nothing to replay, and every number in the report renders 0.

If that's right, native routing and `caveman trial` are mutually exclusive, and there's no way to tell from the output.

**Expected**

Either point the child at the trial's listener, or check for a pinned `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` at startup and refuse with an explanation.

Separately, the report shouldn't render "nothing captured" in the same typography as a measurement. `Requests 0 / Total cost $0.0000` laid out like a result reads as "caveman found nothing to save," when the accurate statement is that this trial never saw any traffic. The caveats section also describes retention rules for payloads that were never captured, which adds to the impression that something was measured.

**Related**

This looks like the second half of #908 ("it is wrap's env injection that has no effect"). That issue was closed on the MCP-recovery half via #929. The env-injection half still reproduces, and the trial path makes it visible.

**Platform**
- [x] Claude Code
- [ ] Codex
- [ ] Other: ___

**Version / install method**
- caveman CLI 1.3.4, binary release bin-v1.1.7
- plugin `caveman@caveman` 2.7.0
- Linux x86_64, Node 24.16.0
- Native integration active: `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8787/w/claude`, `_CLAUDE_CODE_ASSUME_FIRST_PARTY_BASE_URL=1`
