title: pi: caveman_retrieve with query returns a silent excerpt, though the handle says one call returns the entire original
body:
## Summary

In pi, a shrunk tool output ends with:

```text
recover: call caveman_retrieve with recovery_handle="ccr://ccr_obj_…" to get these bytes back in full — one call returns the entire original.
```

The `caveman_retrieve` tool also has an optional `query` parameter, described as "One broad description covering every detail needed from this handle". When the agent passes `query`, as that description invites it to, the result is an excerpt and not the entire original:

```text
… [caveman: non-adjacent] …

trial 2: head: '{"protocol_version":1,…}'
…
… [caveman: non-adjacent] …
```

In our session, lines that the agent needed were left out: the first trial and the restore status. Only a second call without `query` returned them. The excerpt does not say how much is missing.

## Environment

pi 1.3.0, the `@caveman-ai/cli` 4.0.1 pi extension, and the `bin-v4.0.2` runtime.

## Why it matters

The handle says that one call returns everything, and the tool schema suggests a `query`. An agent that follows both believes it has the whole output when it has a filtered part. That is a correctness problem: the agent can act on missing lines without knowing. It is also a token problem, because the agent needs a second request to get the rest.

## Suggestions

- Make the handle text match the behavior. For example: "call caveman_retrieve with only recovery_handle to get the entire original; add query to get the matching excerpt".
- Put a header on excerpt results that gives the size, for example `excerpt: 14 of 61 lines; call again without query for all of it`.
- Or leave `query` out of the default pi tool schema, so that one call does return the entire original.

Related: #1365.

title: Corrupt ccr.db stays corrupt after upgrades: recoveries table damage with the #1149 pattern, and no check or repair
body:
**What happen**

My `~/.caveman/ccr.db` is corrupt. The damage has the same pattern as #1149, on a different operating system and a later version. #1149 is closed. #1103 fixed the dropped compression error, so `proxy.log` now shows a WARN line for each failed write. #1149 did not name a cause for the corruption. The two suggestions that #1103 did not fix (an off-state in `caveman status` and a `quick_check` in `caveman doctor`) wait for a maintainer decision.

`PRAGMA quick_check` on my store, from a read-only connection, on 2026-10-23:

```
*** in database main ***
Tree 2 page 19153 cell 4: Rowid 418 out of order
Tree 2 page 1095 cell 1: Rowid 8 out of order
Tree 2 page 1095 cell 1: 2nd reference to page 1054
wrong # of entries in index sqlite_autoindex_recoveries_1
```

`PRAGMA quick_check` in #1149 (macOS arm64, `bin-v2.0.0`):

```
*** in database main ***
Tree 2 page 2 cell 0: 2nd reference to page 8014
Tree 2 page 3868 cell 2: Rowid 42 out of order
Tree 2 page 3868 cell 2: 2nd reference to page 3876
Tree 2 page 2604 cell 1: Rowid 25 out of order
Tree 2 page 2604 cell 1: 2nd reference to page 2590
wrong # of entries in index sqlite_autoindex_recoveries_1
```

The two reports have these facts in common:

- Tree 2 is the `recoveries` table in both stores.
- The damage is out-of-order rowids, pages with two parents, and a wrong entry count in the handle index `sqlite_autoindex_recoveries_1`.
- In my store, `PRAGMA integrity_check('typed_objects')` reports `ok`. Only the `recoveries` table and its index are damaged.

The same damage in the same table on two machines points to a defect in how Caveman writes the store, not to a disk fault.

Details of my store:

- No frame in `ccr.db-wal` contains a damaged page. So the damage is in the main file. A checkpoint wrote it on or before 2026-10-16 11:38, the last change of the main file.
- The handle index has 2,351 entries for 2,348 rows.
- Four rows are affected. All four are from 2026-09-01 to 2026-09-05:

  | Handle | Created | Problem |
  |---|---|---|
  | `ccr_c0183cc37945b915e0a32d94ae92d371` | 2026-09-01T18:36:16Z | The stored bytes do not match the handle. A lookup by handle does not find the row. |
  | `ccr_511ff30464a57a06df3c4ee7934f9994` | 2026-09-05T13:56:11Z | The bytes match, but a lookup by handle does not find the row. |
  | `ccr_e9d1f58a7c6f578bddf150f9e561d0d5` | 2026-09-01T18:02:37Z | The bytes match, and the lookup finds the row. SQLite `.recover` drops the row. |
  | `ccr_41cbf5a2c2aafb8e87d313bfb3c8816a` | 2026-09-05T08:17:53Z | The bytes match, and the lookup finds the row. SQLite `.recover` drops the row. |

  A handle is `ccr_` plus the first 32 hex characters of the SHA-256 of the original bytes (`Handle`, `engine/ccr/store.go:218`). So a row whose bytes do not match its handle returns wrong data for that handle.
- Eight processes had the store open at the same time: the proxy, and 7 `caveman-mcp` processes. Five Claude Code sessions and the Codex app server started the `caveman-mcp` processes. Each process held `ccr.db`, `ccr.db-wal`, and `ccr.db-shm` open. The design allows this: the comment on `SQLiteDSN` (`engine/ccr/store_sqlite.go:72`) says that several processes share one store through WAL mode and `busy_timeout`.
- The store also reached its page cap on 2026-10-17. That failure is separate, and #1370 reports it. The cap blocks new writes, so the damage did not grow after that date.
- `~/.caveman/caveman.db` passes `PRAGMA quick_check`.

The probable cause is #1008, which is fixed. In that issue, the maintainer found that `secureSQLiteFile` opened and closed a separate descriptor on `ccr.db`, `-wal`, and `-shm`. On POSIX, the close of any descriptor removes every record lock that the process holds on that file, the SQLite locks included. The proxy then used the store without its locks. In #1008, a short-lived `caveman-mcp` or `caveman-engine` process took itself for the last connection, checkpointed the store, and deleted the live WAL while the proxy continued to write. The fix uses an `O_PATH` descriptor (`engine/ccr/sqlite_file_security_linux.go:47`). It reached `main` on 2026-09-14 (`bd739e15`, #1015). The first binary release after it is `bin-v1.1.7`, published on 2026-09-15.

The four damaged rows in my store are from 2026-09-01 to 2026-09-05, before that fix. When a process writes without its locks, two processes can write pages of the same tree from different snapshots. That can give pages with two parents and out-of-order rowids. #1149 saw the damage on `bin-v1.1.7` and `bin-v2.0.0`, but its store can also be older than the fix. `PRAGMA quick_check` cannot tell when damage occurred, and the damage stays in the file across upgrades. So the #1008 fix probably stopped new damage, but nothing detects or repairs a store that was damaged before it. I cannot prove the cause from the damaged pages alone.

I did not attach the damaged store, because it contains prompt text and tool output. I kept a backup of the damaged files, and I can run queries on it on request.

**Expected**

- The maintainers confirm that the #1008 fix covers this damage, or they find the other cause.
- A store that was damaged before an upgrade gets a check after the upgrade, for example one `PRAGMA quick_check` when a new release first opens the store. Today the damage stays hidden until a write fails.
- `caveman doctor` runs `PRAGMA quick_check` on `ccr.db`, reports a damaged store, and names the repair. This was suggestion 3 in #1149.
- `caveman status` shows that compression is off when the store refuses writes. This was suggestion 2 in #1149.
- No migration or cleanup writes to a store that fails `PRAGMA quick_check`. New writes to a damaged tree can spread the damage.
- Caveman provides a repair that keeps every row whose bytes match its handle. SQLite `.recover` alone does not do this (see the procedure below).
- Retrieval never returns bytes that do not match the handle. A check of the SHA-256 on read turns the wrong row above into an error instead of wrong data.

**Decisions for the maintainers**

The check of the bytes on read needs no decision. These parts need one:

1. The cause. Does the #1008 fix cover this damage, or is another cause possible?
2. Detection. Does `caveman doctor` run `PRAGMA quick_check`, and does `caveman status` show that compression is off? #1103 left both open.
3. A check after an upgrade. Does a new release run one `PRAGMA quick_check` when it first opens the store? The check reads the whole file, so it delays that first open.
4. The repair. Does Caveman provide a repair command? It must stop every CCR client, keep the native hooks from starting a new proxy, and replace the file. The procedure below shows the steps.

**Repair procedure**

This procedure kept every row whose bytes match its handle, on a copy of my damaged store:

1. Stop every process that uses the store: the proxy and every `caveman-mcp`, `cavemem`, `caveman-engine`, and `caveman-browse` process. Then keep the proxy stopped until step 6 is complete. The `caveman <agent>` wrapper and the native hooks (`caveman-proxy native-hook`) start a new proxy when port 8787 does not listen (`ensureLocalProxyForNative`, `packages/cli/src/index.ts:7139`). On my machine, a new proxy started 11 seconds after the stop and opened the store again. Close every agent session, or keep port 8787 busy with a placeholder listener until the swap is complete.
2. Copy `ccr.db`, `ccr.db-wal`, and `ccr.db-shm` to a backup directory.
3. Run `sqlite3 ccr.db .recover | sqlite3 recovered.db`.
4. In `recovered.db`, delete each `recoveries` row whose `original` does not match its handle.
5. Copy each `recoveries` row from `ccr.db` that `.recover` dropped and whose bytes match its handle. Read the old rows with `NOT INDEXED`, because the handle index is damaged.
6. Make sure that `PRAGMA quick_check` on `recovered.db` reports `ok`. Then replace `ccr.db` with `recovered.db`, and remove the old `-wal` and `-shm` files.

Results on the copy:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Damaged copy | 2,348 rows in `recoveries`, 2,347 with bytes that match the handle, 159,338 typed objects |
| After step 3 | 2,346 rows, 2,345 with matching bytes, 159,338 typed objects, `quick_check` reports `ok` |
| After steps 4 and 5 | 2,347 rows, all with matching bytes. A lookup by handle finds all 2,347. `quick_check` reports `ok` |

On 2026-10-23, I applied the procedure to the live store, with a placeholder listener on port 8787. The results were the same as on the copy. After the swap, `PRAGMA quick_check` reported `ok`, and the proxy started again with its old environment. The repaired store had 129,042 pages, near the cap of 131,072 pages. The page cap is a separate problem, and #1370 reports it. I keep a backup of the damaged files.

**Before/after example**

```
Input: ccr.db that 8 Caveman processes share, written since 2026-09-01
Got:   PRAGMA quick_check reports damage in the recoveries table (tree 2) and
       its handle index. One handle returns wrong bytes, and two handles
       cannot be found. caveman doctor reports nothing
Want:  no damage. If damage occurs, caveman doctor reports it, and a repair
       keeps every byte-exact row
```

**Platform**
- [x] Claude Code
- [x] Codex
- [x] Other: Pi. All three agents on my machine use the store through the proxy.

**Version / install method**

`@caveman-ai/cli` 4.0.1 (`binary_release: bin-v4.0.1`), installed with the mise `npm:` backend. Linux x86_64. The driver is `modernc.org/sqlite` v1.59.0. Line numbers refer to checkout `b4531dfc`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Input compression stops when ccr.db reaches its page cap below the 512 MiB payload budget, and nothing removes old typed objects
body:
**What happen**

After the upgrade to `bin-v4.0.1`, the proxy compresses no input. Every compression attempt fails, and the proxy forwards the block uncompressed:

```
{"level":"WARN","msg":"compress failed; forwarding the block uncompressed","error":"ccr put: ccr: storage budget exceeded","path":"segment-query"}
```

The proxy started on `bin-v4.0.1` at 2026-10-17 11:55. The first error came at 11:58. From then until 2026-10-23, `proxy.log` has 432 of these errors, and the `requests` table in `caveman.db` has 0 compressed requests. In the 8 days before the upgrade, the proxy compressed 7 to 37 requests each day.

The store reached this size on earlier versions, before the cap existed (#1023 describes one cause of the growth). So the store was already full when `bin-v4.0.1` started for the first time.

Four gaps in the code combine. All line numbers refer to checkout `b4531dfc`.

1. The page cap and the payload budget measure different things. `configureStorageBudget` (`engine/ccr/store_sqlite.go:387`) sets `PRAGMA max_page_count` to `maxBytes / page_size`. That cap counts every page: rows, indexes, overflow pages, and unused space in pages. The budget checks in `checkRecoveryBudget` (line 542) and `putObject` (line 660) count only payload bytes (`storageBytes`). In my store, the payload was about 384 MiB when writes stopped. The insert then failed with `SQLITE_FULL`, and `isFull` (line 568) maps that error to `ErrBudgetExceeded`. `isFull` also matches a full disk, so the error does not tell the two causes apart.
2. Old duplicate repository maps keep full copies. The dedup for #1023 (`b710bd8d`, `92d606ec`) applies only to new puts. `ensureDataRefColumn` (line 442) adds the `data_ref` column, but it does not convert existing rows. Each `RepositoryMap` row stored before that fix still holds its own copy of the data. In my store, these copies hold 36,964,452 bytes.
3. The failure is silent. `caveman status` still shows `on input wired`. `Summary` (line 890) sets `StorageFull` from payload bytes alone, so it reports false after an insert fails with `SQLITE_FULL`. Only the WARN lines in `proxy.log` show that new recovery writes fail. #1149 had the same symptom with a corrupted `ccr.db`.
4. The page cap belongs to one connection. `max_page_count` is a setting of the connection, not of the file. The store uses one pooled connection (`SetMaxOpenConns(1)`, line 203). If `database/sql` replaces that connection after `ErrBadConn`, the new connection has no cap. Another program that opens `ccr.db` also has no cap.

Nothing in `engine/ccr/store_sqlite.go` deletes rows. A simple rule that deletes `archived` or `cold` objects is not safe:

- Typed objects provide exact recovery. `Retrieve` (`engine/engine.go:240`) resolves `ccr_obj_` handles through the object table.
- `deferredMaskContext` (`proxy/internal/nativeruntime/runtime.go:469`) writes `ccr://<id>` into the context and then sets the object to `cold` (line 492).
- `transitionAfterCompaction` (line 749) sets most object types to `cold`. `archiveSession` (line 771) sets every object of the session to `archived` at `session.end`.
- A resumed session loads its transcript again, and the transcript still contains these references.
- A `RepositoryMap` row can own the data for rows in other sessions through `data_ref`. `resolveObjectData` (line 735) requires that owner to exist.

The dedup lookup (line 643) also reads the whole table for each `RepositoryMap` put. The only index on `typed_objects` is `(session_id, created_at DESC)`. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` reports `SCAN typed_objects` and `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY`. The query also has no tie-breaker for equal `created_at` values.

My store on 2026-10-23:

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| `ccr.db` main file | 526,774,272 bytes = 128,607 pages × 4,096 bytes (about 502.4 MiB) |
| Cap at the default budget | 131,072 pages (512 MiB) |
| `PRAGMA freelist_count` | 0 |
| Payload in `recoveries` | 7,973,947 bytes (2,348 rows, 2026-09-01 to 2026-10-16) |
| Payload in `typed_objects` | 394,774,974 bytes |
| Payload in `typed_objects` with `lifecycle = 'archived'` | 336,998,210 bytes |
| Pages for the `typed_objects` table and its indexes | 471 MiB and 30 MiB |
| Newest row in `recoveries` | 2026-10-16T09:36:12Z |
| `ccr.db-wal` file | 37,949,352 bytes, 6,337 valid frames, 853 commits, last change 2026-10-17 14:00 |
| `PRAGMA page_count` with the WAL present (read-only connection) | 131,072 pages |
| Database size in the header of the last WAL commit frame | 131,072 pages |
| `CAVEMAN_CCR_MAX_BYTES` in the environment of the proxy | not set, so the budget is the default 512 MiB |

The main file is 2,465 pages below the cap, but the WAL holds pages that no checkpoint has copied to the main file yet. With the WAL, the logical database is 131,072 pages, which is exactly the cap: 536,870,912 bytes / 4,096 bytes. So the page cap stopped the writes, not the payload budget and not the disk. The disk has 161 GB free. No write reached the store after 2026-10-17 14:00.

Payload of `typed_objects` on 2026-10-23, from a read-only connection. The table shows the 8 largest of 32 groups:

| `object_type` | `lifecycle` | Rows | Data bytes |
|---|---|---|---|
| FileObservation | archived | 2,257 | 87,389,057 |
| CommandResult | archived | 24,969 | 77,911,280 |
| RepositoryMap | archived | 442 | 62,550,152 |
| TaskDecision | archived | 101,449 | 47,818,088 |
| DiffSnapshot | archived | 2,065 | 45,069,895 |
| FileObservation | hot | 227 | 20,182,264 |
| RepositoryMap | warm | 93 | 17,871,561 |
| TestResult | archived | 4,168 | 6,275,049 |

```sql
SELECT object_type, lifecycle, COUNT(*), SUM(length(data))
FROM typed_objects GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 4 DESC;
```

Duplicate copies of repository maps: 45 groups, 183 duplicate rows, 36,964,452 bytes.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(n) - COUNT(*), SUM(dup_bytes) FROM (
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(length(data)) - MAX(length(data)) AS dup_bytes
  FROM typed_objects
  WHERE object_type = 'RepositoryMap' AND data_ref = ''
  GROUP BY content_hash HAVING COUNT(*) > 1);
```

From 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-16, the store added 229,470,623 bytes of typed object data (by `created_at`), about 14.3 MB for each day. The largest day added 43,421,391 bytes. So the data that consolidation frees is about 2.6 days of growth at the average rate. Consolidation alone does not keep the store below the cap. A lasting fix needs expiry.

A probe measured the consolidation from part A on a page-exact copy of the store. The copy came from the SQLite backup API, with a read-only connection to the live file. The probe applied the cap of 131,072 pages to the copy:

| Measure | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `page_count` and `freelist_count` | 131,072 and 0 | 131,072 and 8,955 |
| Payload (`storageBytes`) | 402,748,921 bytes | 365,784,469 bytes |
| `RepositoryMap` rows whose resolved data matches `content_hash` | 535 of 535 | 535 of 535 |
| Recoveries of 3,396 bytes (the average size) that fit below the cap | 0 | 8,880 (30,156,480 bytes) |

The consolidation committed while the cap applied. It kept every object ID, did not change other object types, and left no reference to a reference. The 8,955 free pages hold about 2 days of new data at the average rate.

On 2026-10-23, I repaired the corruption that the next paragraph describes, and then applied the consolidation to the live store. I stopped every CCR client first, and kept port 8787 busy with a placeholder listener, so that no hook started a new proxy. The script checked every handle inside the transaction before the commit. The results were the same as on the copy: 536 of 536 maps returned data that matched `content_hash`, and 8,955 pages went to the freelist. The store then had 129,223 pages and 8,955 free pages, so 10,804 pages remain below the cap. That is a few days of growth. It does not replace expiry.

My store was also corrupt. `PRAGMA quick_check` reported damage in the `recoveries` table and its handle index, with the same pattern as #1149. #1369 reports the damage and a repair. The corruption did not cause this failure. The page cap refused the writes first. `typed_objects` passes `PRAGMA integrity_check('typed_objects')`, so the measurements above are valid.

**Expected**

- The proxy continues to compress over time. The store removes old typed objects under a contract that keeps every reference that a session can still use, and the store stays below the cap.
- Consolidation frees the space of duplicate repository maps, and every existing handle continues to return byte-exact data.
- The page cap applies to every CCR connection.
- When new recovery writes fail, `caveman status` and `caveman doctor` report it, give the cause (page cap, payload budget, or full disk), and name the fix.
- If no space can be freed safely, the proxy continues to forward the original input, as it does now.
- No change deletes an object that a reference can still need.
- No migration or cleanup writes to a store that fails `PRAGMA quick_check`.

**Proposed fix**

The fix has three parts. Each part has a different risk. Parts A and B can ship first. They unblock the store for a few days and make the failure visible. Part C is necessary for a lasting fix.

Part A: consolidation. This part deletes no object.

1. Stop and upgrade all CCR clients before the first consolidation. The comment on `SQLiteDSN` (line 72) names `caveman-mcp`, `cavemem`, `caveman-engine`, and `caveman-browse`, in addition to the proxy. An older reader can read C with `data_ref = B`, and the migration can then change B into a reference. The older reader then reads empty bytes. A stop of only the writers does not prevent this.
2. Select the owner with `ORDER BY created_at ASC, object_id ASC` in the dedup lookup and in the migration, so that both select the same row.
3. Add the partial index `CREATE INDEX typed_objects_owner ON typed_objects(object_type, content_hash, created_at, object_id) WHERE data_ref = ''`. With this index, the plan for the dedup lookup is `SEARCH typed_objects USING COVERING INDEX typed_objects_owner (object_type=? AND content_hash=?)`.
4. In one transaction, point every existing reference to the retained owner, and convert the other copies of the group to references (`data = x''`, `data_ref = <owner>`). Keep all other fields unchanged. `resolveObjectData` follows only one reference, so a reference to a reference returns empty data.
5. Run the migration before `configureStorageBudget`, so that the cap does not block the cleanup. Decision 2 below asks what starts the migration, because a migration in `openWithBudgetHooks` runs while older clients can still have the store open. On a copy of this store, the consolidation also committed while the cap applied, so this order is a safeguard. Make the migration idempotent, because several processes open the same store. Run `PRAGMA quick_check` first, and do not migrate a store that fails it.
6. In `put` (line 481) and `putObject`, run the lookup, the budget check, and the write in one transaction that starts with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`. The migration uses the same lock. The driver accepts `_txlock=immediate` in the DSN. Give the helper functions (`storageBytes`, `checkRecoveryBudget`, `recoveryUnchanged`, and the owner lookup) an interface with `QueryRow` and `Exec`, so that they run on the `*sql.Tx`. A call to `s.db` inside the transaction deadlocks, because the pool has only one connection.
7. In `getObject` (line 747) and `listSessionObjects` (line 794), run the row read and the resolution in one read transaction (`BeginTx` with `ReadOnly: true`). In WAL mode, each statement outside a transaction reads its own snapshot, so a migration can commit between the two reads. The driver sends a plain `begin` for a read-only transaction, also when `_txlock=immediate` is set. Close the cursor before the resolution, as the comment at line 807 requires.
8. In `resolveObjectData`, compare the SHA-256 of the resolved data with `obj.ContentHash`. If they differ, look up one row with the same `object_type` and `content_hash` and `data_ref = ''`, and check its hash. Return an error if no row passes. Report SQL and storage errors as errors, not as missing content. This fallback is an additional defense for damage that already exists. It does not replace the coordinated upgrade.

Part B: capacity.

1. Add a CCR-only function that builds the DSN with `_pragma=max_page_count(N)`, from the actual page size of the file. The driver runs each `_pragma` value on every new connection. Do not change `SQLiteDSN`, because `mem/store.go:116` also uses it. Do not use `RegisterConnectionHook`, because it applies to every SQLite database in the process.
2. Keep the existing file-identity checks when the store reads the page size and opens the configured connection.
3. Confirm the applied cap. SQLite cannot lower the cap below the current page count.
4. Record when a write fails with `SQLITE_FULL`, and use that state and the page count for `StorageFull`. Report it in `caveman status` and `caveman doctor`, as decision 3 below decides. Describe it as blocked new recovery writes. `recoveryUnchanged` (line 519) can still accept an identical recovery without a write.

Part C: expiry. This part needs its own issue and a decision from the maintainers. In my store, archived objects hold most of the data: `FileObservation`, `CommandResult`, `TaskDecision`, and `DiffSnapshot` together hold 258,188,320 bytes in the archived state. Archived data by age on 2026-10-23, by `created_at`:

| Age | Archived rows | Archived data bytes |
|---|---|---|
| Older than 30 days (before 2026-09-23) | 31,978 | 107,486,655 |
| 14 to 30 days | 70,522 | 134,285,845 |
| 7 to 14 days | 39,683 | 94,115,348 |
| Newer than 7 days | 10 | 203,757 |

No object is newer than 2026-10-16, because the store has refused writes since then. Objects older than 14 days in the `hot`, `warm`, and `cold` states hold 33,998,101 more bytes. Their sessions never reached `session.end`, so `archiveSession` never ran for them. 12 archived owners hold data that rows in other states use through `data_ref`.

At the average growth of 14.3 MB for each day, a 30-day limit keeps about 430 MB of data. That is more than the 402,748,921 bytes of payload at which this store reached the cap. A 14-day limit keeps about 200 MB.

The maintainers must decide these questions:

1. How long must a `ccr://` reference stay recoverable after its session ends? A resumed session needs the references in its transcript. The hooks keep session state for 14 days (`SESSION_TTL_MS`, `src/hooks/caveman-config.js:672`).
2. What does retrieval return for an expired object? Today an unknown handle returns `ErrNotFound`. The comment on `Retrieve` (`engine/engine.go:240`) says that a handle that cannot resolve invites repeated retrieval attempts. A small tombstone row with the object ID and the expiry time lets retrieval report "expired" instead of "unknown".
3. Do objects of sessions that never ended expire? Today they stay `hot`, `warm`, or `cold` forever.
4. Is the limit only an age, or also a size? A size limit removes the oldest archived objects first when the store is near the cap.
5. Can the user configure the limit, for example with an environment variable such as `CAVEMAN_CCR_MAX_BYTES`?
6. Do blob recoveries in `recoveries` also expire? They hold 7,973,947 bytes. The comment on `OpenWithBudget` says that the store never evicts them.

For every option, an owner that a kept row uses through `data_ref` must stay until that row expires, or until its data moves to the kept row.

**Decisions for the maintainers**

Part B, except its display, and the building blocks of part A (steps 2, 3, 6, 7, and 8) need no decision. These parts need one:

1. Expiry: the six questions in part C.
2. The trigger for the consolidation. The consolidation is safe only when no older CCR client runs. A migration when the store opens is not safe during an upgrade, because older `caveman-mcp` processes keep the store open, and the native hooks start a new proxy when port 8787 does not listen. Option A: `caveman update` runs the consolidation after it stops every CCR client. Option B: a command such as `caveman doctor --fix` runs it on request.
3. The display. How do `caveman status` and `caveman doctor` show refused recovery writes and their cause? #1103 left the same question open for #1149.

**Tests**

- Page exhaustion while the payload is below the budget, and payload exhaustion.
- An archived owner whose data a retained map in another session uses.
- Equal `created_at` values in one group.
- An interrupted migration, and a migration that runs again.
- A concurrent recovery put and a concurrent object put during the migration. Rollback, and reuse of an unchanged recovery.
- A reader that reads C, a migration that commits, and the same reader that resolves B. The reader gets the bytes from its snapshot. The same case for `listSessionObjects`.
- A store with a reference to a reference before the reader opens it.
- A replaced connection, and an existing database whose page size is not the default.
- A store with nothing that can be removed safely. The proxy forwards the original input.
- After cleanup and reopen, all old recovery handles return byte-exact data, and a new recovery write succeeds.
- A store that fails `PRAGMA quick_check`. The migration does not run.

The existing test `TestPutObjectReturnsStorageFullInsteadOfMintingHandle` lowers `max_page_count` by hand and checks only that `PutObject` returns an error. With `umask 077` and a private `TMPDIR`, the 7 tests that match `Budget|Full|Dedup|RepositoryMap` in `engine/ccr` pass on `b4531dfc`.

**Workarounds**

Do not raise the budget on a damaged store. New writes to a damaged tree can spread the damage. Run `sqlite3 -readonly ~/.caveman/ccr.db 'PRAGMA quick_check;'` first.

1. If the check reports `ok`, set `CAVEMAN_CCR_MAX_BYTES` to a larger value, and restart every CCR client. `Open` (line 146) reads the variable, and each open applies the new cap. The value also raises the payload budget. The disk must have space for the larger file. This workaround is not tested.
2. If the check reports damage, repair the store before any other step. #1369 gives a repair procedure that keeps every byte-exact handle. On a copy of my store, the repaired file had 129,039 pages, so it was still close to the cap. After the repair, consolidate the duplicate maps or raise the budget.
3. Destructive cleanup is a last resort. Stop every process that uses the store, and make a consistent backup of `ccr.db` and its `-wal` file first. A deletion of typed objects can break `ccr://` references in active sessions and in resumed sessions. A deleted owner can also break `RepositoryMap` rows in other sessions.

**Before/after example**

```
Input: ccr.db at 131,072 pages with its WAL, which is the cap at the default
       budget, 337 MB of archived typed_objects, bin-v4.0.1 proxy,
       Claude Code session through the proxy
Got:   every compress attempt forwards the block uncompressed with
       "ccr put: ccr: storage budget exceeded". caveman status shows "on input wired"
Want:  the store removes old typed objects that no reference can still need,
       and the recovery write succeeds. If no space can be freed safely,
       caveman status shows that new recovery writes fail, and why
```

**Platform**
- [x] Claude Code
- [x] Codex
- [x] Other: Pi. The failure is in the proxy, so all three agents on my machine are affected.

**Version / install method**

`@caveman-ai/cli` 4.0.1 (`binary_release: bin-v4.0.1`), installed with the mise `npm:` backend. Linux x86_64. The only commit on `main` after 2026-10-17 is `fix(release): patch Go CVE-2026-111943`, so `bin-v4.0.2` has the same CCR code. The driver is `modernc.org/sqlite` v1.59.0.

title: caveman stats times out because each requests row stores up to 1,024 cache component digests, which every report read must pass over
body:
**What happen**

`~/.caveman/caveman.db` grows without a limit, and almost all of the growth is one column. Because of this column, `caveman stats` reads about 930 MB for the default 30-day report. When the machine is under load, the read can exceed the 60-second timeout of the CLI:

```
failed to read stats via ~/.caveman/bin/caveman-proxy: spawnSync ~/.caveman/bin/caveman-proxy ETIMEDOUT
```

`stats()` in `@caveman-ai/cli` 4.0.1 runs `caveman-proxy stats --report --write-report` through `execFileSync` with a fixed `timeout: 60_000` (`packages/cli/src/index.ts:18725`). `execFileSync` uses `spawnSync`, which explains the text of the message.

Size of `caveman.db` on 2026-10-23:

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| `caveman.db` file | 1,056,575,488 bytes |
| `requests` table | 994 MiB, 96,439 rows since 2026-09-01 |
| `provider_cache_component_sha256` column | 895 MiB, 90% of the file |
| Indexes on `requests` | none |

All line numbers below refer to checkout `b4531dfc`.

Each value in `provider_cache_component_sha256` is a comma-separated list of SHA-256 hex digests, one digest for each cache component of the request. `sanitizeRequestRecord` accepts up to 1,024 digests (`validDigestList(rec.ProviderCacheComponentSHA256, 1_024)`, `proxy/internal/store/store.go:533`), so one value can have 1,024 × 65 − 1 = 66,559 characters. On 2026-10-22, the proxy wrote 4,264 rows with an average of 20,392 bytes in this column, which is about 314 digests for each row. That day added 86,949,383 bytes to the column. From 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-22, the column grew by 382,367,706 bytes, about 54.6 MB for each day. The smallest day in that period added 12,005,142 bytes.

Most of each list repeats the list from the previous request. In a sample of 395 pairs of consecutive requests in the same session, 74% of the digests in a row were also in the previous row.

No Go or TypeScript file in the repository contains `DELETE FROM requests`, so the table grows without a limit.

On an idle machine, `caveman stats --plain` finished in 13.9 seconds. A direct run of `caveman-proxy stats --report` took 9.9 seconds and read 1,820,112 file system blocks (about 930 MB). So the default 30-day report reads almost the whole file. The timeouts occurred while other work loaded the machine, a VM. With this much disk input for each run, the margin to the 60-second limit is small, and it gets smaller as the file grows.

The report reads most of the file because of the position of the digest column, not only because no index exists:

- SQLite stores the columns of a row in schema order. If a value is larger than about 4 KB, SQLite moves the rest of it to a chain of overflow pages. To read a column after that value, SQLite must read every page in the chain.
- In `CREATE TABLE requests`, `provider_cache_component_sha256` is at line 60. `BuildStatsReport` reads columns that come after it, for example `request_tokens_before` (line 102) and `price_reasoning_per_million` (line 117).
- The `requests` table first appears in `82864c8f` (2026-08-11, Caveman 2.0.0), and that `CREATE TABLE` already contains the digest column. Commit `9f6398ff` (2026-09-08) added the accounting columns with `ALTER TABLE`, and SQLite appends an added column at the end of the row. So every store that 2.0.0 or a later version created has the digest column before the accounting columns.
- In my database, `PRAGMA table_info(requests)` confirms the order. The table has 76 columns. `provider_cache_component_sha256` has `cid` 15. `request_tokens_before` has `cid` 56, and `price_reasoning_per_million` has `cid` 71.
- The report therefore reads the full digest list of each row in the window, but it does not select that column.

A local probe with SQLite 3.54.1 shows the effect. It uses 4,000 rows, a 20,391-byte digest value, and a 64 KiB page cache. `SELECT SUM(tokens)` read these amounts:

| Table layout | File size | Bytes read |
|---|---|---|
| Digest column before `tokens` | 81,965,056 | 81,928,328 |
| Digest column after `tokens` | 81,965,056 | 16,425,103 |
| Digest column before `tokens`, after `UPDATE ... SET digests = NULL` | 81,965,056 | 16,425,111 |
| The same, after `VACUUM` | 98,304 | 98,431 |

The probe counts bytes that read system calls returned. It does not measure physical disk reads or production latency.

The report query also cannot use a plain index on `ts`. `proxy/internal/store/stats.go:214` filters and sorts with `julianday(ts)`, because older rows use different timestamp formats. An in-memory query-plan probe still reported `SCAN requests` and a temporary sort with an index on `ts`. An index on `(julianday(ts), id)` gave an indexed range search with no sort. That index skips only the rows outside the window. Each row inside the window still costs its full digest list. In my database on 2026-10-23, the default 30-day window starts at 2026-09-24. It holds 75,797 of 96,945 rows (78.2%) and 823,239,659 of 944,234,025 digest bytes (87.2%). So the index alone avoids about 13% of the digest bytes for the default report.

The stored list is evidence for export, not the input of the live cache-bust detector. `providerPrefixEvidence` (`proxy/internal/gateway/proxy.go:1097`) builds the list for telemetry. `observeCachedPrefix` (`proxy/internal/gateway/prefix_monitor.go:237`) compares prefixes in memory. `AgentEvidenceForBuild` (`proxy/internal/store/store.go:788`) reads the list for at most 500 rows of one session, build, and plan, ordered by `id`. The `agent-evidence` command of `caveman-proxy` (`proxy/cmd/caveman-proxy/main.go:70` and line 188) prints these rows as `caveman.agent.evidence.v1` JSON. A program outside this repository reads that JSON.

In 26,050 rows (19,216 in the window), the column holds an empty string. No row holds `NULL`. An empty string means that the proxy recorded no list, or that `sanitizeRequestRecord` refused the list. In both cases, the row has no usable component list.

The measurements in this section come from a read-only connection on 2026-10-23. The scan of the whole table took 27 seconds.

**Expected**

- The 30-day report reads only the small accounting part of each row, and finishes in a few seconds on this database.
- The digest lists are stored apart from the accounting rows, and they expire by age. Request counts, token totals, recorded prices, and lifetime reports stay unchanged.
- The exported evidence states for each request if its component list is available. A consumer must not take an unavailable list as evidence of an unchanged cache prefix.
- If the proxy does not finish in time, the CLI error names the size of `caveman.db` and says that the report timed out. After the index on `(julianday(ts), id)` exists, the error can also suggest a smaller `--days` value. Without that index, `--days` still scans the whole table.

**Proposed fix**

1. Storage:
   - Move the digest lists to a separate table, for example `request_cache_components(request_id, digests)`, with at most one row for each `requests.id`.
   - Write each request row and its evidence row in one transaction, in all three write paths: `Record` (line 413), the normal `recordBatch` transaction (line 445), and the fallback in `RecordBatch` (line 430) that calls `Record`.
2. Migration of existing databases:
   - Stop every running proxy process before the new binary clears legacy values. An older proxy reads only the legacy column, and it does not check a schema version. Decision 1 below names another option.
   - Copy and clear in batches by `id`. Each batch is one transaction:

     ```sql
     INSERT INTO request_cache_components (request_id, digests)
       SELECT id, provider_cache_component_sha256 FROM requests
       WHERE id BETWEEN ? AND ? AND provider_cache_component_sha256 <> ''
     ON CONFLICT(request_id) DO NOTHING;
     UPDATE requests SET provider_cache_component_sha256 = NULL
       WHERE id BETWEEN ? AND ?
         AND (provider_cache_component_sha256 = ''
              OR id IN (SELECT request_id FROM request_cache_components));
     ```

   - The copy skips `NULL` and empty values. `DO NOTHING` prevents a retry from replacing copied evidence. The lowest `id` with a non-null legacy value is the next start point, so the migration needs no progress row.
   - A `NULL` value takes no space in the row, and SQLite frees its overflow pages. Do not use `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN`. It rewrites the whole table in one transaction.
3. Reader:
   - `AgentEvidenceForBuild` reads `COALESCE(c.digests, r.provider_cache_component_sha256)` through a `LEFT JOIN` on `request_id`. The join adds at most one row for each request, so the limit of 500 rows and the order stay the same.
   - Scan the value as nullable. The current scan at line 825 reads into a Go string, which fails on `NULL`.
   - Keep the existing string field. Add `provider_cache_components_available` to every request in the output, also when its value is false. Calculate it as `validDigestList(value, 1_024)`, with `NULL` converted to `""` first. `sanitizeRequestRecord` stores `""` for a refused list, so SQL nullability alone cannot carry the availability.
   - Document in `caveman.agent.evidence.v1` that an absent flag in older output does not mean that the evidence is available.
4. Retention: expire evidence by age in one transaction that deletes the evidence rows and sets the legacy column to `NULL` for the same `id` values. Otherwise the `COALESCE` fallback returns expired evidence again. Define a bounded cleanup schedule and the treatment of active sessions. Accounting rows stay unchanged.
5. Report speed: add an index on `(julianday(ts), id)` as a separate improvement for narrow windows.
6. File size: the steps above free pages for reuse, but the file does not get smaller. Only `VACUUM` makes the file and the reads of the remaining rows small. `VACUUM` needs free disk space for a full copy of the database, and it blocks writers while it runs. Run it only as planned maintenance, not during a report or when the store opens.

**Decisions for the maintainers**

The index on `(julianday(ts), id)` (step 5) and a clearer timeout error need no decision. The move of the evidence (steps 1 to 4 and 6) needs these decisions:

1. The upgrade path. An older proxy reads only the legacy column. Option A: the upgrade stops every running proxy before the new binary clears legacy values. Option B: one release writes the list to both places and clears nothing, and a later release stops the legacy writes and clears the column. Option B keeps the disk growth for one more release.
2. Retention. How many days of evidence does the proxy keep, and how does it treat active sessions? The accounting rows stay in all cases.
3. `VACUUM`. Does Caveman run `VACUUM` to make the file smaller, and when? It needs free disk space for a full copy of the database, and it blocks writers while it runs.
4. The evidence consumer. The reader of `caveman.agent.evidence.v1` is outside this repository. The maintainers decide the contract for `provider_cache_components_available`, and they add the contract test where that reader lives.

**Tests**

- Refused lists, migrated empty strings, expired evidence, valid evidence, and output without the new flag.
- Migration restart, the `RecordBatch` fallback, and concurrent inserts during the migration.
- Exact round trips of the ordered digest list after migration and restart.
- A contract test with the consumer outside this repository.
- A report benchmark with large rows.
- Request counts, token totals, recorded prices, and lifetime reports before and after the migration.
- The existing mixed-timestamp and UTC-window tests of the report.

**Before/after example**

```
Input: caveman.db at 1,056,575,488 bytes, 96,439 requests rows, VM under load,
       caveman stats
Got:   failed to read stats via ~/.caveman/bin/caveman-proxy: spawnSync ... ETIMEDOUT
Want:  the 30-day report in a few seconds. Each requests row holds only accounting
       data, and old digest lists expire
```

**Platform**
- [x] Claude Code
- [x] Codex
- [x] Other: Pi. The proxy writes the rows for all agents.

**Version / install method**

`@caveman-ai/cli` 4.0.1 (`binary_release: bin-v4.0.1`), installed with the mise `npm:` backend. Linux x86_64.

title: perf(store): index requests by julianday(ts) for stats windows
body:
## Summary

`BuildStatsReport` filters and sorts the `requests` table with `julianday(ts)`. The table had no index, so every report scanned all rows and sorted them in a temporary B-tree. This PR adds the expression index `idx_requests_julianday_ts ON requests(julianday(ts), id)`. The query text does not change. It moves into three constants, and a test checks the query plan against those constants.

Refs #1371. This PR uses "Refs", not "Fixes", because it resolves only part of #1371. A closing keyword closes the issue when this PR merges. This PR does not fix the timeout in #1371 for the default 30-day report. The measurements below show why.

## Changes

- `proxy/internal/store/store.go`: adds the index at the end of the schema. `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` runs on every open, so existing databases get the index on their first open.
- `proxy/internal/store/stats.go`: the WHERE and ORDER BY text of the report query moves into `statsWhereTo`, `statsWhereFrom`, and `statsOrderBy`. The SQL is the same as before.
- `proxy/internal/store/stats_test.go`:
  - `TestStatsQueryUsesJulianDayIndex` runs `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on the production constants. The plan must use the index and must not contain `SCAN requests` or `USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY`.
  - `TestOpenAddsJulianDayIndexToExistingDatabase` opens a database that has no index and checks that the store adds it.

## Measurements

I copied my own `caveman.db` (1,067,204,608 bytes, 97,181 rows) and ran `caveman-proxy stats --report` from 4.0.1 and from this branch. I counted the bytes that `read` and `pread64` returned, with `strace`. The machine was under load, so wall time was not stable. Bytes read do not depend on load.

| Window | Without the index | With the index |
|---|---|---|
| `--days 30` (the default) | 1,084 MB | 1,218 MB |
| `--days 7` | 567 MB | 457 MB |
| `--days 1` | 213 MB | 17.8 MB |

- The 1-day report reads 92% less, and the 7-day report reads 19% less.
- The 30-day report reads 12% more. Almost every row is inside the window, and each row stores a long `provider_cache_component_sha256` value before the columns that the report reads. #1371 describes this cost. Only a move of that column out of the row removes it.
- The reports are identical with and without the index, except for `window.to`, which is the time of the run.
- The first open of this database with the new code built the index. That open and a 1-day report took 0.79 s to 1.1 s. `sqlite3` alone builds the index in 0.22 s. The build holds the write lock for that time, once.

## Tests

- `go test ./proxy/internal/store/ -count=1` with `umask 022` and a private `TMPDIR`: pass.
- `go vet ./proxy/internal/store/`: no findings. `gofmt -l proxy/internal/store/`: no files.
- The store tests reject a group-writable temporary directory. Run them with `umask 022` and a private `TMPDIR`.

title: fix(ccr): refuse recovery bytes that do not match the handle
body:
## Summary

A damaged `ccr.db` row returned wrong bytes as a good recovery. #1369 shows one: the bytes of `ccr_c0183cc37945b915e0a32d94ae92d371` do not match the handle. This PR checks the bytes on every read that returns them to a caller:

- A blob recovery must match its handle: `ccr_` plus the first 32 hex characters of the SHA-256 of the bytes.
- A typed object must match its `content_hash`. This check also covers a `RepositoryMap` that stores a `data_ref` to another row.

A mismatch returns the new error `ccr.ErrCorruptRecovery`. `Engine.Retrieve` falls through from the blob table to the object table only on `ErrNotFound`, so a damaged row does not turn into "not found". The MCP retrieve tool reports `cave_corrupt_recovery` instead of `cave_unknown_handle`. Then the agent does not retry a handle that cannot resolve.

Refs #1369. This PR uses "Refs", not "Fixes", because it resolves only part of #1369. A closing keyword closes the issue when this PR merges. These parts of #1369 stay open, and they need the decisions that the issue lists: the cause of the damage, the repair of existing damage, a check after an upgrade, and output in `caveman doctor` and `caveman status`.

## Changes

- `engine/ccr/store.go`: adds `ErrCorruptRecovery` and `verifyObjectData`.
- `engine/ccr/store_sqlite.go`: `get` checks the handle. `resolveObjectData` checks the content hash for inline data and for `data_ref` data. `getObject`, `listSessionObjects`, and `findTaskDecision` use `resolveObjectData`, so they all check.
- `mcp/engine_tools.go`: `retrieveError` maps `ErrCorruptRecovery` to `cave_corrupt_recovery`, for the normal call and for `verify_only`.
- Tests: `engine/ccr/store_corrupt_test.go` (new), `engine/engine_sqlite_test.go` (new, `//go:build !js`, because the SQLite driver does not build for `js/wasm`), `mcp/engine_tools_retrieve_test.go`.

`getMetadata` returns only the metadata column, so it does not check. Summary and statistics queries read only lengths. `caveman-engine retrieve` and `caveman-proxy native-why` print the error and exit non-zero, with no code change. `browse/` is not changed.

## Behavior change for reviewers

`listSessionObjects` now fails when one object of the session is damaged. The native runtime calls it at compaction, at session end, and for receipts. Four of these callers read `Data`. With this PR, a damaged object stops those calls with an error. Before this PR, they used the wrong bytes. The SHA-256 check also adds one hash for each listed object. A `RepositoryMap` can be several MB.

## Tests

- `go test ./engine/... ./mcp/... ./proxy/internal/nativeruntime/... -count=1` with `umask 022` and a private `TMPDIR`: pass. The store tests reject a group-writable temporary directory, so a default `umask 002` makes them fail.
- `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go test -c` for `./engine`, `./engine/ccr`, and `./mcp`: compiles.
- New tests: a changed blob, a changed typed object (through `getObject`, `listSessionObjects`, and `get` with an object ID), a changed `data_ref` owner, the `Engine.Retrieve` fall-through, and the MCP error code.
- `go vet ./engine/... ./mcp/...`: no findings. `gofmt -l engine mcp`: no files.

title: fix(ccr): apply the page cap on every store connection
body:
## Summary

This PR fixes the capacity reporting of #1370, part B.

1. The page cap applies to one connection only. `configureStorageBudget` sets `PRAGMA max_page_count` once. SQLite keeps that setting per connection and does not store it in the file. If `database/sql` replaces the single pooled connection, the new connection has no cap.
2. A full store looked healthy. The file reached its page cap (131,072 pages) at about 384 MiB of payload, because the cap counts index pages, overflow pages, and unused space. Every write failed with `SQLITE_FULL`, but `Summary` compared payload bytes only and reported `StorageFull = false`.
3. A write that the payload budget refused also left `StorageFull = false` while the retained bytes stayed below the budget. That gap exists on `main` too.

Refs #1370. This PR uses "Refs", not "Fixes", because it resolves only part of #1370. A closing keyword closes the issue when this PR merges. This PR changes no CLI text. These parts of #1370 stay open, and they need the decisions that the issue lists: the trigger for the consolidation, expiry, and the display in `caveman status` and `caveman doctor`.

## Changes

- `engine/ccr/store_sqlite.go`:
  - The store opens its database through `sql.OpenDB` with a private `sqlite.Driver`. A connection hook on that driver sets the applied page cap on every new connection. `SQLiteDSN` does not change, so the `mem` store and other SQLite databases in the process get no cap. The package-level `sqlite.RegisterConnectionHook` is not used, because it applies to every database in the process.
  - `configureStorageBudget` still reads the real page size. It stores the requested cap for the hook, so each new connection requests the same limit. When a database is already larger than the requested cap, SQLite applies its current page count instead. Capacity calculations therefore read the cap that the connection applies (`PRAGMA max_page_count`).
  - Pages on the SQLite freelist count as room below the cap. Deleted or consolidated data therefore frees capacity without `VACUUM`.
  - A refused write records its cause at the time of the refusal. The payload check gives `payload_budget`. For `SQLITE_FULL`, `recordRefusal` compares the write plus 64 pages for b-tree and index pages with the room below the cap, freelist included. Less room gives `page_cap`, otherwise `disk_full`. The next write that adds or changes data clears the recorded cause. A repeated object that adds no row does not clear it, because it does not show that room exists.
  - `Summary` reports `StorageFull` for a full payload budget, for no free page below the cap, or for a recorded refusal.
- `engine/ccr/store.go`: adds the field `StorageFullReason` (`storage_full_reason`, omitted when empty) with the values `payload_budget`, `page_cap`, and `disk_full`.
- `engine/ccr/store_test.go`: `TestPersistentStoreBudgetRefusesNewRecoveryAndPreservesExisting` expected `StorageFull == false` after a payload refusal. It now expects `true` with the reason `payload_budget`, because that was the gap in point 3.
- `engine/ccr/store_reopen_race_test.go`: uses the new test-only `testConnectionHook`, because the package-level hook does not reach the private driver.

`StorageFull` has no consumer outside `engine/ccr` today.

## Tests

New tests in `engine/ccr/store_full_test.go` and `mem/page_cap_test.go`:

- A replaced connection keeps the cap.
- A database with 8,192-byte pages gets a cap of `maxBytes / 8192`.
- Page exhaustion below the payload budget reports `page_cap`. A later successful write clears the state.
- A large write that fails while some pages are still free reports `page_cap`, not `disk_full`.
- A refused write below the cap reports `disk_full`.
- Payload exhaustion reports `payload_budget`. A 50 KiB write refused under a 64 KiB budget with 20 KiB retained also reports `payload_budget`, and a later small write clears it.
- Free pages count as room: a store at the cap deletes rows without `VACUUM`, stores new content, and reports no full store while `page_count` still equals the cap.
- Consolidation frees room: duplicate `RepositoryMap` copies that use overflow pages fill a store to the cap, the consolidation SQL from #1370 moves pages to the freelist, and a new write succeeds with no full store reported.
- A database that is already larger than the requested cap reopens with the applied cap, accepts a new write into free pages, and reports no full store.
- A repeated object keeps a recorded refusal. A new object clears it.
- The `mem` database keeps the SQLite default page limit.

Results:

- `go test ./engine/... ./mem/... ./mcp/... -count=1` with `umask 022` and a private `TMPDIR`: pass. The store tests reject a group-writable temporary directory, so a default `umask 002` makes them fail.
- The two new tests for the applied cap and the repeated object fail on the code before these fixes.
- `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go test -c` for `./engine`, `./engine/ccr`, and `./mcp`: compiles.
- `go vet ./engine/... ./mem/...`: no findings. `gofmt -l engine mem`: no files. `git diff --check`: clean.

title: fix(ccr): serialize writes and pin read snapshots for dedup maps
body:
## Summary

This PR adds the building blocks of #1370, part A. A later consolidation of the duplicate `RepositoryMap` copies needs them, and they also fix races that exist today. This PR does not consolidate anything. The maintainers decide when a consolidation runs, because an older CCR client must not run at the same time.

This PR depends on #1374 (page cap). The hash check of #1373 is already in `main` through #1315. The branch has the three commits of #1374 first, with the same changes. Please review only the top commit, `fix(ccr): serialize writes and pin read snapshots for dedup maps`. I will rebase it after #1374 merges. When the payload check refuses a write inside the new write transaction, the store records the refusal from the page-cap PR without a second database call. `putObject` clears a recorded refusal only after the commit, and only when the insert added a row.

Refs #1370. This PR uses "Refs", not "Fixes", because it resolves only part of #1370. A closing keyword closes the issue when this PR merges.

## Changes

All code changes are in `engine/ccr/store_sqlite.go`.

1. The owner lookup for a deduplicated map orders by `created_at ASC, object_id ASC`. Before, equal `created_at` values gave a random owner.
2. A partial index `typed_objects_owner ON typed_objects(object_type, content_hash, created_at, object_id) WHERE data_ref = ''` supports the lookup. Before, every `RepositoryMap` put scanned the whole table and sorted the result. The plan is now `SEARCH typed_objects USING COVERING INDEX typed_objects_owner`. The store creates the index on open, after `ensureDataRefColumn`.
3. `put` and `putObject` run the lookup, the budget check, and the insert in one transaction that starts with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`. The CCR connection string gets `_txlock=immediate`. `SQLiteDSN` does not change, so the `mem` store is not affected. The helper functions take a small `querier` interface, so that they run on the transaction. A call to `s.db` inside the transaction deadlocks on the single pooled connection, so no helper uses it there. Before this change, two processes were able to pass the budget check at the same time, and a process was able to insert a reference to an owner that another process had just changed.
4. `getObject`, `listSessionObjects`, and `findTaskDecision` read the row and resolve `data_ref` in one read-only transaction. In WAL mode, each statement outside a transaction reads its own snapshot, so another process was able to commit between the two reads.
5. When the resolved bytes do not match the content hash, `resolveObjectData` tries up to four full copies with the same type and content hash, and checks each one. It returns `ErrCorruptRecovery` only if none matches. Storage errors stay storage errors.

## Behavior change for reviewers

A `data_ref` whose owner row is missing returned a wrapped `sql.ErrNoRows` before. It now goes through the fallback, and it returns `ErrCorruptRecovery` when no full copy matches.

## One-time cost

On a copy of my own store (529 MB, 160,013 typed objects), the first open with this code built the index in 1.92 s. A second open took 0.6 ms. `sqlite3` builds the same index in 2.6 s. The build holds the write lock once.

## Tests

New tests in `engine/ccr/store_consolidation_blocks_test.go`:

- The owner tie-break picks the smallest `object_id`.
- The lookup uses the index on a new store, on a store without the index, and on an old store without `data_ref`.
- A reference to a reference resolves through the fallback, for `getObject` and `listSessionObjects`. With no valid copy left, the read returns `ErrCorruptRecovery`. A storage error is not reported as `ErrCorruptRecovery`.
- Snapshot reads: a second store commits a change between the row read and the resolution, and the reader still returns the bytes from its snapshot. With the read transaction removed from `getObject`, this test fails. I checked that.
- Two stores on the same file put the same maps concurrently. No row points to a reference, each content has one full copy, and all bytes are exact.
- Two stores on the same file near the payload budget put concurrently. The retained payload does not exceed the budget.

Results with `umask 022` and a private `TMPDIR`:

- `go test ./engine/... ./mem/... ./mcp/... ./proxy/internal/nativeruntime/... -count=1`: pass. The store tests reject a group-writable temporary directory, so a default `umask 002` makes them fail.
- `go test -race ./engine/ccr/ -count=1`: pass, no data race.
- `GOOS=js GOARCH=wasm go test -c` for `./engine`, `./engine/ccr`, and `./mcp`: compiles.
- `go vet ./engine/... ./mem/... ./mcp/...`: no findings. `gofmt -l`: no files. `git diff --check`: clean.

title: fix(pi): send per-prompt context as a message, keep the system prompt stable
body:
Fixes #1364.

## Problem

In `before_agent_start`, the pi extension appended the per-prompt context (the `UserPromptSubmit` answer and the queued `PreToolUse` context) to the system prompt of the run. That text changes at every prompt. Today the runtime answers, for example, `Caveman repository evidence: warming asynchronously; no path claims injected.`

A provider caches the prompt in order: tools, then the system prompt, then the messages. When the system prompt changes, the cache is re-written from the system prompt onward, so the whole conversation is written again. It happens twice per prompt: once when the context arrives, and once when the next prompt drops it.

## Change

- Core context still rides the system prompt, byte-stable, as before.
- Dynamic context is returned as `message: { customType: "caveman-context", content, display: false }` from `before_agent_start`. pi adds that message to the run, at the tail of the transcript, so the cached prefix stays the same. pi's extension docs prefer this over replacing the system prompt ("Returning `systemPrompt` ... replaces the whole prompt for that run").
- CHANGELOG: an Unreleased entry.

## Tests

- New integration test: "open gate: dynamic context rides a message and the system prompt stays byte-stable". It runs two prompts against the stub provider. It asserts that Core is in the system prompt, that the system prompt of the second request is byte-identical to the first, and that `DYNAMIC_MARKER_ABC` is in a message and not in the system prompt.
- Without the `src/index.ts` change, the test fails on `dynamic context must not enter the system prompt`. With it, the test passes.
- `npm test` in `packages/pi-extension`: 145 pass, 0 fail (144 before, plus the new test). `tsc --noEmit`: clean.

## Measured

pi 1.4.0, Claude Haiku 4.5 through a gateway, `bin-v4.0.2` runtime and proxy in a private `CAVEMAN_HOME`, the same 8 prompts per arm on the same working tree:

| Arm | Cache-write tokens | Cost |
|---|---:|---:|
| No Caveman extension, direct | 38,685 | $0.107 |
| Caveman extension as released (`@caveman-ai/cli` 4.0.1 bundle), through the proxy | 131,658 | $0.234 |
| Caveman extension with this PR, through the proxy | 35,975 | $0.112 |

With the released extension, the same prompts cost 2.2 times as much, and nearly all of the difference is cache writes. With this PR, the cost is back at the level of the run without the extension.

Assisted-by: an AI coding agent (pi). I reviewed and ran every change.

title: fix(pi): state that caveman_retrieve with a query returns only an excerpt
body:
Fixes #1368

The recovery footer on a masked tool output claims "one call returns the entire original". That holds only for a call with `recovery_handle` alone. A call with `query` returns a filtered excerpt with `[caveman: non-adjacent]` markers, and no text reports how much was omitted. Three texts disagreed: the footer, the pi `query` description, and the runtime behavior. Before the change, 0 of the 2 agent-facing texts (footer, pi `query` description) said that `query` narrows the result.

Root cause: the footer is built once, at `proxy/internal/nativeruntime/runtime.go:1279`, and every host reuses it. The pi `query` description at `packages/pi-extension/src/index.ts:168` had no statement about excerpts.

Fix: the footer now says to pass only `recovery_handle` for the full bytes and that adding a query returns only a matching excerpt. The string grew by 53 bytes. The pi `query` description now says to omit it for the entire original and that with it only an excerpt returns, with gaps marked. Recovery bytes are unchanged. `query` stays in the schema.

Evidence:
- Before: the two new asserts in `TestMaskedToolOutputTellsTheAgentHowToRecoverIt` failed (`FAIL github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/proxy/internal/nativeruntime`).
- `go test ./proxy/internal/nativeruntime -run TestMaskedToolOutputTellsTheAgentHowToRecoverIt -v`: `--- PASS`.
- `go build ./...`: exit 0. `go vet ./proxy/...`: exit 0. `gofmt -l proxy`: 0 files.
- `go test ./proxy/...`: 27 packages `ok`, 0 failed.
- `npm test` in `packages/pi-extension`: `tests 116`, `pass 116`, `fail 0`.

Boundaries:
- Only the footer string and the pi `query` description changed. `mcp/engine_tools.go` and the SDK descriptions already state that omitting `query` returns the original.
- `go test ./...` outside `proxy/` was not run. Only macOS arm64 was tested.
- The excerpt size header from the issue (option b, for example `excerpt: 14 of 61 lines`) is not included. It requires a change in `engine/retrieve_query.go`, a different layer. I chose the text change because it fits in 2 lines of production code and removes the contradiction now.

Question: do you want the size header as a separate PR against `engine/retrieve_query.go`? I can open it after this one lands, or drop it.

title: fix(pi): leave tool outputs under 4096 bytes unmasked
body:
Fixes #1365

`afterTool` replaced a 1.8 KB command result with a 296-byte stub that held a `ccr://` handle and no content. The mask threshold was `len(stub)+384`, which is 680 bytes for that stub. Redeeming the handle costs one extra model request. In the reporter's session that request read 27k-31k cached tokens, three times in eight prompts.

Root cause: `proxy/internal/nativeruntime/runtime.go:1283` masked any output above that threshold. The condition applies to every host and every output type.

Fix: I added `minMaskBytes = 4096` and required `len(output) >= minMaskBytes` before masking. Outputs below it leave `afterTool` byte-identical. They are still stored, so the handle stays valid. I changed a "~448 bytes" comment in the pi extension to "~4 KB".

Threshold: 4096 equals the floor the Hermes shrink hook uses (`CAVE_HERMES_SHRINK_MIN_BYTES`). Outputs of 680-4095 bytes now enter context in full, at most 3,800 bytes more than the stub. Question for maintainers: should the floor derive from the cost of a retrieve round trip instead of a constant? I chose the constant because it needs one condition and applies to all output types.

Alternatives not taken:
- Inline excerpt (head, tail, error lines): changes the replacement text, which #1368 also touches. I can send it as a separate PR.
- Round-trip cost in the decision: needs a per-model token model that the runtime does not have.
- Env override: the Go runtime has no existing pattern for one.

Evidence, run from `proxy/` unless noted:
- Before the fix: `go test ./internal/nativeruntime -run TestShortToolOutputIsNotMasked` printed `a ~1800-byte output must pass through unchanged` and `a ~3896-byte output must pass through unchanged`, then `FAIL github.com/JuliusBrussee/caveman/proxy/internal/nativeruntime 0.977s`.
- With the floor applied and the old fixtures, three existing tests failed: `TestMaskedToolOutputTellsTheAgentHowToRecoverIt` (2640-byte output), `TestSessionEndWritesHonestReceiptOutsideModelContext` and `TestDeferredMaskIsInjectedOnceForHostsWithoutDirectOutputRewrite`. I enlarged their fixtures to 5280, 4800 and 4500 bytes. The assertions are unchanged.
- After: `go test ./internal/nativeruntime -run TestShortToolOutputIsNotMasked -v` printed `--- PASS: TestShortToolOutputIsNotMasked (0.04s)`. The test asserts that outputs of at least 1800 and 3896 bytes stay unmasked and keep a recovery ref, and that an output of at least 4296 bytes is still masked.
- From the repo root: `gofmt -l proxy/internal/nativeruntime` printed nothing. `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` exited 0. `go test ./...` exited 0 with 61 `ok` packages, 4 `no test files` and 0 failures.

Not covered: `pnpm test` in `packages/pi-extension` did not run, because the only change there is a comment. The issue reports 800-byte and 1,600-byte outputs passing, which the 680-byte threshold does not predict. I did not find why. I tested on darwin/arm64 only.

title: fix(middleware-python): exclude broken litellm
body:
Fixes #1326.

## Summary

Exclude LiteLLM **1.106.0, 1.106.1, 1.106.2, and 1.107.0** from fresh `caveman-middleware[litellm]` installations while retaining upstream's **`filelock>=4.2.1` security floor**.

- Preserve the package-only exclusions without changing `COMPATIBILITY` or the adapter implementation.
- Set `constraints/latest.txt` to tested **LiteLLM 1.103.10**, preserving upstream's `anthropic==2.1.0` constraint.
- Update the README to describe the exclusions, security floor, and tested LiteLLM/filelock combination.
- Check the installed wheel's LiteLLM requirement by name, rather than assuming the extra contains no other requirements. Keep the existing filelock security tests and assert that the extra does not add MCP.

Current `main` was merged into the existing PR branch in `25ffbb2f`; published history was not rewritten. Relative to `main`, this PR still changes only four middleware files. The original commit and the refresh both carry DCO sign-offs.

## Why

LiteLLM 1.106.0–1.106.2 load the optional MCP gateway on ordinary calls with `tools`, causing a base LiteLLM installation without MCP to fail before a provider request is sent. The upstream report is [BerriAI/litellm#46045](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/46045).

Separately, LiteLLM's [October 21 security notice](https://docs.litellm.ai/blog/security-incident-oct-21-2026) identifies **1.107.0** as compromised. Excluding it prevents its selection by this extra; it does not remediate an already compromised environment. Affected users should follow the vendor's notice. That release was not downloaded or executed during validation.

The exclusions name only the known-bad releases, so later patches remain eligible for the nightly canary if their dependencies can satisfy the extra. The runtime compatibility gate remains unchanged: it checks adapter compatibility, not package security.

## Reconciliation with #1382

The original version of this PR proposed `litellm==1.105.3`. Since then, merged #1382 added `filelock>=4.2.1` to the extra. LiteLLM 1.105.3 requires `filelock<4.0`, making those requirements mutually unsatisfiable; a resolver check reproduced `ResolutionImpossible`.

The refresh retains the security floor rather than weakening it. An unconstrained resolver selected **LiteLLM 1.103.10 + filelock 4.2.4**, with no MCP package. The installed-wheel tests below verify that combination, and the latest constraint and README now match it. More recent LiteLLM releases that require `filelock<4` remain incompatible with the extra until upstream permits patched filelock versions.

Draft #1396 also contains the exclusions. This PR remains focused on the standalone packaging change recommended in the maintainer's October 27 review comment; the overlap can be reconciled at merge time.

## Validation

Tests used built wheels installed into fresh environments, ran from outside the checkout, and required the LiteLLM adapter through `CAVEMAN_REQUIRED_ADAPTERS=litellm`. They used local fixtures and dummy credentials, with no live-provider calls. The final wheel was rebuilt after the documentation update and retested in all three environments.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Updated metadata/security tests against the current-main wheel | **4 failed, 15 passed**: precisely the four missing LiteLLM exclusions |
| Metadata/security tests against the updated wheel | **19 passed** |
| Python 3.12.3, unconstrained extra, LiteLLM 1.103.10 | **190 passed, 244 skipped, 0 failed** |
| Python 3.14.7, latest constraints, LiteLLM 1.103.10 | **190 passed, 244 skipped, 0 failed** |
| Python 3.12.3, floor constraints, LiteLLM 1.95.0 | **190 passed, 244 skipped, 0 failed** |
| `pip check` in all three installed-wheel environments | Passed |
| `python3 tests/verify_repo.py` on the final tree | Passed |
| `git diff --check` | Passed |

All three runtime environments installed **filelock 4.2.4**, had no MCP package, and imported `caveman_middleware` from `site-packages`. The 244 skips in each environment are for unavailable optional adapters. The two LiteLLM 1.103.10 environments emitted one Pydantic `ReadOnly` warning each; the floor environment emitted none.

Not run locally: Python 3.11 and 3.13 interpreter lanes, the other isolated adapter-family environments, full Go/engine tests, macOS/Windows execution, or live-provider calls. These results do not claim that the full hosted CI matrix is green; current CI results are in the PR's Checks tab.

title: fix(cli): retry locked wedge output renames
body:
Windows engine CI failed in the concurrent wedge generator test when `renameSync` returned EPERM before another writer had published matching bytes. The generator deleted its complete temporary file and exited immediately.

Retry EPERM, EBUSY and EACCES up to six attempts with bounded backoff, retaining the complete temporary file until publication succeeds or retries finish. Unrelated errors still fail immediately; permanent locks preserve the previous output and remove the temporary file.

The regression harness converts its preload path to a file URL so Windows drive paths load correctly. Its fixture directory includes `#` to exercise URL escaping on every platform, and missing preload execution reports child stderr.

Validation:
- Real-process filesystem fault regressions failed before the generator fix; seven focused generator tests passed on the original fix with Node 22.22.2.
- All five lock tests failed with the URL-sensitive fixture path before path conversion and passed after it. Retry limits, persistent-lock preservation, unrelated-error handling and temporary-file cleanup assertions remain intact.
- Corrected head: seven focused tests passed. Full root suite: 645 passed, two Windows-only skips with Node 22.22.2 and Python 3.14.2. An initial run using system Python 3.9.6 timed out in PTY fixtures at 180 seconds; the unchanged suite passed with installed Python 3.14.2. Native Windows engine CI must pass before merge.
- CLI `npm run build` passed on the original generator correction with reused installed dependencies; subsequent changes affect only its regression test.
- Original Node 26 broad run failed an unrelated existing stable-PATH-node hook test; that test and the full suite passed on Node 22.

Only generator source and its regression tests changed. Existing generated release-pin drift is outside this correction. No release or deployment performed.
